name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana’s 2nd bobcat hunting season hits statewide quota in 2 weeks
description: Hoosier hunters and trappers hit the 400-b0bcat quota on Saturday — killing an average of 28 per day since the season opened Nov. 8. That was faster than the year before, which had a 250-bobcat limit and was exhausted in four weeks. The Indiana Department of Natural Resources this year expanded the bobcat season to […]
text:
Indiana hunters and trappers already killed 400 bobcats, ending the season. (Photo courtesy of Indiana Department of Natural Resources)Hoosier hunters and trappers hit the 400-b0bcat quota on Saturday — killing an average of 28 per day since the season opened Nov. 8.
That was faster than the year before, which had a 250-bobcat limit and was exhausted in four weeks.
The Indiana Department of Natural Resources this year expanded the bobcat season to include hunting as well as trapping in 40 counties. The quota also increased by 40%.
“Licensed harvesters had a successful bobcat season,” Geriann Albers, Indiana DNR’s furbearer and gamebird program leader, said in a Monday announcement. “DNR will review what we’ve learned from this and past seasons as we move forward with the regulated harvest and management of bobcats in the state.”
The new season permitted methods from just traps to include hunting with a bow and arrow, crossbow, shotgun, handgun, rifle, muzzleloading long gun or handgun, and certain air guns. Trappers may use a cage trap, permitted foothold traps or a snare trap with a relaxing snare lock to trap a bobcat, same as last season.
Samantha Chapman, Indiana state director for Humane World for Animals, said hunters have 24 hours to report their kills so the total killed might rise from the 402 known on Saturday.
“Indiana’s small, shy bobcats never stood a chance against the devices permitted to bait, lure and kill them. Recreational trappers used strangling neck snares, steel-jawed leghold traps and cage traps baited with meat, catnip and animal secretions, while trophy hunters used eight kinds of weapons to kill bobcats,” she said. “The senseless loss of these bobcats is a loss to all Hoosiers who care about the responsible conservation and ethical treatment of wildlife. If the Natural Resources Commission and Governor Braun make this quota increase permanent, we could lose bobcats from Indiana within a decade, according to the Department of Natural Resources’ own projections.”

Bobcats were eliminated from Indiana by the 1960s due to overhunting and habitat loss. They were then protected as an endangered species in the state from 1969 until 2005. They remained protected in Indiana until 2025, when the DNR opened the first bobcat trapping season following legislation that forced the agency to do so. The Natural Resources Commission approved a trapping quota of 250 bobcats for the 2025 season despite widespread public opposition,
DNR used an interim rule to expand bobcat season. More than 95% of the 496 public comments submitted opposed the interim rule, the group said. The interim rule is in effect only for this season. The NRC will vote on whether to make the quota increase permanent in 2027.
Additional information on the bobcat hunting and trapping season can be found at on.IN.gov/bobcat-season.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Here’s Why H-Power Uses So Much Fuel
description: The facility often runs through  thousands of gallons of fuel oil per day to help it burn rubbish. This year's spill was reflected in discrepancies in its daily log numbers at the time.
text:
When H-Power opened 36 years ago, supporters framed it as a win-win: Burning Oʻahu’s rubbish would both create energy and help reduce the amount of trash sent to landfills.
Decades later, the facility and its operations are coming under scrutiny after more than 400,000 gallons of fuel oil spilled from an underground fuel line between late January and early May.
“That is an enormous amount of fuel,” Mayor Rick Blangiardi said Thursday at a press conference announcing the spill, “and I want everyone to understand that we recognize the seriousness of this incident.” 
As city, state and federal agencies work with the private company that operates H-Power to determine how far the fuel has spread, here’s what we know about the plant and why so much fuel was there in the first place.
What Is H-Power?
Unlike the prototypical image of a landfill with mountains of garbage and swirling seagulls, Honolulu’s landfill is 80% ash. That’s because the vast majority of the island’s non-construction rubbish first goes to H-Power in Kalaeloa, where it’s burned and converted into electricity, leaving behind the ash.
Mayor Rick Blangiardi said he only learned  about the spill’s existence in October, and that he learned the scope of it in mid-November.  Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
The city owns H-Power and contracts out the facility’s operations to Reworld, a company that manages 31 other waste-to-energy plants around the United States and Canada. The plants are especially clustered in Florida and the Northeast, in places such as West Palm Beach, Florida; Niagara Falls, New York; and Bristol, Connecticut. 
Waste-to-energy remains a somewhat controversial method of rubbish disposal. 
“It sounds really clean and lovely on paper,” said Nicole Chatterson, sustainability consultant and former executive director of Zero Waste Oʻahu. “But in practice, it’s a lot more complicated.”
Why Do We Need An Incinerator?
In much of the U.S., where land is generally plentiful, landfills are often more viable to build than waste-to-energy plants. Not so on Oʻahu.
By the time it opened in 1990, H-Power – which stands for Honolulu Program of Waste and Energy Recovery – had been discussed for over a decade. Former Mayor Frank Fasi pushed for it for years to help solve Oʻahu’s “mounting trash problem,” according to a 1988 article from the Honolulu Advertiser and Star-Bulletin. 
“It absolutely does decrease the volume of waste that has to get buried at the end,” Chatterson said, slowing the pace of filling up a landfill. “That, I think, is its main benefit.”
What’s The Argument Against Having An Incinerator?
Burning trash pollutes the air. Chatterson said that can be reduced by limiting what kind of trash is burned and by using so-called “scrubbers” to pull pollutants out of the smoke, but these solutions only go so far.
Participants in the city’s 2024 Tour de Trash watch rubbish being moved at H-Power, where it will be burned to create energy. Much of the facility’s infrastructure is dedicated to cleaning its own air emissions. Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024
H-Power requires a certain amount of input of rubbish to be profitable. Without it, the operator can’t make enough electricity. A 2017 city audit referenced this, saying the city’s contract with H-Power states that if there’s not enough trash being delivered to the facility, the city has to make up for the lost revenue.
Chatterson said that creates a perverse and unsustainable incentive.
“Burning as little material as possible is the goal,” she said, “but that’s antithetical to the business model of waste-to-energy plants.”
Not to mention the fuel oil that’s needed to start combustion in the first place — which, of course, can leak.
What Did Company Data Show During The Spill?
At any given time, H-Power’s fuel tanks can hold upward of 20,000 to 30,000 gallons of fuel, according to Reworld’s daily fuel reconciliation data obtained by Civil Beat. The amount used each day varies, sometimes totaling less than 1,000 gallons while other times reaching closer to 10,000. Rainy weather makes it harder to burn rubbish and requires more fuel, Reworld Vice President Michael Van Brunt said at Thursday’s press conference.
During the time of the leak, the fuel data shows discrepancies between the amount of fuel expected in the storage tanks based on calculations and the amount of fuel actually observed.
Before the leak, the daily discrepancy was usually below 1%. During the leak, however, it was often above 10%, sometimes reaching levels above 30% and at one point even hitting 78%.
An H-Power official said Thursday that taxpayers will not bear the cost of the cleanup. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Instructions at the top of the sheet say the operations night shift supervisor should double-check the numbers if the discrepancy is over 3%. If it’s over 6%, the supervisor should walk down to ensure there are no leaks. 
The supervisor is then supposed to make a note explaining the discrepancy and confirming all checks were completed, according to the instructions. But the notes column is largely blank during the spill’s duration from January until May 4, at which point it includes just two words: “Leak identified.”
Company spokesperson Neal Yokota said Friday that Reworld declined to comment for this story, but at Thursday’s press conference Van Brunt said the extra fuel needed to ignite rubbish during this year’s rainy spring obscured how much fuel they were losing during the leak. Honolulu had its wettest March in 20 years thanks to back-to-back storms during the Kona lows.
The EPA, which regulates aboveground fuel tanks such as the ones that leaked at H-Power, is actively investigating the situation, public affairs specialist Alejandro Díaz said in an emailed statement. He said the EPA does not comment on ongoing investigations. 
The EPA was informed of the spill in May — when it was initially thought to be approximately 6,500 gallons — but the state did not update the EPA on the situation until Aug. 21, Díaz said. He said the EPA has been assisting with the spill response since then.
What Other Options Exist For Waste Disposal?
Similar to an incinerator, plasma arc gasification is a technology that essentially disintegrates waste, though it does so by zapping it at a very high temperature rather than burning it with fire.
“Plasma arc is much more effective than H-Power, cheaper, more environmentally friendly, and also produces electricity,” University of Hawaiʻi civil and environmental engineering professor Amarjit Singh said in an email. “It beats me why it’s not selling in Honolulu where the landfill matter has become very serious.”
Mayor Rick Blangiardi held a press conference Thursday morning to announce that roughly 400,000 gallons of fuel oil were spilled at the city’s H-Power waste-to-energy plant earlier this year. (Ben Angarone/Civil Beat/2026)
Chatterson, on the other hand, is skeptical of supporters’ claims that the technology reduces the amount of toxic byproducts to the extent they say it does. 
“I’m not sold that they’re impact-free enough to be worth the cost to the public to fund them,” she said. 
She would like to see a future where waste is reduced as much as possible – to zero would be ideal, per the name of her nonprofit. 
Council member Andria Tupola, whose district includes both H-Power and the city’s only municipal landfill, has been leading the End Landfills Task Force since August with the goal of submitting a final report of recommendations in November 2027. After Thursday’s press conference, she called for answers about how the leak occurred and why the public didn’t know sooner.
“This was a massive release, it went undetected for months, and the people who live and work near it were left in the dark far too long,” she said Friday in a press release. 
Beyond new technology, Chatterson thinks conversations about lifestyle changes to reduce waste are what’s ultimately needed to solve Oʻahu’s ʻōpala conundrum.
“Those feel harder to us than just believing that human engineering is undefeatable,” she said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Grove Farm Shares Early Plans To Redevelop Plantation Camp
description: The major landowner is exploring its options for the former Kōloa Camp site and asked the Kōloa community to share their ideas.
text:
Kaua‘i’s South Shore may in the coming years see dozens of new single-family workforce homes under a nascent plan by one of the island’s largest landowners to redevelop a former plantation camp. 
The Waihohonu project is part of Grove Farm’s larger vision for 2,500 new homes on the island over the next five years. Kaua‘i needs 4,900 more homes by 2027, according to the 2024 Hawai‘i Housing Planning Study
The over 100-year-old Kōloa Camp, once part of Japanese Camp C, housed sugar plantation workers. The roughly 24-acre property sits behind the county’s Anne Knudsen Park and is adjacent to part of the Waihohonu Stream. 
The company, which gathering community input as part of early planning, expects to present a more solid plan for the Waihohonu project sometime next year. 
“There’s nothing locked in stone,” Don Horner, chairman and CEO of Grove Farm, said at a community meeting last week. “We don’t have engineering done. We don’t have technical plans done, etc. So we’re exploratory.”
Don Horner, chairman and CEO of Grove Farm, talked with Kōloa community members about the company’s plans for the region at a Nov. 12 Kōloa Community Association meeting. (Noelle Fujii-Oride/Civil Beat/2026)
Grove Farm evicted the last tenants of the plantation camp in 2012 to build a 50-unit housing subdivision, also called Waihohonu, that never came to fruition. Back then, prices for the homes were expected to range from $260,000 to $485,000, according to reports in the Honolulu Star-Advertiser. 
The western half of the property is divided into 46 lots. Horner said the company doesn’t yet have a set number of homes for the development but that the preliminary target would be 40 to 60 lots.
Grove Farm is looking at potentially selling lots and then letting buyers build their homes. That’s what the company has been doing for its Pīkake and Puakea subdivisions in Līhu‘e. 
It’s also looking at creating plans for two-bedroom, two-bathroom model homes to give buyers another option. Those homes would have to align with South Kaua‘i’s building code which outlines what types of homes can be built in certain areas, he said. 
Community Concerns 
Horner invited the Kōloa community to share their ideas for the Waihohonu project at a recent Kōloa Community Association meeting. He was especially interested in what adjacent neighbors wanted to see and introduced the company’s new project manager who will continue engaging the community. 
Residents at the meeting questioned Grove Farm’s plans to address flooding and wastewater on the Kōloa site and ensure that the homes go to local community members.  
Part of the site is in a flood zone, and Grove Farm will need to conduct analysis on how to best mitigate flooding. 
‘At the meeting, some community members were concerned about heavy rains and flooding in 2024 that damaged dozens of nearby Kōloa homes and the Kōloa Early School.   
The Waihohonu development is outside the Visitor Destination Area, so homes cannot be used for transient vacation rentals. 
Grove Farm is also considering placing deed restrictions on the lots so that the homes can only be sold to Hawai‘i residents. That’s in response to the community’s concerns about speculators purchasing new homes for second homes. 
Horner added at the meeting that the company wants to give property owners on Wailani Road, which is next to the development site, the first option to purchase the lot behind their homes. 
In July, Hawai‘i Gov. Josh Green signed a law that requires affordable housing projects to place such perpetual deed restrictions on their units in order to qualify for fast-tracked permitting. 
Horner said that regulations for how that law is implemented have yet to be drafted. For example, it’s not clear if buyers of deed-restricted homes can get first mortgages. 
Grove Farm focuses on “gap housing” — meaning it targets residents who make too much money to qualify for affordable housing but not enough to purchase market-rate homes. Horner often uses police officers and teachers as examples of who Grove Farm builds for. 
Over the last 160 years, Grove Farm has built more than 2,194 homes.  
Community Feedback
Several community members at the meeting expressed concerns about how the development would handle its wastewater, especially when the state’s mandated 2050 cesspool conversion deadline is fast approaching. Kōloa is challenged by its lava rock terrain, which makes conversions costly. 
Horner said that one idea is to have a septic system for every two homes or potentially connect to other sewer lines that already exist in Kōloa. Grove Farm is looking at revisiting its plan for a sewage treatment plant. In 2009, the company completed an environmental impact statement for such a facility on part of the former Kōloa Mill site. 
Other Kōloa community members asked that Grove Farm consider creating plans for larger homes since many Kōloa families live in multigenerational homes. 
Horner said that he’d like to see Waihohonu have community garden space and access to the Anne Knudsen Park. He also wanted to explore whether there’s ways to access the development that don’t burden the existing neighborhood around it. 
Grove Farm will continue to engage South Shore residents to help inform its plans for Waihohonu. 
“We are listening,” he told Civil Beat, “and we will modify where needed.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Cost of using WA National Guard to protect drop boxes could reach $350K
description: Gov. Bob Ferguson’s call up of the state National Guard to keep watch on ballot drop boxes ahead of the Nov. 3 election may cost Washington taxpayers up to $350,000. In total, 105 people took part in the mission, dubbed Election Neighborhood Watch by the governor, that marked the state’s first large-scale activation for the […]
text:
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson inserts his ballot into a drop box on the campus of South Puget Sound Community College in Olympia, Washington on Oct. 30, 2026. Thurston County Auditor Mary Hall is walking away after depositing her ballot. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
Gov. Bob Ferguson’s call up of the state National Guard to keep watch on ballot drop boxes ahead of the Nov. 3 election may cost Washington taxpayers up to $350,000.
In total, 105 people took part in the mission, dubbed Election Neighborhood Watch by the governor, that marked the state’s first large-scale activation for the express purpose of safeguarding ballots. 
National Guard members were deployed in seven western Washington counties —- King, Pierce, Snohomish, Thurston, Clark, Lewis and Island. Their role consisted mostly of driving around at night and overnight, making visual checks between Oct. 26 and Nov. 3. 
They dressed in civilian clothing, were unarmed and instructed to be inconspicuous and not interact with voters. If they saw anything suspicious they were to notify local law enforcement.
Seven incidents were reported, all in King County and none serious, the Washington Military Department said. 
One report was of a box that had been spray painted and another of a suspicious bag seen near a box. There were three reports of people loitering near a ballot box, though in one case the person said they were using the wifi of the nearby library. Authorities were also called for a person seen sleeping near a ballot drop box.
“I appreciate the service of our National Guard. They have stepped up for our communities in times of flooding, fires, and now to make sure everyone’s vote is counted,” Ferguson said in a statement. 
“We were happy to work with county auditors who requested this assistance,” he added.
‘Unexpected expense’
County auditors didn’t actually seek help as they had not detected any credible threats to drop boxes.. Rather, Ferguson reached out to all counties on Oct. 19, offering the services of the National Guard. Seven accepted, appreciative of an added layer of security.
Ferguson signed the activation order two days later. It covered the period of Oct. 26 through Nov. 10.
Brionna Aho, Ferguson’s communications director, said the final cost of the mission is still being calculated, but initial estimates from the Office of Financial Management are that it will be under $350,000. 
“The Secretary of State’s Office agreed to pay for the activation out of their election funds,” she said in an email.
That wasn’t the initial understanding of Secretary of State Steve Hobbs.
On Oct. 19, when the governor’s office shared its plans, “we understood that they had identified a funding source to support the deployment,” said Stefanie Randolph, director of communications for the secretary of state’s office.
On Oct. 23, which was two days after Ferguson signed the activation order, officials from his Office of Financial Management contacted the secretary of state’s office to find out if the National Guard deployment could be paid for with existing election funds.
“We agreed to cover the costs through our existing agreement with the Washington Military Department and seek reimbursement,” Randolph said. “The funds we are using support ongoing election administration and security activities. Because the activation was an unexpected expense, we have emphasized the importance of reimbursement.”
She said the final tab may be closer to $260,000.
“Many different resources exist to support election security. When county elections officials request additional assistance, we want to make sure they have the resources they need,” Hobbs said.
‘A serious matter’
This wasn’t the first time the Washington National Guard had played a role in an election.
Cybersecurity professionals from the guard have been activated to assist with cybersecurity tasks for every election since 2016, according to the governor’s office. 
In 2024, Gov. Jay Inslee activated the guard after a drop box in Vancouver was set on fire and several hundred ballots inside were damaged.. 
More recently white powder has been sent to offices of numerous elected officials in the state and across the country.
“Amid these recent developments and the highly charged atmosphere of this election, my administration is taking every precaution to ensure that every vote counts and that counties have the resources they need to monitor and respond to potential threats,” Ferguson wrote auditors when he offered services of the National Guard.
It’s too soon to speculate on whether a similar offer will be made ahead of the 2028 election.
“Calling up the National Guard is a serious matter,” said Hobbs, who is a National Guard member. “It requires a clear picture of the threat environment and what resources are available, which isn’t possible when the 2028 election is still two years away.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Brisk bidding in Alaska oil lease sales dominated by a single company
description: A Texas-based company that recently expanded its Alaska holdings drove a pair of state oil and gas lease sales to the highest dollar total in more than a decade. The Alaska Department of Natural Resources reported that this year’s auctions of onshore North Slope acres and offshore Beaufort Sea acres generated $35.6 million in total […]
text:
The Badami pipeline, which carries oil from Badami west toward Prudhoe Bay, is seen in this undated photo. The Badami field is located on the eastern North Slope, between Prudhoe Bay and Point Thomson. Texas-based APA Corp., which is taking over the Badami field and its associated infrastructure, was the dominant bidder in annual lease sales held by the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas. (Photo by David Houseknecht/U.S. Geological Survey)A Texas-based company that recently expanded its Alaska holdings drove a pair of state oil and gas lease sales to the highest dollar total in more than a decade.
The Alaska Department of Natural Resources reported that this year’s auctions of onshore North Slope acres and offshore Beaufort Sea acres generated $35.6 million in total high bids for more than 427,000 onshore and offshore acres.
APA Alaska LLC, owned by Texas-based APA Corp., dominated the bids, which were opened on Wednesday by DNR’s Division of Oil and Gas.
APA Corp. is the holding company for Apache Corp., an oil and gas company that has been active in Alaska. APA, which has already been engaged in Alaska exploration, announced in June that it had struck a $70 million deal to buy the Badami field and associated assets on the eastern North Slope from Savant Alaska LLC. The transaction includes about 75,000 acres in a prospect called the Grey Owl Unit.
Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is leaving office in a little over two weeks, said the overall lease sale results show that Alaska is an attractive place to explore for oil.
“Companies are continuing to invest in the North Slope renaissance because they recognize the strong resource opportunities our state offers, as well as the benefits of a stable tax and permitting regime, and the promise embodied in Alaska’s motto North to the Future,” Dunleavy said in a statement released by the Department of Natural Resources.
The three auctions were part of the Division of Oil and Gas’ regular program of areawide lease sales in different regions of the state. The program, in place since 1999, ensures that there are regular lease sales offering all available state territory in the main regions for oil and gas activity, the North Slope and Southcentral Alaska’s Cook Inlet basin. Arctic lease sales are usually held in the late fall, while sales for the Cook Inlet region are usually held in the spring.
In Wednesday’s onshore North Slope lease sale, APA won 218 of the 254 tracts sold and submitted $30.2 million of the total $33.29 million in high bids, according to preliminary results.
APA’s participation pushed the sum of high bids to the highest amount for an annual state lease sale in that region since 2014, when $39.85 million in winning bids were submitted for 254 tracts, according to Division of Oil and Gas records.
Last year’s North Slope areawide lease sale, in comparison, generated a bit over $16.97 million in high bids for 271 tracts.
Ten other companies submitted successful bids in this year’s North Slope lease sale. Those include Oil Search Alaska, which is owned by Australia-based Santos; Burgundy Xploration; and Captivate Energy Alaska Inc.
Hilcorp, the privately held company that now operates the Prudhoe Bay oil field and other assets previously owned by BP, submitted successful bids for two tracts, according to the preliminary results.
HEX North Slope LLC, which is part of Anchorage-based HEX LLC, was the successful bidder on four tracts, according to the preliminary results. Those tracts are located on state land bordering a lease within the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that HEX bought in a federal auction conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management in June.
In all, the North Slope areawide lease sale offered 1,741 tracts comprising 2.7 million acres of state-owned land.
APA said in June, when it announced the Badami purchase deal, that it intends to drill two exploration wells this winter.
The company was also active in the state’s annual Beaufort Sea lease sale on Wednesday, which offered 298 tracts comprising 865,000 state-owned offshore acres.
APA submitted $1.5 million of the $2.33 million in high bids received and won six of the 11 tracts sold, according to the preliminary results.
Other successful bidders in that sale were investor Samuel Cade, Epoch Oil and Gas LLC, Hilcorp and Narwhal Exploration LLC, according to preliminary results.
The sum of high bids for the Beaufort Sea sale was the highest since 2014, when $4.5 million was submitted in winning bids for 42 tracts, according to Division of Oil and Gas records.
A third annual lease sale held by the division, offering 817 tracts comprising 4.3 million acres in the Brooks Range Foothills, drew no bids. The foothills area is well south of the area where most North Slope activity has occurred, and it generally attracts less industry interest.
A map released by the state shows the tracts that received bids in the just-completed 2026 North Slope areawide lease sale. (Map provided by the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas)

name: California
title: Measles is spreading in the U.S. What it means for California
description: Measles is spreading in the U.S., but experts say Californians don’t have to freak out just yet.  We also dive into the lives of five people who lifted themselves out of homelessness and shared what support made a big impact in their journey to get off the streets. Then we get into colleges creating their […]
text:
A lab assistant loads blood samples for automated serology testing for measles immunity status at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health laboratory in Downey on Feb. 26, 2026. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters




Measles is spreading in the U.S., but experts say Californians don’t have to freak out just yet. 
We also dive into the lives of five people who lifted themselves out of homelessness and shared what support made a big impact in their journey to get off the streets.
Then we get into colleges creating their own AI platforms to avoid being totally dependent on AI products from Google, Microsoft and other tech companies. Finally, public health experts are inviting you to take part in a new survey. 
Though they are urging caution, public health officials say that Californians shouldn’t panic yet when it comes to the measles outbreaks spreading across the U.S. 
As CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang explains, more than twenty years after the country gained measles-elimination status, international health officials stripped the U.S. of its standing last week. Since 2025, outbreaks in Pennsylvania, Texas, South Carolina, Arizona and Utah sickened more than 8,000 people and killed more than a dozen.Measles can cause pneumonia, inflammation of the brain, pregnancy complications and death.
California has witnessed 60 confirmed cases of measles so far this year — more than the previous two years combined. Pockets of unvaccinated communities have driven local outbreaks in the state, including two earlier this year in Shasta and Riverside counties, and a regional outbreak in Sacramento and Placer counties.
The Sacramento-Placer outbreak sickened 21 people, all of whom were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak began when a family member of a Placer County resident traveled to South Carolina, and health officials estimate that fewer than half of the people were vaccinated in the communities where the virus spread.
Nonetheless, California has one of the highest immunization rates in the nation — a bulwark that helped prevent these outbreaks from growing much larger. People usually get vaccinated for measles before the start of kindergarten and in California 96% of kindergarteners are vaccinated.
But Californians should still be careful and get vaccinated if they’re not already. Though no vaccine guarantees 100% protection, it can protect someone who has contracted measles against severe complications and hospitalization. 
If you’re not sure of your vaccination status, talk to your primary care doctor to check whether you need to be tested for measles immunity, or receive an updated shot.

Dr. Sanchi Malhotra, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at UCLA Health: “Measles is the most infectious disease we have. It’s a canary in the coal mine. If we’re seeing measles outbreaks, it makes us worry what other vaccine-preventable diseases are on the horizon.”

Read more.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


Clawing oneself out of homelessness


Top left, clockwise: Mike McCarthy, Jennifer Su, Ifalayo Harper, John Janosko, Judy Cleborne and James Presley. Photos by Sarahbeth Maney, Anna Hoch-Kenney, Zoë Meyers and Alisha Jucevic for CalMatters




With nearly 180,000 unhoused people in California, the state’s homelessness crisis can seem like an intractable problem. But every year, thousands of Californians overcome the odds and find safer places to live.
In her latest report, CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall profiles five, formerly homeless residents who share what interventions, accountability measures and community support helped them secure stable housing. 
Judy Cleborne was in her 70s when she was living in an RV parked on the streets in San Diego. After suffering multiple break-ins, she embarked on a journey to find housing — a long, and at times “soul-destroying” process, she said.
Cleborne got help from Dawn Contreras, a case manager with the nonprofit PATH, who eventually found her an apartment through a group chat with other caseworkers. Someone in the chat knew of a building that had an opening, and Contreras pounced. Cleborne moved into the $1,550-a-month apartment in March. Her income includes a rent voucher that expires soon, plus Social Security and a part-time job.

Cleborne: “It’s a big rent payment, and I have a car payment, and it’s all scary. But that’s my challenge, to make it all work.”

Read more.
More on homelessness: Marisa also reports that a new rule barring families with undocumented immigrants from federally funded housing has the potential to cause thousands of Californians to lose housing. Read more.



CA colleges’ quest to create their own AI


The data center at the San Diego Supercomputer Center at UC San Diego in San Diego on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by McKenzie Patterson for CalMatters




Some California public colleges are developing their own data centers and artificial intelligence platforms to save money and exert more control over their AI tools in lieu of being solely reliant on commercial AI providers, writes CalMatters’ Adam Echelman.
Commercial AI platforms can be more advanced and intuitive to use. But they can be expensive: Individual subscriptions can hit $200 a month. Meanwhile, university-brokered deals with commercial platforms cost students nothing but require the campuses to pay up. As an alternative, California’s three public college systems are either exploring or expanding using in-house AI products that are cheaper and ensure more privacy over student data.
UC San Diego has the most advanced, university-controlled AI platform. Its supercomputing center helped create TritonGPT, and the university has assisted other UCs to develop their own chatbots. California’s community college system also cited UCSD as a partner in its formal proposal to the state to develop a more independent AI network.
Read more.



And lastly: What do you want public health officials to know?


Vials of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley on Jan. 26, 2015. Photo by Justin Sullivan, Getty Images




Have an opinion on what health issues should be prioritized in California? CalMatters is partnering with Your Local Epidemiologist to make the real concerns and questions from Californians heard by public health officials and journalists.
Every Monday, we’ll ask about health topics affecting Californians, and it’ll only take two minutes to answer.
This week, we’re asking about the health impacts of measles and mold. Take the survey.






California Voices
While union members are moving earth and pouring concrete for the high-speed rail project, politicians aren’t doing their job to pass laws that’ll help the project finish faster, better and for cheaper, write Carter Lavin and Avery Barrett, of the Bay Area transit rider group Transbay Coalition.

title: Unpacking voting trends in Massachusetts’s Latino communities
description: This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon senior reporter Chris Lisinski speaks with Rafael Pérez Medina, Latino policy analyst at the UMass Boston Gastón Institute, and Julio Mejia, executive director of the Merrimack Valley Project, about how heavily Latino communities swung back to the left this year, voter registration trends, and how to achieve bett[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Chris Lisinski
Guests: Rafael Pérez Medina, Latino policy analyst at the UMass Boston Gastón Institute; Julio Mejia, executive director of the Merrimack Valley Project








PLENTY OF INK was spilled two years ago when Vice President Kamala Harris won Lawrence by only 17 points. While her margin of victory was comfortable, it was also about 26 percentage points narrower than Gov. Maura Healey’s win in 2022, part of a shift toward President Donald Trump in Latino communities across Massachusetts and nationwide.
That was far from the case this year. Healey carried Lawrence by an even bigger margin than she did in 2022, just as she did in other places with significant Hispanic and Latino populations like Chelsea and Holyoke.
So what can we learn from the back-and-forth swings? One conclusion, according to Rafael Pérez Medina, Latino policy analyst at the UMass Boston Gastón Institute, is that no one can “take the Latino vote for granted.”
This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon senior reporter Chris Lisinski interviews Pérez Medina and Julio Mejia, executive director of the Merrimack Valley Project, about voter registration, trends, and turnout in Latino communities.
In Massachusetts, Latino voters cast about 7.5 percent of ballots in 2024, a larger share than any other racial or ethnic minority. And they could gain significantly more political power as the state’s demographics continue to evolve.
Yet gaps in participation and representation linger, leaving plenty of work for people like Mejia to drive consistent civic engagement even when the spotlight of a national election has powered down.
In this episode, we discuss the pendulum of election results in Latino communities (6:00), increases in turnout rates in cities and towns with significant Latino populations (19:40), and what it will take to grow the ranks of the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus in the State House (30:00).

name: California
title: What it took for 5 Californians to pull themselves out of homelessness
description: CalMatters interviewed five Californians who successfully left homelessness behind. Each story provides clues into what types of interventions can work for others.
text:
On the surface, California’s homelessness crisis often seems unsurmountable: Tents and RVs line city streets and nearly 180,000 people have nowhere to call home. 
But every year, thousands of Californians successfully claw their way out of homelessness. Each person’s story of how they did it is unique, influenced by what led them there in the first place, their individual needs and their past traumas. 
CalMatters interviewed five Californians who have survived homelessness and come out the other side, and we are sharing those stories here as examples of interventions that can work. 
Some common themes flow through them, showing that housing, while crucial, isn’t always enough. People need a reason to keep going – a passion such as music, helping others, or spirituality – and a community to support them and keep them accountable. 
‘Let them grow together’
John Janosko depended on his friends and community during the years he lived in Oakland’s largest homeless encampment. 
“That’s what kept me sane,” he said. “Because those are the ones who understand you the most.”
When city workers tore down the camp in 2023, they offered Janosko and many of his friends something unusual: the chance to stay together and move as a group into temporary tiny homes. That opportunity meant he could lean on his community as he transitioned back into mainstream society after nearly a decade of homelessness.
Now, at 58, he has his own apartment, is sober and dedicates his time to helping other people who are homeless.
John Janosko, 58, who was previously unhoused for ten years, at his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
Janosko’s time on the streets, which he refers to as an “adventure,” started in 2013, when he lost his job and apartment after struggling with an addiction to crack cocaine, and later methamphetamine. 
Around 2019 he helped launch the Wood Street camp, which grew to more than 300 occupants. Residents fashioned make-shift amenities including an outdoor kitchen, shower and community clothing closet, hosted parties and protests, launched a GoFundMe and started a registered nonprofit. Janosko was a driving force behind it all, and he thrived on it. 
But Janosko, who’d recently had a heart attack, knew he couldn’t live there forever. The city of Oakland and Caltrans were making it increasingly clear that the campers were no longer welcome. So when the city offered to move him and several dozen of his friends into new tiny homes down the street, he agreed. 
The miniscule unit, big enough for a cot and a mini fridge, was a stepping stone that helped Janosko get ready for independent living. He got re-accustomed to having the privacy of a locked door. He started taking culinary classes and settled into a regular schedule. 
“It was the stability I needed,” he said.
John Janosko shows old photographs from his time being unhoused that hang on a wall in his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
An obvious pitfall of tiny homes, which have gained popularity recently as a solution to homelessness, is that while they’re supposed to be temporary, occupants often can’t find permanent housing once they leave. Janosko estimates fewer than half of his Wood Street friends secured permanent housing after the tiny homes. 
He was one of the lucky ones. In 2024, after about a year in the tiny home, he found a subsidized apartment where he now pays $258 a month in rent using his Social Security income. 
Part of it was chance: Janosko thinks having a heart attack placed him at a higher priority in the county’s housing queue. But the support of his Wood Street friends also helped keep him from getting discouraged along the way, he said.
It’s common for people living in encampments to form close bonds with their street families, and people sometimes become isolated and depressed when moved alone out of those communities and into shelters or housing. Some programs try to account for that by keeping street communities together – such as Los Angeles’ Inside Safe program, which moves entire encampments into hotels. But it’s not the norm. 
John Janosko opens a photo book of childhood memories from growing up in the Bay Area, at his apartment in Oakland on Aug. 28, 2026. His adoptive parents gave Janosko the book after he experienced homelessness. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
To Janosko, it’s an obvious solution. 
“Keep them together,” he said. “Let them grow together. They do better that way. Don’t dismantle everything that they know.”
From overdose to accountability
Ifalayo Harper’s third try at sobriety, during her 11th year of homelessness, was the one that worked.
That’s because this time, when she finished rehab in 2023, there was something different waiting for her on the other side. She moved into a unique, self-governed sober-housing community with two dozen formerly homeless people called Homefulness. 
“There’s always somebody to keep me accountable,” said Harper, 43. 
The other key to her success is her faith: She embraced traditional Yoruba religious practices during a trip to Nigeria in the midst of her recovery.
Ifalayo Harper inside her apartment at the Homefulness community in Oakland on Sept. 14, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters
Harper, whose birth name is LeaJay, became homeless in 2012, after her drinking cost her her job, and then her home. Once on the street, she started using methamphetamine, then heroin, and then fentanyl, getting sucked deeper and deeper into addiction. 
Like Janosko, Harper lived in the Wood Street encampment. But while that camp was a lifeline for him, Harper’s relationship with it was more fraught: The camp made it far too easy for her to get drugs. So when the city cleared the encampment, it was “bittersweet,” Harper said. The city moved Harper and her RV to a city-sanctioned “safe parking lot” all the way across town. It was isolating, but it gave her the nudge she needed to start thinking seriously about recovery. 
Two months later, Harper overdosed in the backseat of her college-age daughter’s car after injecting a shot of fentanyl into her neck.
When she woke up in the hospital, her friend, Homefulness founder Lisa “Tiny” Gray-Garcia, offered to get her into rehab. After that, Harper moved into Homefulness in December 2023. She recently got a job in the same San Francisco drug treatment program where she was a patient three years ago. 
Unlike other homeless housing programs, Homefulness has no nonprofit setting rules for residents and no government funding. Residents decide things as a group and take turns doing chores that include feeding the chickens and goat. There’s no rent. Residents contribute toward utilities and other group expenses if they can, but no one pays more than $300 a month, and most pay less, if anything. 



First: Ifalayo Harper spends a moment with Cappuccino the goat during a stroll around the Oakland Homefulness community. Last: Ifalayo Harper makes jewelry in the attic of her apartment, which she transformed into a creative workshop. It is her favorite part of her apartment and where she spends hours sewing and beading. Harper, who was previously unhoused for years, said making jewelry helped when she was going through recovery. Photos by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters
It’s a novel – even radical – approach, but it’s slowly gaining momentum. In addition to the East Oakland property where Harper lives, Gray-Garcia and her group own a second lot down the street where they’ve built two tiny homes and plan to add 12 more, and a third lot in San Francisco where they’re planning a four-story building. The group also is raising money for sites in Los Angeles and Washington. 
By and large, the people who have moved in, stay. Many of them are people who have been labeled hard to help, or “service resistant,” by society.
Gray-Garcia says the reason it works is simple: community.
“We need each other,” she said. “We don’t need to be alone in a room with a door and a lock and a key. That’s not a human way to live, at all.”
Help from a stranger
After more than a decade of methamphetamine use and homelessness, Mike McCarthy figured eventually he would die on the streets.
“I got tired of the lifestyle,” McCarthy said. “It got old after a while. I just kept begging for help, kept praying: ‘I want out. I want help. I don’t want this anymore.’”
Then he met Jennifer Su. 
Mike McCarthy, 36, at Jennifer Su’s home in Pacheco, on Aug. 21, 2026. McCarthy overcame addiction and currently lives with Su. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
At the time McCarthy was sleeping at a camp in Pleasant Hill, an upper-middle class suburb in Contra Costa County, and Su often stopped by to visit her own son, who was also homeless. She and McCarthy made an unlikely pair. He’s a 36-year-old tattooed metal music fan. She’s a 57-year-old county government employee who’s active in her church. 
One day, Su asked McCarthy if he could use some help. She took him to the DMV to get an ID card. She helped him sign up for public assistance benefits, Medi-Cal, and, eventually, addiction treatment. 
When he initially got assigned to an outpatient treatment program – meaning he’d have to try and get sober while living in a tent during a winter of torrential rain – she pushed to get him reassigned to in-patient treatment. When he got admitted to a program that didn’t allow pets, Su took in his beloved pitbull mix, Rose. 
McCarthy graduated from the program in January 2025 and moved into a sober living home. But conditions at the home were challenging. He slept in a bunk bed in a room he shared with three other men, and there were strict rules about chores and possessions. 
Mike McCarthy and Jennifer Su at her home in Pacheco on Aug. 21, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
In July 2025, Su offered McCarthy a spare bedroom in her own home in Pacheco, which she shares with her husband and dogs. McCarthy accepted. Now, he pays rent when he can and helps with chores, including cleaning the bathroom and picking up after the dogs. He got a job at the Safeway he used to sleep behind, he’s working toward getting his GED and he plays guitar in a band that just had its first gig in Berkeley. His passion for music is a major reason he stays sober, McCarthy said – he knows if he started using again, he’d be out of the band. And, he doesn’t want to disappoint Su. 
For Su, each of McCarthy’s successes have been a balm to her heart. She’s been trying for years to help her own son, who has schizophrenia, uses methamphetamine and has been in and out of psychiatric facilities. But like so many people who love someone with a serious mental illness, she’s found that getting him the treatment he needs often seems impossible. When she felt like she’d failed her son, McCarthy helped her see it wasn’t her fault. Where she couldn’t help her son, she could help McCarthy.
“It was really healing for me,” Su said, “and just a blessing in my life to see him doing so well.” Her own son recently went into residential treatment, but she continues to worry about how long he’ll stay there and what will happen to him once he gets out.
McCarthy believes he’d still be on the street without Su. 
“I just don’t think I would have been able to do it on my own,” he said. “I pretty much needed somebody to help me get out of there.”
Mike McCathy plays the guitar at Jennifer Su’s home in Pacheco, on Aug. 21, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
While McCarthy’s story proves recovery is possible, it also highlights how difficult it is to navigate the system without someone like Su. 
Su believes her relationship with McCarthy could be an example. What if programs matched their unhoused clients with housed families to guide them back into society, helping with everything from going to the DMV to filing taxes?
“You don’t just…put a roof over someone’s head and expect that they’ll be able to thrive,” Su said. “People have to have a reason to live. People have to have things that they enjoy, and friendships.”
Crowdsourcing an apartment
Judy Cleborne was in her 70s, feeling unsafe after multiple break-ins to her RV, when she decided she couldn’t keep spending her nights parked on the street in San Diego. 
That was in 2024. This year, she finally sold her RV and moved into her own apartment. But when she embarked on her journey to find housing, she had no idea how long, frustrating, and at times she says “soul-destroying,” that process would be.
She got help from Dawn Contreras, a case manager with the nonprofit PATH, who would eventually find her an apartment. 
Judy Cleborne in her new apartment in San Diego on Oct. 5, 2026. Cleborne got into housing this year after living out of her RV for several years. Photo by Zoë Meyers for CalMatters
The search was slow at first. Between the two of them, Contreras and Cleborne called more than three-dozen properties with no luck. Even in low-rent buildings, Cleborne’s income was a barrier – she received about $1,650 a month in Social Security. And competition was sky-high. 
“Just when you think you’ve found a perfect spot, they’re like, ‘nope, we’re not taking anybody today, call this place,’” Contreras said. “And you call, and they’re like, ‘nope our waitlist is long.’”
Cleborne got a job at Goodwill to boost her income and give herself a better chance at qualifying for an apartment. At the same time, Contreras was consulting her secret weapon – a group chat of other caseworkers who shared tips and resources. Someone in the chat knew of a building that had an opening, and Contreras pounced. Cleborne moved in this past March. 
Judy Cleborne was able to decorate her new apartment in San Diego with the help of Humble Design. Cleborne got into housing this year after living out of her RV for several years. Photo by Zoë Meyers for CalMatters
It’s not uncommon for it to take a year or longer for her clients to find housing, Contreras said. They sometimes get so discouraged that they lose hope. Trauma from years of homelessness also often erodes people’s ability to persevere through numerous rejections. And not everyone has a Contreras in their corner. 
Today, Cleborne’s struggles aren’t over. She’s using a rapid rehousing voucher to cover part of her rent, which is set to expire in January. Then, she’ll have to start paying the entire $1,550 a month herself. 
“It’s a big rent payment, and I have a car payment, and it’s all scary,” Cleborne said. “But that’s my challenge, to make it all work.”
A forced choice: Jail or treatment?
James Presley’s pathway to recovery and housing started in a jail cell.
Presley, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, was sleeping on benches in Santa Monica, hearing and seeing things that weren’t there, when he was arrested in 2025 on a breaking and entering charge. He says he biked to his grandmother’s house, where he’d lived before she kicked him out, broke in through a back window, and laid down on the bed in his old room. When he woke up the next morning, the police were there. 
For someone who is unhoused and has a serious mental illness, an arrest often starts a vicious cycle of jumping between jail and the street. But 31-year-old Presley was selected for a program by Los Angeles County’s Office of Diversion and Reentry, which gives people the option of completing mental health treatment instead of jail.
Presley graduated from the program in May, and moved into an apartment last month. He’s no longer experiencing hallucinations, or using alcohol or marijuana. 
“My mind is clear,” Presley said. “Plus, I’m sober. So it helped a lot.” 
James Presley at his new apartment in Los Angeles on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Alisha Jucevic for CalMatters
Presley spent about a month in jail before he was accepted into the diversion program and started a six-month in-patient hospital stay. Then he moved into a halfway house with about 20 other men also participating in diversion programs. 
Presley doesn’t believe he would have chosen to enter treatment if he hadn’t faced time in jail. 
That’s true of many program participants, said Dr. Clemens Hong, who leads the county’s diversion programs. 
“The big piece, though, is: Can we treat them long enough and successfully enough to allow them to understand the benefits of treatment beyond staying out of jail?” he said. “That’s what leads to the ultimate success of the program…I think we achieve that in a lot of folks.”
To qualify for diversion, participants must be homeless, have a serious mental illness, and be charged with a crime. The idea is to catch people who have fallen through the holes in all the other safety nets. A judge orders them into treatment, and in some programs, can also order them to take medication. Each person’s treatment plan includes housing and other services tailored to their individual needs.
James Presley in the courtyard of his new apartment in Los Angeles on Oct. 17, 2026. After four years on a waiting list for Section 8 housing, he moved into the apartment in mid-October. Presley is now working on getting furniture and setting up his new home. He said he is celebrating two years clean and sober and feeling positive about this new chapter. Photo by Alisha Jucevic for CalMatters
The 11-year-old diversion program is similar in some ways to the state’s newer CARE Court, which uses the courts to place people with severe mental illnesses into treatment. Unlike CARE Court, where participants have not necessarily been charged with a crime, the diversion program has the teeth to force participants to comply with their treatment plans. 
The average diversion participant has been incarcerated 10 times before starting the program. After entering diversion, 56% don’t go back to jail in two years, and some never go back, Hong said. That means the program helps more than half of participants turn their lives around, which Hong called a very high success rate.
Last month, Presley moved into a one-bedroom apartment in Los Angeles’ Silver Lake neighborhood. He has a Section 8 housing voucher, which means he pays a third of his Social Security income in rent and the rest is subsidized by the voucher. It’s been a long time coming. Presley spent four years on the waitlist for a voucher before he got to the top of the queue. 
He also serves on the “lived experience board” for the county’s Office of Diversion and Reentry, where he finds fulfillment by suggesting improvements to the programs he once belonged to – his way of helping others who are on their recovery journey. 
“I feel like I’m balanced,” Presley said. “I feel good. I feel like I accomplished a lot and came a long way.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada health officials warn of waning vaccination rate as measles becomes endemic in U.S.
description: While there haven’t been reported measles cases among Nevada residents this year, local health officials warn that the U.S. losing its measles elimination status makes local communities more vulnerable. Health officials also stress the importance of investing in public health infrastructure to ensure it can prevent the spread of a potential outbreak.   The P[...]
text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. Under the Trump administration, federal health officials have cut back the number of recommended vaccines, and more states are offering exemptions for parents who don't want to vaccinate children entering public schools. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)While there haven’t been reported measles cases among Nevada residents this year, local health officials warn that the U.S. losing its measles elimination status makes local communities more vulnerable.
Health officials also stress the importance of investing in public health infrastructure to ensure it can prevent the spread of a potential outbreak.  
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional office of the World Health Organization, concluded in 2000 that the U.S. had essentially eliminated measles because spread had been squashed for 12 months or more. 
After a year of surges across the country, the elimination status for the country was reversed Nov. 17. 
The news means “that now all of our communities are more vulnerable than they ever have been,” said Dr. Cassius Lockett, the district health officer at the Southern Nevada Health District.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 5,800 cases across the country as of Nov. 19, which Lockett notes is “more measles cases in the past 11 months this year than all of the entire previous 24 years combined.“
“That’s alarming,” he said. “We forget measles definitely spreads like wildfire, and I really truly mean that because it’s really good at infecting up to 90% of unvaccinated people it meets. It’s really good at that.”
The Nevada Division of Public and Behavioral Health said that measles cases in Nevada are rare. Prior to 2025 the state hadn’t had one since 2018.
“This makes Nevada 1 of 5 total states that has not had a reported measles case so far in 2026,” Daniel Vezmar, a spokesman with the division, said in an email. “The loss of U.S. elimination status does not mean that measles is spreading in Nevada, and it does not change vaccine recommendations or school requirements.”
Nevada is not among the list of states with reported cases, but a CDC map  shows Nevada completely surrounded by states with reported cases. 
“What I might take away from the map, even though it’s not showing any cases in 2026, what that map means to me — because we have to always be reminded how good measles is at finding unvaccinated people — is that measles does not recognize state boundaries,” Lockett said.
Though no cases have been reported among residents, the health district indicated in March that a visitor who visited the Las Vegas Convention Center tested positive for measles. 
The last reported residential measles cases in Washoe County was Dec. 25, 2025.
“Our neighboring states have seen activity surge,” said Chad Kingsley, district health officer for Northern Nevada Public Health. “Our history of high vaccine coverage has likely helped us by reducing the number of susceptible individuals. However, if vaccination rates continue to trend downwards while the number of outbreaks continues to rise, it could lead to even more exposures among susceptible individuals and, likewise, more cases.
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has a history of repeating false claims about vaccines and has opposed many vaccine mandates. DHHS this year began recommending fewer vaccines for children. Medical groups denounced the move.
Since then, the MMR vaccination rate in school-age children has since declined nationwide, reaching a new low of 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, according to KFF.
The MMR vaccination rate in Nevada is less than 90%, making the state “more vulnerable,” Lockett said. The herd immunity benchmark is 95%.
“The data is telling us, especially for Clark County here locally, that the coverage has declined over a four-year period by four percentage points,” Lockett said. 
More concerning, he said, is that some pockets within Southern Nevada have severely low vaccination rates. 
The health district provided Nevada Current with a list of the ZIP codes that had the lowest number of kindergarten students vaccinated for measles. 
The health district noted that “vaccination coverage estimates reflect kindergarten students attending schools within each ZIP code and may not represent coverage among children residing in those areas.”
At the bottom of the list was 89121, which had a less than 53% vaccination rate. While 858 kindergarten students are enrolled in schools in that ZIP code, only 451 were up to date on MMR vaccinations.
Lockett said he is worried about the rise in nonmedical exemptions for vaccinations, saying the number of exemptions in Clark County rose from 5.4% to 8.8% in a four-year period. 
Both health districts stressed they are prepared to respond to any potential surge in cases.
“Measles surveillance is already a high priority because of its potential to cause serious complications or death, particularly among vulnerable populations, and its infectiousness,” Kingsley said. “When we confirm a case, it becomes an all-hands-on-deck response involving multiple programs and collaboration with our healthcare providers”
There is “multi-layered approach to measles preparedness,” Lockett said, pointing to the wastewater surveillance systems as one part. 
“It could be a tourist. It could be a resident here. But it allows us to start thinking we have to ramp up and get prepared,” he said. 
Kingsley said that the national benchmark for local health department staffing is 1.7 epidemiologists per 100,000 residents.
“NNPH currently has fewer than one epidemiologist per 100,000,” he said. “With continued rising disease transmission and continued uncertainty around public health funding and diminished resources, securing sustainable financial support for epidemiology and contact tracing is a key to ensure our community has the resources needed to protect public health.”
Ahead of the 2027 Legislative Session, which starts Feb. 1, Lockett said state lawmakers should look at what it means to have sustained investment in public health infrastructure as some federal grants could end next year.
SNHD is planning for a federal Public Health Infrastructure Grant, which provided $21 million in funding to help pay for epidemiologists, laboratory professionals and disease surveillance investigators 
Lockett also said he has heard rumblings that lawmakers might consider a bill draft request to address the rise in non-medical exemptions.
“From my standpoint, I think it should be a balance of evidence-based considerations while balancing individual protections,” Lockett said.
