name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Kentucky politicos need to open minds – and primaries – to independent candidates and voters
description: As is the nature of politics, elections are followed by both sides doing whatever they can to claim victory. Democrats have been simply over the moon about a national shift towards their party, while Republicans in this state are pleased that they managed, more or less, to continue their dominance of politics in Kentucky.  However, […]
text:
On Thursday, the first day of early voting in Kentucky, people formed a line outside the Tates Creek Library in Lexington to make their choices. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)As is the nature of politics, elections are followed by both sides doing whatever they can to claim victory. Democrats have been simply over the moon about a national shift towards their party, while Republicans in this state are pleased that they managed, more or less, to continue their dominance of politics in Kentucky. 
However, both parties are ignoring the rapid growth of political independence among Kentucky voters. Perhaps because it is uncomfortable to dwell upon, both major parties tend to ignore the undeniably tidal wave of people who object to both Republicans and Democrats and then as a result, decide to go without any party at all.
The most obvious sign of this demographic shift lies in the simple number of registered independents in the state. Though Republicans have been rightly proud to have surpassed the number of Democrats in the state a couple of years ago, they are ignoring that most of the people leaving the Democratic Party are refusing to register with either side.
On its own, this simple statistic seems indicative of a potential seismic shift in Kentucky politics. Further data shows just what a big deal this could be. Throughout the state, the most recent midterms came with a marked shift in favor of Democrats. For instance, my own deeply Republican county voted for Charles Booker by 24 more percentage points than we did Kamala Harris. Even more significant, 73% of Kentuckians under the age of 29 voted for Booker.
None of this should be read by Democrats as a sign that the Commonwealth is about to suddenly go blue. But combined with the shift to independent voters, these statistics reveal that by and large Kentuckians — and young Kentuckians in particular — are increasingly nonpartisan.
In so many ways this is a positive development for the state of Kentucky. One-party dominance almost inevitably leads to poor policy outcomes, apathetic politics, corruption, and voter disenchantment. This has been the story of our commonwealth for the last century or so. As a state we have been dominated by one party and then another. To suddenly become a state independent of one party would no doubt be one of the greatest political developments we could hope for.  
However, Kentucky politics is arbitrarily and despotically designed to suppress the exact sort of political independence that our voters crave. Steps must be taken – in truth they will probably have to be forced upon a reluctant General Assembly – to actually open the state to true political independence. 
First, our primaries are stolidly closed, and the ability of third-party and independent candidates to make it on the ballot is designed to be nearly impossible. As a state we really must do better. We also – to an unusual degree – have the political institutions of our state crafted upon the assumption of Democrat and Republican dominance. Should a large third party or group of politicos with no party ever enter the state there would be no outlet for them to protect themselves from the two current parties. 
To improve Kentucky’s political system, our first goal should be to open our primaries. Allowing our citizens — regardless of their party affiliation or lack thereof — to take part in our primary elections is honestly a step towards having a basic level of democracy that we currently lack. In addition, we need to build more avenues to open elections and the institutions of political accountability in the state to independents.
The idea of an increasingly independent Kentucky is unquestionably deeply uncomfortable for both of our major parties. There can be little doubt that they would both prefer to do what they can to silo the average Kentucky voter firmly into their own political camp. However, political independence is a sign of true political maturity within the state. It should be embraced. If not, the voters may yet unleash the dread force of the popular will to force change upon a stultified and antiquated political system.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. school health committee OKs plan to require a nurse in every school; funding concerns linger
description: The School Health Services Committee backed a plan to require a nurse in every Virginia school, with some implementation flexibility and a one-year phase-in, despite concerns about forcing schools to cover the cost. The effort to staff every school is designed to close healthcare gaps by placing experts in schools to manage complex medical conditions. […]
text:
A school nurse takes a student's temperature. (Photo by Carl Court/Getty Images)The School Health Services Committee backed a plan to require a nurse in every Virginia school, with some implementation flexibility and a one-year phase-in, despite concerns about forcing schools to cover the cost.
The effort to staff every school is designed to close healthcare gaps by placing experts in schools to manage complex medical conditions. Under current law, Virginia permits school divisions to employ nurses, but it does not require them to.
Not every school has a full-time registered or licensed practice nurse. The most recent Virginia Department of Health data indicate that approximately 108 licensed nurse positions would need to be added statewide.
Most of the discussion at Wednesday’s committee meeting focused on the potential for an unfunded mandate, which some members argued could create a significant challenge for already underfunded school divisions.
The proposal could carry a fiscal impact of approximately $18 million if the nurse requirement were decoupled from the specialized student support personnel category.
“We can endorse this concept and also endorse the idea of a budget amendment, and appropriators will decide whether or not they’re going to add the additional money,” said Senate Education and Health Chair Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, at Wednesday’s committee meeting.
Under the proposed plan, which would not take effect until July 1, school boards would be required to designate one support position as a nurse for every school. For larger districts with schools of 1,300 students or more, the goal is one nurse per 325 students.
The cost would be covered under existing support personnel allocations within the Standards of Quality (SOQ) formula, which determines how much funding a school division needs, though some members worried that this would still amount to an unfunded mandate.
Committee staff noted that the waiver provision was expanded to allow school boards to request waivers based on good-faith efforts or other good cause, as determined by the Board of Education.
Schools may access Medicaid and other cost-sharing opportunities to help offset expenses.
Betsy Looney, a committee member who championed the concept, argued that nurses are essential for student health and that many schools already meet the requirement, in hopes of easing concerns.
Looney said. “It should not matter what zip code a student lives in; all students deserve to have access to a full-time licensed nurse in their school,” Looney said. “School nurses are essential in keeping children healthy, in school, and ready to learn.”
While many members expressed similar support for the concept, money remained a key concern.
“If we are going to mandate these things to our school systems, and we should, it has to come with the funding to ensure that they are successful,” said Sen. Stella Pekarsky, D-Fairfax.
Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, said he loves the idea, but the state has to pay for it.
“If we’re going to get the budget amendment, I am happy to vote for this when it comes across the House floor, but for now, until we can assure the funding is there, I have to stand on (that) we can’t send another unfunded mandate down,” Cherry said.
Lawmakers will begin discussing legislation and budget amendments in Richmond on Jan. 13.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: How a tiny Virginia grassroots group helped oust a 19-year congressman
description: Wittman Watch, a grassroots Virginia political advocacy organization, was born in a June 2025 Zoom call among a handful of ordinary citizens discussing how to make lawmakers accountable to their constituents. The group is not affiliated with the state’s Democratic party and didn’t receive any money from the party’s pocketbook. But on Election Day, it […]
text:
A "Where's Wittman?" town hall attendee holds up a sign outside the event held in Henrico County, April 26, 2025. (Photo by Ian Stewart/Virginia Mercury)Wittman Watch, a grassroots Virginia political advocacy organization, was born in a June 2025 Zoom call among a handful of ordinary citizens discussing how to make lawmakers accountable to their constituents.
The group is not affiliated with the state’s Democratic party and didn’t receive any money from the party’s pocketbook. But on Election Day, it helped unseat U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, who has represented Virginia’s 1st Congressional District for  19 years.
Warner wins fourth term, Luria ousts Kiggans in VA-02, Taylor triumphs in VA-01

Wittman Watch was an information engine, pumping out reams of reliable data at an awe-inspiring rate. The metrics representing the intense information campaign and targeted outreach by the small citizens’ group boggle the mind:

 From Aug. 5, 2025 through Election Day, the group posted 1,327 times across social media channels and a website,  racking up almost 2 million views. 
 In addition to running a website, Wittman Watch published 106 newsletters. 
 Roughly 3,000 Wittman Watch newsletter subscribers received timely updates on Rob Wittman and the 1st District from Jan. 8 through Election Day.

“It was the first time we had a group outside the party doing really high-quality research,” Jen Tierney, chair of the Historic Triangle Democrats, told me. “You could count on it. A campaign would have to pay tens of thousands of dollars for this kind of research.”
The thing is, the small Wittman Watch crew working out of their homes for dozens of hours a week never collected a dime. 
Nor were they formally affiliated with any political party or advocacy group, despite attacks from online trolls who accused them of being “Democratic Socialists” or “communists” paid to spread lies.
Wittman constituents host town hall in his absence to address immigration, federal funding concerns

“We weren’t trying to say all Republicans are bad and all Democrats are good,” said David Cassidy, who with his wife Shana and a few other folks, operated Wittman Watch. “We were rooting for the 1st District. We did this because we care about where we live.”
Wittman had stopped holding in-person public town hall meetings with rank-and-file constituents over the past year, as he voted for President Donald Trump’s budget and policies, which hurt people the congressman supposedly represented, the couple told me. 
While Wittman’s staff was “unfailingly polite” during limited mobile office hours, responsiveness to concerns remained a problem, the Cassidys said. 
Worse, Wittman Watch’s research showed that many of their representative’s stated positions did not align with his voting record or behavior.
“The hope was to flip a seat,” said Shanna Cassidy. “But our real goal was to shine a light on things people should know. We did shine that light, win or lose.”
In Republican-leaning Essex County, that light became a beacon for county Democratic chair Cayanne Yates. 
She initially saw Wittman Watch on a public Facebook account. Yates also ran a private Facebook account where Essex Democrats gathered called Wittman Watch.
“I called Dave and said ‘We have a Wittman Watch already,’” she told me. “He said his was different.”
It was, Yates discovered.
“They were smart people. They kept us informed,” she explained. “They gave us factual information. If someone said we had said something wrong, we showed them the record. I depended on Dave and Shana. Other Democratic chairs in Republican counties would use them, too. All of us moved the needle.”
The needle in question measured the number of Democratic votes cast in 2026.
Voting records show that while traditionally Republican counties in the 1st District voted to return Wittman to Congress, all but two of them saw more Democratic votes cast in 2026 than when Wittman ran for reelection in 2024. 
As election results across America showed, Trump’s failed policies – the Iran war, tariffs and inflation that drove up gas and grocery prices, along with mortgage rates – certainly brought out Democratic voters. But people on the frontline in Virginia’s 1st District say Wittman Watch made a difference. 
Rural GroundGame, a political group, got permission to use Wittman Watch content in two digital ad campaigns.
The facts Wittman Watch dug up allowed Democrats to start conversations with voters who were still deciding who to vote for or who assumed Wittman was so entrenched their vote would change nothing, Tierney told me.
Shannon Taylor was the first Democrat in nearly two decades to beat Wittman. She won by less than 3%.
Wittman won the 1st District by roughly 13% in 2022 and 12% in 2024. In 2026, Wittman lost by 2.8%.
In 2024, Wittman won James City County by 3% and the staunch Republican stronghold of York County by 15%. In 2026, Wittman lost James City County by 11%, a 14-point flip. He even lost York County by a few votes, a remarkable 15-point flip.
No one can measure the exact impact  Wittman Watch had on those numbers. But politics is a game of persistence and patience. In 2026, a small group of unpaid researchers from the upper Virginia Peninsula showed determination over a grueling 16 months and offered a model for regular Americans across the country who want to hold their leaders to account.   
Jen Tierney said it best: “They definitely mattered.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Commentary: Are you sick and tired of the Blueprint? You shouldn’t be
description: The Blueprint for Maryland's Future will come up for an overdue reboot next year, but that does not mean abandoning its commitment to all our children, writes Kalman Hettleman. We should renew our resolve and make courageous decisions for our schools.
text:
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future education reforms is halfway through a decade-long plan that has added billions of dollars in state funding annually for public schools -- making it a possible target as lawmakers face a $3 billion budget shortfall next year. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)One thing that didn’t change in the historic election of 2026 are prospects for a reboot of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future. It’s overdue.
An old saying goes, I am sick and tired of being sick and tired. That’s how so many people, for so many reasons, feel about the Blueprint.
And its fate is on the line in the upcoming session of the General Assembly.
Legislators will have to confront the Blueprint’s so many unrealized promises, so many cracks in its policy pillars, so much disappointment, and so many critical words said and written. (I’ve written more than my share, with about 10 articles going back to 2019.)
Still, we cannot in good conscience abandon the historic vision of the Blueprint, and the fight to achieve it. And we dare not abandon the extraordinary effort of state and local educators to make it work.
The evidence of the fraying of the Blueprint has been oft told, and need not be retold. In short, the Blueprint is too much to do in too little time with too little money.
We’re past the half-way point in its implementation, and there are some accomplishments, notably large expansions of pre-K programs and community schools. But overall progress in raising student achievement is far below the pace necessary to meet the Blueprint’s goals.
So, where do we go from here?




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




There has been endless public comment about the need to do “something” to strengthen, if not save, the Blueprint, but there has been little discussion of specific reform proposals.
I attempt in this commentary to suggest paths forward.

One, we have to resist the large cuts in Blueprint funding that Gov. Wes Moore and legislative leaders – because of the state’s looming fiscal deficits – threaten. The fiscal crisis is legitimate; still, Annapolis must recognize that the state should have no higher priority than honoring the commitments in the Blueprint.
Two, if cuts are unavoidable, they should largely occur by extending the timelines for implementation of Blueprint programs, not by curtailing or eliminating the programs.
Three, even if timelines are extended, priorities must be set here and now for the most cost-effective ways to spend available Blueprint funding. Moving funds from one program to another is a tough political bullet to bite: Each major program has its own entrenched supporters and political influence.

Still, the governor and General Assembly must make hard decisions about priorities. And, though less obvious, advocates must do the same. Advocates combine to support the Blueprint as a whole but they represent special constituencies and, by and large, have not coalesced around specific priorities.
I have two major recommendations. First, to shift money from concentration of poverty “wraparound” grants to early literacy and math instruction. And second, if necessary, I would further delay funding for grants to reduce teacher time in the classroom and increase planning time.
It’s devilishly hard to pull money from these programs, even for the short term. They are vitally important. Yet, research overwhelmingly shows that they would provide considerably less bang for the limited buck than other priorities.

Four, Annapolis should accelerate the search for revenue sources that would enable the Blueprint to provide an adequate education for all children as mandated by the Maryland Constitution. Because current funding is endangered, we overlook the fact that current funding already falls significantly short of the costs of true adequacy.

These recommendations will be controversial. Yet, they are straightforward, unlike the vague statements floating around Annapolis so far. Further, the governnor and legislative leaders have not acted transparently in the decision-making process; that should change.
The governor bears a singular responsibility for leadership. Yet he has not walked the walk; he has not used his political capital to strengthen the Blueprint. (In part, this seems to reflect the political fact that he can’t take much credit for the Blueprint since it was enacted before he took office. He can’t, like many other governors nationwide, claim ownership of a major school reform initiative.)
Let’s hope he still steps up. Ditto for legislative leaders. We should all be sick and tired of the Blueprint’s problems, but not weary of the struggle. We must renew our resolve, make courageous decisions, and honor the Blueprint’s commitment to all our schoolchildren.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Building On Hawaiʻi’s Investment In Wildfire Resilience
description: The hazard resilience portion of the green fee is could support that work.
text:
Wildfire is the one natural hazard we can exert some control over to minimize the likelihood of ignition and spread. Our everyday choices can help prevent fires from starting, and work across our lands, yards and homes can interrupt their spread.
The hazard resilience portion of Hawaiʻi’s “green fee” funding is an important start toward supporting that work.
Prevention begins with care around things that can accidentally ignite a fire: barbecues, campfires, fireworks, equipment and vehicles. Put campfires and cooking fires out cold, use equipment carefully, and keep vehicles off dry grass when driving, parking or idling. These actions help reduce wildfire risk wherever we live, work or visit.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

We can also influence what happens if a fire starts. Fires follow the fuel, and reducing or removing that fuel can interrupt their spread. Managing vegetation and clearing leaves and debris can reduce the pathways fire takes across the landscape and toward homes.
Making homes less vulnerable to ember-caused ignitions and managing vegetation across communities and the broader landscape are practical ways to reduce wildfire’s impacts.
Everyone has a part to play, and those parts connect. Residents can address hazards around their homes and yards. Through programs like Firewise USA™, neighbors can assess shared risks and develop plans linking household efforts with projects benefiting the whole community.
A wildfire in June 2025 prompted more than 100 evacuations and destroyed 330 acres in the homestead community of Kahikinui. (Photo posted to Maui County’s social media) Maui County/2025
Land managers can extend that work into fields, forests and open spaces through vegetation management and maintained fuel breaks. Conservation, ecological restoration and agriculture also reduce wildfire risk. Fire departments, counties and state agencies connect these efforts with planning, emergency access, infrastructure and public land management.
Working across property boundaries is what makes these individual efforts more effective. A neighborhood’s vegetation management project is strengthened by coordinated work on adjacent lands. Community plans become more useful when residents, emergency responders and neighboring landowners understand their roles and work together to carry them out.
This work takes coordination, technical assistance and resources. A community may have a plan but need equipment and crews to carry it out. Funding and supportive policies help turn these opportunities into work on the ground.
Resilience Work Needed
Government is beginning to make important investments in wildfire resilience, but public funding alone cannot reduce the risks we face. We all have a responsibility to do our part, whether that means preventing sparks, managing vegetation around our homes or working with neighbors and land managers on larger projects.
Green fee funding is beginning to support connected parts of the wildfire resilience work Hawaiʻi needs: community risk reduction and Firewise USA efforts, fire management planning for state parks, early wildfire detection, and coordination across these and other initiatives.
The Hawaiʻi Urban Interface, or HUI, Wildfire Grant Program shows what investment in locally developed projects can accomplish. Administered by the Department of Land and Natural Resources Division of Forestry and Wildlife in partnership with the Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization, the program awarded $1.8 million to eight organizations across five islands in 2026, up from $1.5 million in 2025. Projects include hazardous vegetation removal, managed grazing, fuel breaks, landscape restoration, emergency access improvements and community planning.
We all have a responsibility to do our part.
These projects reflect different needs across Hawaiʻi. Some communities are ready for larger landscape projects; others are focused on defensible space around homes, vegetation along neighborhood boundaries, or developing risk assessments and action plans. Other green fee priorities include a statewide fire management plan for state parks and Pūlama I Ka ʻĀina, a statewide early wildfire detection effort through the Department of Law Enforcement.
Across Hawaiʻi, communities are putting time and effort into this work. Some have high-impact, shovel-ready projects that need resources. Green fee investment via programs like the HUI Grant Program can help turn that preparation into completed work, reducing identified risks before the next fire starts.
Following through means maintaining what we accomplish. Vegetation grows back, fuel breaks need upkeep, temporary measures need to become sustained land management practices, and community plans need to reflect changing conditions. Sustained funding and supportive policies help preserve completed projects’ benefits and allow communities and land managers to take on new priorities.
Public investment brings responsibility to show where funding goes, what gets completed and how work will be maintained. Learning from these projects — including what helps them succeed and what gets in the way — can make future investments more effective.
The green fee’s wildfire resilience initiatives build on work already underway and provide an important start toward getting more done. Government investment is an important part of that effort, but lasting progress will depend on all of us doing our part to prevent ignitions, reduce the fuels that carry fire, and maintain that work together, across property boundaries and across our whole system.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: What Indiana counties and taxpayers can expect from 2027 property taxes
description: Indiana’s statewide gross assessed value is projected to grow 7.9% for 2027, while net assessed value is projected to grow just 1.6%. That gap matters to local officials budgeting for services and taxpayers trying to understand their next bill. Levy growth, debt decisions and school referendums will also shape how much local governments collect and […]
text:
A look at how property taxes could play out in 2027. (Getty Images)Indiana’s statewide gross assessed value is projected to grow 7.9% for 2027, while net assessed value is projected to grow just 1.6%. That gap matters to local officials budgeting for services and taxpayers trying to understand their next bill. Levy growth, debt decisions and school referendums will also shape how much local governments collect and who pays.
Property values are rising. Taxable values tell a different story.
The Association of Indiana Counties (AIC) and Policy Analytics found that gross assessed value, excluding tax-exempt property, increased in all 92 counties, partly reflecting rising market values. Eight counties saw growth below 5%, while 36 saw growth of 10% or more. Yet data from the Indiana Department of Local Government Finance’s Gateway system show net assessed value declining in 25 counties. Personal property assessed value fell 5.3% statewide, partly reflecting changes under Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025.
Gross assessed value is the value assigned to property before exemptions and deductions. Net assessed value is what remains taxable after they are applied. As SEA 1 deductions phase in, a homeowner’s taxable value may fall even if the home’s gross assessment rises. When the amount a taxing district needs to raise in property taxes grows faster than its taxable property value, its tax rate tends to rise.
Levy growth and debt decisions affect collections
Indiana’s statewide Maximum Levy Growth Quotient, which sets the growth factor for levies subject to the maximum levy limit, rises to 6% for 2027 after three years at 4%. Enhanced growth factors for 97 school corporations exceed 6% and reach as high as 10%.
A growing tax base can lower the tax rate needed to pay existing debt. If a taxing unit takes on additional debt while holding its debt service rate steady, the same rate raises more revenue from the larger base. Property owners whose taxable values rise may pay more even at the same rate. A higher debt levy subject to property tax caps can also push more bills to those caps. The resulting circuit breaker credits can reduce collections for local governments serving the same area, even if their own levies stay steady.
AIC found that certified debt and referendum levies totaled about $3.30 billion statewide in 2026, up $148.1 million, or 4.7%, from 2025. School corporations accounted for nearly 89% of the total, and their combined debt and referendum levies rose $171.8 million, or 6.25%. Additional borrowing that used taxable value growth to maintain target debt service rates was a major contributor.
Revenue decisions can shift costs to taxpayers
House Enrolled Act 1392 of 2025 expanded flexibility over financial institutions tax and commercial vehicle excise tax revenues. Beginning January 1, 2027, HEA 1210 extends that flexibility to additional excise tax distributions. The potential impact on property tax bills is greater because the amounts involved are larger. In 2025, schools alone received about $274 million in excise revenue, including $150.7 million allocated to debt and referendum funds. Reported financial and commercial excise tax revenues totaled $18.3 million and $11.4 million, respectively. If local units redirect revenue now used to pay existing debt and have no replacement funding, they may rely more heavily on property taxes to make those payments.
Tax increment financing uses property tax revenue from growth in assessed value within a designated area to finance projects such as roads and utilities that support development. Statewide, assessed value captured in these areas is estimated at $66.7 billion for 2027, up 15.2%. Higher tax rates applied to that growing base can generate more tax increment revenue than originally projected while the tax base available to overlapping taxing units grows more slowly.
New development can also increase demand for services such as road maintenance and emergency response. If no assessed value is released and local units fund those added services through the tax base outside the tax increment area, taxpayers outside the area effectively subsidize those services.
What taxpayers should look for on their bills
An individual bill depends on the property’s taxable value, combined local rates, credits and applicable caps. In November 2026, 38 Indiana school districts sought voter approval for property tax funding. A renewal can continue an existing obligation, while a new or increased levy can add to a bill. The timing depends on the approved measure and collection schedule. Voter-approved referendum taxes are outside Indiana’s property tax caps, so taxpayers who receive circuit breaker relief can still owe those taxes above the cap.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: The night the lights went out on my MBTA train home to Providence
description: An outbound MBTA commuter rail train heading toward Wickford Junction suddenly stopped inside a dark tunnel in Roxbury, just outside Jackson Square. Moments later, the power went out, plunging hundreds of passengers into complete darkness. No lights and no ventilation prompted a collective gasp, followed by silence. As the seconds became minutes, passengers [...]
text:
Passengers from MBTA train 6023 wait to enter Ruggles Station at 6:33 p.m. after departing the replacement train. (Photo by Dorree Ndooki Hosokawa for Rhode Island Current)An outbound MBTA commuter rail train heading toward Wickford Junction suddenly stopped inside a dark tunnel in Roxbury, just outside Jackson Square. Moments later, the power went out, plunging hundreds of passengers into complete darkness. No lights and no ventilation prompted a collective gasp, followed by silence. As the seconds became minutes, passengers tried to stay calm. Fifteen minutes later, parents were scrambling to arrange emergency childcare. The minutes turned into hours.
I was one on the train. I live in Providence, and since returning to grad school in September, I travel to Boston twice a week. I’ve grown accustomed to the frequent delays that come with commuting on the MBTA. The afternoon of Oct. 27, I was eager to take the express train home, leaving Back Bay at 3:52 p.m. Instead, my standard 90-minute commute became a five-hour ordeal.
At 4:06 p.m., the train came to a halt just past Ruggles, the next train station after Back Bay. It wasn’t until nearly two hours later, at 6:04 p.m., that passengers were directed to evacuate onto the tracks and make their way to a replacement train to bring them back to Ruggles. 
That meant passengers had to descend 4 to 5 feet onto the track, and then climb industrial stairs to reach the next train parked alongside it. Without ramps or accessible paths, riders with mobility challenges relied on conductors and fellow riders for help. 
One older woman seated next to me told me she was recovering from back surgery. She said MBTA staff almost dropped her as she attempted to board the replacement train. 
Confusion persisted back at Ruggles station, making it feel as though the entire ordeal was starting all over again. A massive crowd overflowed the platform around the station’s stairwell and spilled past the ticketing machines. Meanwhile, electronic departure screens consistently displayed optimistic arrival estimates. Yet no trains appeared.
I finally made it home at 9:06 p.m. thanks to a shared ride with another passenger who lived in Providence I had never met before, arriving to find home-cooked dinner waiting from thoughtful friends. But my routine commute should never have to depend on luck and the kindness of others to get home safely. 
The next day, I contacted Keolis Commuter Services, the company responsible for operating the MBTA’s commuter rail service, seeking an explanation. I heard back on Oct. 29 from the company’s media relations manager Jack O’Neill, who identified “slippery rail” as the cause of the disruption.
During autumn, fallen leaves get crushed beneath train wheels, leaving an oily residue that reduces traction and affects braking, O’Neill said. The MBTA uses laser systems and high-pressure washing equipment to address this seasonal hazard.



Quotation







My routine commute should never have to depend on luck and the kindness of others to get home safely.


But explaining why a train stopped is not the same as explaining why hundreds of passengers were not supported when it happened. And ironically, the MBTA’s new fall/winter schedule had taken effect just the day before the incident. Demonstrating that officials were organized enough to account for seasonal weather changes on paper, yet somehow remained entirely unprepared for the actual impact of autumn weather on the rails. 
Why were passengers required to navigate such a physically demanding evacuation with no accessible options provided?
Keolis has operated MBTA’s commuter rail system since July 2014 under a multibillion-dollar contract. The agreement expires on June 30, 2027, giving Massachusetts an opportunity to reconsider how its commuter rail system should be operated.
An email I received Nov. 3 from Keolis customer service stated:
“During this event, train crews and other staff members were present to help guide passengers and facilitate the transfer to alternate equipment as safely as possible. We recognize that such situations can be especially challenging for elderly passengers and those with disabilities, and we regret any difficulties experienced during the transfer.”
Although the company acknowledged the challenges, its statement failed to clarify what specific accommodations were provided, if any, or whether emergency protocols would be improved to avoid similar situations.
The MBTA has shortlisted three companies for the next contract: incumbent Keolis in partnership with British consulting and engineering firm Amey Ltd.; Mass Regional Rail; and a partnership between Transdev and Transport UK. The MBTA’s board of directors is expected to recommend which finalist should get the contract when it meets in December.
No matter who wins the contract, however, there remain concerns about the regulators who oversee it. 
A March 2025 performance audit by the Massachusetts Office of the State Auditor examining the MBTA’s administration of its Keolis contract between June 2020 and December 2023 identified significant problems. Among its findings, approximately $3.32 million in performance-based penalties that should have been assessed were not. The audit also identified incorrectly assessed penalties, errors involving performance incentive payments and weaknesses in reporting and documentation.
The MBTA must also ensure that contractual standards are frequently monitored and enforced.
We all deserve safe and reliable rail service, especially during emergencies.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan decarbonization roadmap presents path to reducing manufacturing emissions
description: As state leaders continue work toward mitigating Michigan’s contributions to climate change, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy has released a policy roadmap detailing how to cut greenhouse gas emissions in the state’s industrial sector while strengthening manufacturing.  Building on the MI Healthy Climate Plan and the state’s Com[...]
text:
The Ford Rouge Plant in Dearborn on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)As state leaders continue work toward mitigating Michigan’s contributions to climate change, the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy has released a policy roadmap detailing how to cut greenhouse gas emissions in the state’s industrial sector while strengthening manufacturing. 
Building on the MI Healthy Climate Plan and the state’s Comprehensive Climate Action Plan, the roadmap, prepared by clean energy consultants at 5 Lakes Energy, examines the factors involved in reducing emissions across Michigan’s industrial sector. 
Manufacturing provides more than 600,000 jobs and contributes $100 billion to the state’s gross domestic product annually, making it a central part of Michigan’s economy. 
However, industry accounts for 17.5% of the state’s greenhouse gas emissions, with the roadmap noting that Michigan will need to significantly reduce the amount of industrial emissions if it is to hit its 2050 goal of carbon neutrality.
Because Michigan’s industrial sector includes facilities of varying sizes, the roadmap emphasizes that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to decarbonization. 
At Michigan climate conference, Inslee says states still hold power on clean energy

While targeting decarbonization investments at major industries will allow the state to take a major step toward its goal, the roadmap notes that small and mid-sized manufacturers will need technical assistance, financing and help implementing these improvements. 
Although technologies to reduce emissions are available, the roadmap identifies high upfront costs, energy prices and production risks as major barriers to their adoption.
In developing their recommendations, consultants prioritized practical, actionable policies, distinguishing between near-term actions, long-term strategies and efforts that may require additional authority, funding, engagement with utility companies or federal government support.
During a Thursday webinar hosted by EGLE, Andrew Hoffmeister, a senior consultant on 5 Lakes Energy’s industry team, noted that the report also focused on four technological pathways facilities can pursue to reduce emissions: energy efficiency, electrification, fuel switching, and carbon capture, utilization and storage.
As for its recommendations, the roadmap suggests eight core policy measures.
The first suggestion was to establish recurring grants for industries to  modernize and decarbonize their technology. Hoffmeister also recommended the state develop additional financing options to support the grant program. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
To address the ongoing costs of producing clean industrial heat, 5 Lakes Energy also encouraged the state to create a clean heat production tax credit that would help facilities offset the cost difference between electricity and natural gas while incentivizing the use of clean heat technologies. 
The consulting firm also advised state energy regulators to look into developing an electricity rate structure for industrial facilities using technology that displaces fossil fuels.
“Of course, we don’t want those rates to work by shifting costs onto existing customers,” Hoffmeister said. “The objective would be to develop rates that reflect the actual costs of serving those loads and recognize the benefits that manufacturers using those technologies can provide to the system.”
While the first few recommendations focused on lowering the cost of lower carbon-producing products, Hoffmeister noted that 5 Lakes’ fourth recommendation was centered on creating a stronger market for those products. 
By establishing a “Buy Clean, Buy Michigan” program that utilizes the government’s ability to purchase materials, the state can create demand for lower-carbon construction and manufactured materials, the roadmap explains.
Expanding and targeting existing workforce programs to support modernization and industrial decarbonization programs was also a priority. 
The roadmap also advocated for an expedited permitting pathway for projects that reduce emissions and improve air quality.
Using recycled materials in manufacturing is another way to reduce industrial emissions, Hoffmeister explained, with the roadmap advising the state to expand its investment into recycling, support the development of a market for these materials and coordinate with the previously suggested “Buy Clean, Buy Michigan” program to create a demand for these materials.
In its final recommendation, the roadmap encourages the state to look into the feasibility of a cap-and-invest program. This would set a limit on the amount of greenhouse gases major industrial facilities can emit in a region while allowing the state to auction emissions allowances. 
The state can then use that auction revenue to provide funding for industrial decarbonization projects, workforce development, technical assistance or community investments, Hoffmeister explained.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Employers can pay disabled people pennies on the hour. Indiana is moving away from the practice.
description: Melody Cooper spent the earliest years of her career earning below the minimum wage, sometimes bringing home $25 a week while working for a sheltered workshop in Indianapolis. Shawn Fulton earned as little as half-a-cent for each part he sorted at a sheltered workshop in Grant County. “You’d have to do a lot to make […]
text:
Melody Cooper, a self-advocate for the Arc of Indiana, works at her desk at the Arc's Indianapolis office on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Melody Cooper spent the earliest years of her career earning below the minimum wage, sometimes bringing home $25 a week while working for a sheltered workshop in Indianapolis.
Shawn Fulton earned as little as half-a-cent for each part he sorted at a sheltered workshop in Grant County.
“You’d have to do a lot to make any money when you did that job,” he said.
For decades, employers could pay a sub-minimum wage through sheltered workshops.
The workshops function like modified assembly lines where people with intellectual and developmental disabilities spend hours sorting, assembling and labeling parts, often for a piece rate that at times amounted to as little as pennies on the hour — far below Indiana’s $7.25 minimum wage.
Evolving attitudes on employment
The federal Fair Labor Standards Act permits certain employers and vocational rehabilitation programs to pay disabled people a sub-minimum wage through a waiver known as a 14(c) certificate.
Work is typically performed in a sheltered workshop: a heavily supervised facility kept separate from mainstream workplaces, where people with disabilities are offered work and vocational training.
The sheltered employment model, popularized in the 1950s as an alternative to institutionalization for intellectually and developmentally disabled people who couldn’t find work elsewhere, is becoming obsolete as the rehabilitation programs serving them transition to employment in the community instead.
Only six community rehabilitation programs and one business in Indiana had active 14(c) certificates as of Nov. 1, according to the U.S. Department of Labor.  
Collectively, those institutions employ just shy of 400 people across the state at a sub-minimum wage, federal records show.
Thirty-six organizations held 14(c) certificates as recently as 2022.
The sheltered employment model itself is controversial: Some parents support them as a safe place for their adult children to spend the day, said Kim Dodson, chief executive officer of the Arc of Indiana, a disability rights organization. 
But other advocates like Dodson now see the concept as belittling of the skills disabled people can bring to the workforce.
“It wasn’t valuing people and showing them the respect that they deserve for their time and their skills,” she said. 
A ‘step ladder’ to work
Noble, a chapter of the Arc of Indiana, sunsetted its sheltered workshop in 2021.
Now, clients work with job coaches to find employment in the community or sign up for the Noble Employment Workforce, which employs its own team to perform housekeeping, lab support and other jobs for major companies like Eli Lilly and Corteva.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Noble CEO Wade Wingler said the program is similar to a sheltered workshop, with a key difference: workers are not paid a sub-minimum wage.
“I like to call it a mini-career step ladder,” he said. “There may be three or four different jobs they can do there, with the ultimate goal — if they want to — is to get to community-integrated employment, where they have a job that’s not in place specifically for folks with disabilities.”
The Arc of Indiana’s other chapters have been making the same transition.
“We are trying really hard to prove to businesses that hiring people with disabilities is good business, not just good charity,” Dodson said.
Still, Wingler said sheltered workshops are meaningful to a subset of people with disabilities, and the option should still exist for people who prefer it.
“Our philosophy is that we want folks to be as integrated into the community as they want to be, and that extends to employment,” he said.
Indiana supports transition
The gradual dissolution of sheltered workshops is part of a broader shift toward independent and community living for disabled people.
Dodson said disability rights advocates considered filing a lawsuit to end the practice of paying sub-minimum wages — until Indiana started to phase out the practice on its own.
Shawn Fulton, center, testifies before the Indiana House Ways and Means Committee. (Photo courtesy of the Arc of Indiana)
A 2017 law established competitive integrated employment as the preferred outcome for people with disabilities, with grants available for sheltered workshops to begin the transition.
The new model brings disabled people into traditional workplaces, where they are paid at least the minimum wage.
By next year, the Family and Social Services Administration’s Division of Disability and Rehabilitation Services will no longer reimburse facility-based prevocational services, which are often associated with sheltered workshops.
“Providers may decide whether to continue operating under a 14(c) certificate, regardless of the state’s funding decision,” said Marcus Barlow, spokesperson for the agency.
Still, fewer than 200 people were receiving services through a prevocational workshop as of Nov. 5, according to Barlow.
The agency is redirecting its resources to community-based prevocational services and employment supports.
“By focusing resources on these supports,” Barlow said, “Indiana is creating more opportunities for people with disabilities to pursue meaningful careers, achieve greater independence and earn wages comparable to those of other workers in the community.”
‘Self-advocates’ for independence
Cooper, who was born with cerebral palsy, said she left sheltered employment after six years when she found a job pushing carts at Meijer and eventually got married.
She’s happier now working as a self-advocate at The Arc of Indiana: traveling to Washington, D.C. and the Indiana Statehouse to testify about legislation affecting people like her. The job more closely resembles a traditional career — a far cry from the days she labelled parts for hours.
She sees her own trajectory as an example each time she hears someone say they can’t leave sheltered employment.
“They don’t know that they can have that same kind of life as anybody else,” Cooper said.
Fulton transitioned out of sheltered employment by becoming a self-advocate for the Arc too. Rather than sort parts for pennies, he does voter outreach and visits the Statehouse.
He recently finished a project informing people with disabilities about online romance scams, “because people with disabilities are prone to get scammed like that,” he said.
Fulton is glad to see fewer sub-minimum wage jobs in Indiana.
“I love it,” he said. “It should have happened a long time ago.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Budget secretary calls on school systems to prepare flat budgets for next year
description: State budget officials wrote school systems across the state this weekend, asking them to flat-fund their budgets for the coming year, when the state faces a projected $3 billion spending shortfall, according to a copy of the letter obtained by Maryland Matters.
text:
Budget Secretary Yaakov "Jake" Weissmann asked school systems to prepare their fiscal 2028 budgets based on the current year's spending, as the state prepares to grapple with four years of projected budget shortfalls. (Photo Bryan P Sears/Maryland Matters)School systems across the state are being asked to flat-fund their budgets for the coming year, when state leaders will be grappling with a nearly $3 billion projected spending shortfall.
The request was part of a letter sent Sunday to schools in all 24 jurisdictions by state Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann. He wrote that the administration is “proud” to support schools, but that the state will “enter this year knowing that there are hard choices to make,” according to a copy of the letter obtained by Maryland Matters.
“Working with all of you, the administration and the Maryland General Assembly will collaborate on long-term solutions to this challenge,” Weissmann wrote. “In order to ensure predictability in your budget process, I urge you to develop your Fiscal Year 2028 budget based on your Fiscal Year 2027 funding allocations.”
Weissmann cited “gains in academic outcomes” especially in high poverty areas. But his letter also notes that the pace of education spending is proving difficult for the state budget to absorb.
The coming year’s budget shortfall is expected to be the first of several years of projected budget deficits that would reach nearly $16 billion combined between fiscal 2028 and fiscal 2032.
In September, Weissmann asked state departments to trim their budget requests for next year by roughly 3%. He also asked Cabinet level agencies to prepare a 10% budget cut scenario.
State budget analysts warn that a moderate recession could add $1 billion to projected budget gaps over the next four years. (Chart courtesy Department of Legislative Services)
“While no final decisions have been made on the budget, this letter is an effort to ensure Maryland schools have an understanding of the fiscal realities facing the State heading into next session so they can plan ahead to best serve our students” Weissmann said in a statement to Maryland Matters.
“We’ll continue working with our partners in the legislature and school systems on a fiscally responsible budget that continues supporting our K-12 system,” his statement said.
Front and center are a looming projected shortfall for fiscal 2028. Larger structural deficits loom in each of the following three years.
The five-year combined deficit projections are an amount that is more than half the current year general fund budget and more than 20% of the state’s total fiscal 2027 budget.
Driving much of those shortfalls are the escalating costs of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future education reform plan. The state will exhaust money set aside to pay for its phased-in implementation in the coming year. After that, the general fund budget will cover billions of dollars in costs from the plan.
This year, the state sent $10.1 billion to local governments for K-12 education — slightly more than half of every dollar spent on public schools.
“Our state has increased funding by 45% to improve our schools, an increase of $3.2 billion between Fiscal Year 2020 and Fiscal Year 2027,” Weissmann wrote in his letter.
When increases to the state’s childcare subsidy are included, that increase grows to $3.7 billion.
The gap projected for the coming year is roughly 10% of the state’s general fund budget. Stagnant revenues and a flagging economy exacerbate the problem.
Local governments have called for changes to Blueprint funding requirements that are putting pressure on their budgets. But changes to the Blueprint have proven politically difficult. Often, the House and Senate have been on opposite sides.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Budget analysts last week offered a peek into how a moderate recession would factor into an already tough budget outlook. The results would add roughly $1 billion to those projected shortfalls.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and the leaders of the House and Senate face what all agree is a difficult 2027 session. Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) told the Maryland Chamber of Commerce that the session will include “a candid review of our spending.”
“We have to figure out where we can reduce spending and limit growth that does not hurt our economy or our most vulnerable,” Ferguson said. But we know if that’s all we do, if we just focus on this one year, we will come back again a year from now with continued uncertainty and lack of predictability.
“The real choice that we have this upcoming term and this upcoming year in particular is whether we keep lurching from one budget cycle to the next, or if we build something that is more durable and will be more difficult to accomplish,” he said.
Moore, Ferguson and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) recently agreed to develop a long-term budget plan to get away from continued structural budget gaps.
“My, and I hope the Senate’s, number one goal this session will be to work with our colleagues in the House and with the administration on delivering a true and real four-year plan that closes our structural shortfall and puts our finances on a sustainable path that is going to require difficult choices for every sector that government touches,” Ferguson said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Trump administration rescinds rule that would boost staff recruitment and retention for Head Start
description: Head Start programs just got another regulation change.  Last week, the Trump administration announced that it would roll back a Biden-era initiative to increase wages and benefits for Head Start teachers and staff.  In 2024, the Biden administration made several regulatory changes to Head Start Program Performance Standards in an effort to “support and stab[...]
text:
New rules from the Trump administration will revoke a past rule change that would require Head Start teachers and staff to get paid more. Here, a Head Start program on Silver Street in Manchester. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)Head Start programs just got another regulation change. 
Last week, the Trump administration announced that it would roll back a Biden-era initiative to increase wages and benefits for Head Start teachers and staff. 
In 2024, the Biden administration made several regulatory changes to Head Start Program Performance Standards in an effort to “support and stabilize the Head Start workforce and improve the quality of services.” Rules around wages and benefits, breaks for staff, and enhanced support for staff health and wellness, as well as improved mental health services integration for students, would be required to change. 
However, the Administration for Children and Families rescinded the mandatory wage and benefits increase for teachers, stating that the rule change was “not in line with the plain language of the Head Start Act” and is “costly and overly prescriptive to Head Start programs and staff.” 
Head Start is a federal program that provides early education and other comprehensive services, such as childcare and developmental supports, to low-income families with children ages 0 to 5, as well as expectant parents. It is considered the nationwide leader for early care and education and provides services for free to those eligible. There are 33 Head Start programs in New Hampshire.
The 2024 rule change would have required those programs to implement four standards for staff wages. Under these changes, programs would be required to: 

Update their salary scale or pay structure that promotes competitive wages for all positions;
Ensure salaries for educators were comparable to local public preschool or kindergarten teachers;
Ensure that all Head Start staff “receive pay that is at least sufficient to cover all basic costs of living” in their area;
And ensure that wages are comparable across Head Start and Early Head Start staff serving in similar positions with similar qualifications.

“For decades, the Head Start programs have been subsidized by low paid workers committed to the mission; now is the time to enact clear Federal requirements for staff compensation,” the Biden administration wrote in the Federal Register when it finalized the decision.
The regulation changes, which came amid “severe staffing shortages” of Head Start programs nationwide, were required to be implemented by Aug. 1, 2031. The Biden administration said the changes would help programs retain high-quality staff and that not doing so would disrupt relationships between teachers and families, negatively impacting children. 
The Trump administration estimated revoking the rule change would save over $2 million in future cost savings. It said increasing wages and benefits without more congressionally approved spending for Head Start would result in enrollment loss, since money would be moved away from staffing for classroom capacity and go toward higher salaries for existing staff.
“The current Administration has reconsidered the approach adopted in the 2024 final rule and does not believe that a one size fits all approach to staff compensation is the appropriate way to address these challenges, particularly when doing so may reduce access to Head Start services,” the Trump administration wrote. “Instead, ACF has determined that programs should have maximum local flexibility to design compensation packages and provide services that best meet the needs of their communities.” 
According to enrollment data collected by the National Institute for Early Education Research, Head Start enrollment nationwide and in New Hampshire has been declining, in part due to staffing issues, for the past 15 years.





Like private childcare programs, Head Start is required to maintain teacher-to-child ratios for safety and developmental reasons. When fewer teachers are employed in a program, classrooms cannot be filled in order to maintain the ratio.

In New Hampshire, five regional Community Action Partnership organizations manage Head Start and Early Head Start programs in their region and are responsible for their paychecks. None of the five CAPs responded to questions from the Bulletin about current employment numbers or whether they had started to implement the 2024 rule change into their programs before the new guidance. 
Based on yearly enrollment numbers and required ratios, however, as of 2025 at least 109 teachers would have been needed to staff Head Start programs in New Hampshire, down from at least 201 in 2011.
Programs can still voluntarily choose to implement the 2024 change requirement. However, with a separate impending rule change from the Trump administration to drastically overhaul Head Start curriculum, safety, ratio and administrative requirements, programs may be wary of taking on another set of changes.

title: A little-seen change in maternity billing codes could reveal a fuller picture of care
description: For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way. Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of […]
text:
A change to billing codes for pregnancy-related care beginning Jan. 1 will change the insurance process from one lump-sum payment billed at the end of a full pregnancy to separate services for the first time in 30 years. Providers say it won’t change much for patients, but will have many upsides for the overall provision of maternal care. (Photo by Noelle Straub/Stateline)For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way.
Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of the codes providers use to bill insurance and receive payment for their services. The five-digit codes are used to describe the type of care a patient received, including specific procedures and testing. 
While it isn’t expected to change much for patients, providers say it will make it easier to transfer care among clinics and hospitals, ease revenue burdens and perhaps most importantly, provide a more detailed and data-driven picture of maternity care nationwide that is opaque under the current system — though it remains somewhat unclear how private health insurance companies and Medicaid programs will respond to the change.
Black mothers around US say pregnancy, postpartum needs are often unmet

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, known as ACOG, worked with the American Medical Association to develop the new codes, which are then communicated to health insurers, including Medicaid. Pregnancies that began in the 2026 calendar year will likely still be billed under the global code, but those that have their first visit after Jan. 1 will use the new system.
Lisa Satterfield, vice president of practice, sustainability and workforce initiatives for ACOG, said the group started working on this change in 2022, after feedback from providers that the system was outdated.
“The way they were designed was for one provider to get billed from the very first prenatal visit to the very last postpartum visit,” Satterfield said. “It was not practical anymore.”
In the vast majority of cases, nothing should change about how much patients are paying for care, Satterfield said, because maternity visits are considered preventative care under the federal Affordable Care Act and not subject to cost sharing. Patients may just see more statements in the mail with an explanation of their benefits.
With the current global payment, no services are billed after the confirmation of a pregnancy until the last postpartum visit, Satterfield said, which leads to a long delay in the revenue from each visit in between. On average, Satterfield said, the global payment from health insurers to OB-GYNs or midwives was about $3,500 for an entire pregnancy, regardless of whether it was a patient with relatively few or no complications along the way, including delivery, or someone who needed many more interventions and had a long, complicated delivery.
“It didn’t matter, they got paid the same, regardless of the services that were being provided,” Satterfield said.
If patients switch among providers or clinics for various reasons, sometimes a provider isn’t even aware that the patient had seen someone else until the claim is denied, leaving that provider to try to negotiate with the insurer or ask the other provider to share their payment. Many times, it just results in lost revenue for the health providers, she said.
The current bundled code also has allowed some insurers to try to lump other services into that same payment, she said, such as the insertion of a birth control implant, which some women opt to do after delivering a baby, that otherwise could be charged separately.
Study shows sharp increases in maternal deaths over two decades

Dr. Barbra Fisher, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist in central California, said there is a separation of billing if someone is referred to the specialist clinic for various reasons in pregnancy, such as a fetal anomaly or high-risk conditions like gestational diabetes or hypertension. Some specialist clinics use the global code for their services as well, she said, but they also have the option to bill separately for services. The biggest changes will come for standard OB care rather than specialists, she said.
But she added there are some concerns among obstetrics providers about how insurers will adjust to the changes, particularly private health insurance.
“I think practices are worried because they just don’t know what the reaction is going to be,” Fisher said. “We don’t know what state Medicaid payers and private insurance will do.”
Dr. Mark Simon, chief medical officer of the national OB Hospitalist Group, said the insurance providers he spoke with earlier in the fall didn’t have set plans yet on how they would respond to the changes, so there are still unknowns. But he said he sees many upsides to the changes, including how closely researchers can track the details of obstetrical care and its variations by patient.
Maternal mortality rates in the United States remain stubbornly high compared with peer countries. In 2024, the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 17.9 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, compared with 8.4 per 100,000 in Canada and 5.5 in the United Kingdom. That rate in the U.S. also varies significantly by state and race, with a much higher rate of 44.8 deaths per 100,000 births among Black women.
Simon said the global payment made it difficult to know how to improve those rates when there was little information about how many times a patient was seen during pregnancy and afterward, what kind of delivery and labor management they had, and what types of providers they saw.
“You lose a lot of quality data that you need to help systems improve,” he said. “We’re trying to improve the healthcare system with one hand tied behind our back, because we don’t have full information on what’s actually happening.”
The new data will lag behind until 2026 pregnancies are out of the global billing system, he said, but once full data is returned starting late in 2027 and into 2028, Simon thinks there will be many opportunities to make more informed decisions about maternity care.
“I’m very hopeful that with this kind of information, we’ll be able to direct efforts to areas where we identify weaknesses, as it were, that were leaving patients behind,” he said.
Fisher said she’s looking forward to the change as well.
“This has been a long time in the making, and I think it will be much more equitable. I think it will be good for the patients and good for the practices,” she said.

title: Eviction prevention program faces uncertain future as funding runs out
description: Maine’s eviction prevention program is running out of money just two months after opening applications for the year, prompting advocates to call for a larger, permanent investment as thousands of households seek rental assistance. MaineHousing and Portland-based nonprofit Project Home announced Wednesday that the program’s current waitlist is expected to exh[...]
text:
There are over 150,000 renter households in Maine, a majority of which are "cost burdened" and pay more than a third of their salary for rent. (Photo by Nevada Current)Maine’s eviction prevention program is running out of money just two months after opening applications for the year, prompting advocates to call for a larger, permanent investment as thousands of households seek rental assistance.
MaineHousing and Portland-based nonprofit Project Home announced Wednesday that the program’s current waitlist is expected to exhaust the $11 million lawmakers allocated earlier this year. The announcement comes as advocates plan to push the incoming administration and Legislature to make the program permanent and significantly increase its funding starting next year.
The need to shorten the application period “definitely demonstrates how urgently people needed the support,” said Rep. Ambureen Rana, a Democrat from Bangor who sponsored the eviction prevention program bill earlier this year. “We’re recognizing that it’s about to run out of funds, and honestly it’s not surprising, given that it was funded at the level that it was.”
According to MaineHousing’s dashboard, more than 2,500 households applied to the program since Sept. 21. A vast majority of those are still being processed, but 187 applicants have received benefits and 114 have been rejected. 
The program targets Mainers making less than 60% of the area median income and who pay less than 125% of their area’s fair market rent. People who live in subsidized housing or use federal housing vouchers are not eligible.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since the program launched in 2024 as a response to increasing post-pandemic evictions, it has helped more than 1,400 households avoid eviction “and the devastating ripple effects it can have on employment, education, and family stability,” according to Victoria Morales, executive director of Project Home. 
When it launched as a pilot in 2024, the Legislature allocated $18 million, with participants receiving $800 a month in rental assistance. Rana had proposed earlier this year increasing the funding to $25 million, but lawmakers ultimately reduced it to $11 million. The program in its current iteration offers an average monthly rent benefit of $573 and average overdue rent benefit of $4,180. 
The program has already proven to be effective. MaineHousing’s 2026 report showed that the number of evictions dropped for the first time since 2020, from 5,977 in 2023 and 4,663 in 2024 to 4,057 last year (based on 11 months of data).
“It is safe to assume that the program has contributed to this decline,” the report states. 
Morales agreed. “It’s rare that you have a program anywhere that in the first full year has that much of an impact,” she said. “I just hope that that’s what everyone is thinking about: If we can stabilize households, we also prevent them from deeper crises of becoming unhoused, of needing shelter services, of then needing emergency room services.”
Morales and Rana both told Maine Morning Star they hope the new governor and incoming Legislature will make the program permanent and increase the state’s investment in eviction prevention. 
Neither have spoken with Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree’s team, but both said they are encouraged by her experience working on affordable housing. Pingree declared housing to be one of her administration’s priorities on the campaign trail, and her spokesperson Mary-Erin Casale echoed that on Friday, reiterating her commitment to invest  $100 million in housing programs.
“The governor-elect is committed to working with the Legislature and stakeholders to determine how best to use that investment, and to find a way to support eviction prevention efforts as part of the broader housing agenda. No Mainer should live without a safe, stable home,” Casale said.
“Eviction prevention programs, especially for seniors, families with children and other vulnerable Mainers, help households avoid instability and homelessness.”
Rana said even the $25 million she had initially proposed this year may not be enough going forward, given people’s economic precarity and the increased cost of living. Morales estimated that between $26 and $30 million would be needed to meet the statewide need.
“The fact that this program is closing within two months, it really does show how big the need is and how big that investment is going to have to be,” Rana said.
“Our hope is that this administration realizes that 78,000 households in crisis — who are lower-income renter households — is really too big to fail for this economy,” Morales added. “We’d be spending a lot more on the potential crisis than we would be on actually stabilizing people’s housing.”

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Developers have proposed a data center in Windsor Township in Eaton County, WILX’s Brayden Willis reports, with developer Related Digital planning an open house on the project next months.

Updates

Lenox Township officials canceled a public hearing for a 1,400 acre rezoning request for a suspected data center, after a local business sued developers for alleged deficiencies in their rezoning application and issues with the public notice for the project, Lucas Smolcic Larson reports for MLive. The hearing has been rescheduled for  6 p.m., Friday, Dec. 4.
The University of Michigan Board of Regents approved the $795 million Los Alamos computing center project, Planet Detroit’s Brian Allnutt reports, with Regent Paul Brown acting as the sole vote against moving forward with the project.

Legislative Action

U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence was among a group of Democrats who joined labor advocates, political organizers and environmentalists calling on the next Congress to demand a federal moratorium on data center development until guardrails can be put in place.

News of Note

A new study published in Nature Sustainability analyzing the operations of 403 hyperscale data centers across the United States determined these facilities could be using the same amount of energy in a year as states like Michigan, Simmone Shah reports for TIME.
Sinclair Statewide Political Reporter Remington Hernandez breaks down what Michigan lawmakers could do about data centers, as Democrats take control of the Michigan House in January, while retaining a majority in the state Senate and holding onto the governor’s seat.
