name: Mississippi Today
title: By electing Scott Colom, Mississippi has done what most other states have not
description: U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., speaks with journalists alongside Scott Colom, Mississippi's Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Colom won the November election and will serve in the U.S. Senate starting in January, along with Warnock and five other Black senators.
text:
It has been difficult in recent days to tune to a television news show and not see Scott Colom or at least people talking about Scott Colom.
He has become sort of a national sensation – the next big thing for political nerds and perhaps even for many who take a more casual interest in politics.
In the Nov. 3 midterm election, Colom, a Democratic district attorney from the Lowndes County area, upset Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black person elected through popular vote to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi.
The watershed election has to be viewed against the historical backdrop of Mississippi’s sordid racist history.
Regardless of one’s political views, it could be argued that Colom’s victory provides Mississippi a good dose of needed redemption.
Mississippi is only the third state from the footprint of the old Confederacy – and all of the lingering segregation and racism that followed the downfall of the Confederacy – to have elected a Black person to the United States Senate.
South Carolina elected Republican Tim Scott in 2012, and Georgia elected Democrat Raphael Warnock in 2020.
Perhaps more impressive in terms of Colom’s accomplishment is that only nine Black people before this year have ever been elected via popular vote to the United States Senate.
Come January, Colom will join five other Black senators, including the aforementioned fellow Southerners, Warnock and Scott. Being sworn in with Colom will be Juliana Stratton, the second Black woman elected to the Senate from Illinois and the fifth Black woman ever elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
Illinois has elected the most Black senators – three – and had another who was appointed to succeed Barack Obama after he was elected president.
Only nine states – California, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, South Carolina and now Mississippi – have elected Black senators.
It is worth noting that a Mississippi native, Laphonza Butler, was appointed to fill one of California’s U.S. Senate seats in 2023 after the death of Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Butler service until December 2024 and did not seek election to the post.
It is also worth noting that Mississippi was the only state after the Civil War during Reconstruction to have Black citizens serve in the U.S. Senate – Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce. They were selected by the state Legislature instead of via popular vote.
Again, regardless of one’s politics, it is fair to say Mississippi is a trendsetter in this particular instance.
But an important question for us here in Mississippi is: What took us so long to elect a Black person to a statewide office?
Before Colom, Mississippi had not elected a Black person to statewide office since Reconstruction, despite currently having the largest percentage of Black residents in the country – around 38%.
Mississippi has had some Black candidates get relatively close in statewide election efforts.
In the 2003 race for state treasurer, Democrat Gary Anderson, who was the state fiscal officer under Gov. Ronnie Musgrove, garnered 46.6% of the vote in a losing effort against Republican Tate Reeves, a political unknown running his first campaign.
In November 2018, former U.S. Agriculture Commissioner Mike Espy captured 46.4% of the vote in losing a special election to Hyde-Smith, who had been appointed by Gov. Phil Bryant earlier that year to serve temporarily after fellow Republican Thad Cochran retired. Hyde-Smith and Espy competed to fill the remaining years of Cochran’s term.
Two years later when Hyde-Smith was running for a full six-year-term, Espy received 44.1% of the vote in a rematch.
It should be pointed out that the 2020 election was a presidential year and the highest vote-total election in the state’s history. In that election, Espy captured nearly 100,000 more votes in a losing effort than Colom received in his recent winning effort.
Election turnouts are normally much lower in midterm elections than in presidential elections.
Mississippi is one of few states that elect a governor, other statewide offices and state legislators between the presidential and midterm elections.
So, next year Mississippi will elect eight statewide officials, including for the open office of governor because Reeves cannot seek a third term.
A big question now: Will another Black candidate replicate Scott Colom’s success to win a different statewide office?

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont state employees’ health insurance premiums will increase 9% next year
description:
The union representing state employees is using the news of the increase to call on the governor to implement hospital price caps for their plans, as some other states have.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont state employees’ health insurance premiums will increase 9% next year.
text:
Vermont deals with loss of health care subsidies after last summer’s federal budget bill. Photo from Adobe Stock

The roughly 26,000 Vermonters who receive their health insurance through the state employees’ plan will see a 9% increase in their healthcare premiums starting Jan. 1, according to a memo from the Vermont Department Human Resources. 
This increase matches last year’s 9% raise, which followed steep, double-digit increases between 2023-2025, according to Ted Fisher, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Human Resources. He said that this year’s rates are a hopeful signal that Vermont has “turned the corner on the trend in annual increases for our state employees.” He is hopeful that it means next year could see a “lower or no increase next year.” 
Still, the state employees’ union has used the announcement as an opportunity to call on the governor to fast track price caps on hospital care for those on the state employee plans. In June, Gov. Phil Scott vetoed the Legislature’s effort to implement this kind of price cap for school employees and Affordable Care Act marketplace plans.
“I think the governor needs to really put reforming the healthcare system at the forefront of his agenda,” Steve Howard, executive director of the Vermont State Employees’ Association, the union representing state workers, told VTDigger.
Though Vermont is in the process of putting price caps on hospital prices for all commercial health insurance in the state, the union is urging Scott to sign an executive order to implement these lower prices tied to a benchmarked price of what Medicare pays for the service for state employees. Montana established this type of reference-based pricing for its state employees’ health plans in 2016, but has since sunset it. Oklahoma, South Carolina, West Virginia and eight other states have some version of the price caps for public employee health plans.
Vermont is unique among states in its emphasis on price caps across the entire commercial market. 

READ MORE

Scott supports the price caps for all payers, not just a subset of insurance plans, his spokesperson Amanda Wheeler told VTDigger, adding that the governor signed the broad reference-based pricing plan into law. It’s the same reasoning he gave for vetoing this spring’s attempt to fast-track the plan first for public schools’ and marketplace plans. 
“Implementing it for just one subset of the insurance market would mean other Vermonters would be excluded from those affordability gains, while adding further complexity, inequity, and cost to an already complicated healthcare system,” Wheeler wrote in an email.
A 2024 report by the independent healthcare regulator that was ultimately tasked with implementing Vermont’s reference based pricing plan, analyzed the impact a price cap for hospital charges could have on public school employees’ and state employees’ healthcare plans. They found that if the state kept hospital charges for those plans at two times Medicare rates — rather than the status quo of an average 289% of Medicare’s charges — the state could have prevented $400 million of claims payments during the five-year study period. In 2022 alone, the cap could have cut $79 million.
Health insurance, broadly, is a measure of the cost of services times the number of services used. Less costly hospital claims means the insurer needs to collect less in premiums to cover them, which means the state would pay less to cover those premiums.
For the VSEA plans, the state covers 80% of employees’ premiums.
In 2027, the least expensive plans available to state employees have a monthly price tag of $747 for an individual, $1,494 for two people and $2,054 for a family of three or more. 
“That eats into people’s wages at a time when — because of the president’s tariffs and the economy and the price of gas and the war in Iran and all that stuff — it’s harder and harder for state employees to make ends meet,” Howard said. 
The increase comes as other insurance groups across Vermont are starting to see the impacts of efforts to lower costs. In August, plans sold on the state’s Affordable Care Act exchange received some of the smallest increases they’ve ever had. That’s due to reduced hospital budgets, reductions in BlueCross BlueShield’s 2026 contract with the state’s largest hospital network, and a 2025 law that capped the cost of some expensive drugs. The same forces influenced Vermont public school employees’ health insurance plans, which expect to see some of the smallest premium increases in more than a decade.
Fisher, with the state’s human resources department, said that the state employees’ plans are on track to follow those trends. Before the pandemic, the plans had very small annual increases, he said, but following it, they saw a “spike” in claims and utilization — which is not uncommon as many people went without optional care during the height of COVID-19. 
That spike pushed the state employee medical fund into a deficit, he said, which $18.5 million of FY25 state general funds have worked to stabilize. This year’s rates seek to do the same kind of stabilization.
“As a result of this money and utilization rates stabilizing, we anticipate the fund being in surplus by the end of FY28 (barring unforeseen economic/healthcare factors),” Fisher added.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont state employees’ health insurance premiums will increase 9% next year.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Commentary: Believe it or not, there are things to be thankful for in Arkansas politics
description: Political journalists are the worst people to ask for hopeful news. It’s hard to find optimism among a group of people whose job is covering the latest political fight or crisis. That’s especially the case over the past couple weeks, when a wayward router in El Dorado can ground thousands of planes and online glitches […]
text:
(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Political journalists are the worst people to ask for hopeful news. It’s hard to find optimism among a group of people whose job is covering the latest political fight or crisis.
That’s especially the case over the past couple weeks, when a wayward router in El Dorado can ground thousands of planes and online glitches affect banking, email and other critical systems on a near-daily basis.
But in honor of the approaching Thanksgiving holiday, it feels fitting to highlight some trends in Arkansas politics that offer some hope as the year comes to an end:
 
A chance for bipartisanship on healthcare 
The Trump administration’s decision to not renew Arkansas’ hybrid Medicaid expansion threatens coverage for thousands of low-income residents and could destabilize an already shaky healthcare system.
That’s the bad news.
The good news is that Democrats’ gains in the Legislature mean both parties are going to have to work together to come up with a solution. With Republicans losing the 75-vote supermajority needed to pass most budget bills strictly on party lines, working across the aisle will be crucial.
If recent history is any guide, Arkansas has come up with some of its best health solutions under divided government. The state’s hybrid approach to Medicaid expansion was crafted as a compromise between Republicans who controlled the Legislature and then-Democratic Gov. Mike Beebe.



Let us know what you think...


 


That kind of cooperation can also be seen under former Gov. Mike Huckabee, a Republican who championed and signed legislation creating the ARKids First children’s health insurance program and an indoor smoking ban with the help of a majority-Democrat Legislature.
Coming up with a solution that wins support in the Legislature and the federal government’s approval — under a tight 6-month timeline — is a long haul. But such cooperation isn’t unheard of in Arkansas.
 
A growing consensus on reining in AI
Another potential area for bipartisanship in the Legislature could come next year on the need to address growing concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence.
Polling conducted during the midterms showed the widespread concerns Arkansans have about the impacts of AI as well as data centers.
With President Donald Trump dismissing calls for guardrails at the federal level, it’s increasingly likely the state will have to step in.
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has indicated a willingness to break from Trump on the issue, writing in her new book about the need to protect children and the workforce from AI’s consequences. And Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin has also sued OpenAI, saying the company has misled consumers about the safety of ChatGPT.
The moves don’t guarantee consensus on every issue surrounding AI and technology, especially over what additional restrictions data centers should face in the state.
But it at least signals there’s more common ground on finding a way to protect Arkansans from the technology.
 
Hope for protecting civic institutions
The state public television commission’s decision to reverse course and not break ties with PBS was a victory for supporters of programs ranging from Sesame Street to Ken Burns’ documentaries.
It also demonstrated that there’s support for civic institutions like public television and libraries that have faced Republican-led attacks over their content and programming.
That support was also on display in this month’s midterm elections in Saline County, where voters rejected an attempt to cut funding for the library system that’s been the focus of book-banning efforts.
Challenges still remain, as Arkansas public television’s decision to drop two PBS programs from its lineup. And the state’s libraries still face an attempt to tie their funding to restricting minors’ access to materials, though a state board’s decision to revise that proposal indicates second thoughts.

title: Gov.-elect Foulkes announces in-person listening sessions
description: Even after receiving more than 1,200 constituent ideas through her transition website, Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes wants more feedback. Foulkes’ transition team on Friday announced a four-part listening tour to hear from Rhode Islanders in person about how to improve state government under her administration.  The events are open to the public, but RS[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes, shown outside her polling place on Election Day, will hold a four-part listening tour to seek feedback from constituents. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Even after receiving more than 1,200 constituent ideas through her transition website, Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes wants more feedback.
Foulkes’ transition team on Friday announced a four-part listening tour to hear from Rhode Islanders in person about how to improve state government under her administration. 
The events are open to the public, but RSVPs are requested beforehand.
All four sessions take place from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Dates and locations are:

Tuesday, Nov. 25, at Elmwood Community Center in Providence
Monday, Nov. 30, at the Newport campus of the Community College of Rhode Island 
Tuesday, Dec. 1, at Warwick Public Library
Wednesday, Dec. 2, at Woonsocket Education Center 

Submissions can also be sent to Foulkes’ transition website, where she is also soliciting expressions of interest from people who want to work in her administration or serve as a volunteer on a state board or commission.
Foulkes takes office on Jan. 5. A separate, 501(c)4 organization was set up the day after the Nov. 3 election to raise money for her inauguration, although details on events, schedules and cost have not been determined, Jon Carvalho, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ transition team, said.

title: Salesianum Advances to 2026 DIAA Class 3A Football Semifinal with Win over Cape Henlopen
description: Salesianum defeated Cape Henlopen, 44-6, to advance to the semifinal round of the 2026 DIAA Class 3A Football State Tournament.    WILMINGTON, Del. — Salesianum football scored 37 points in the first half and defeated the Cape Henlopen Vikings, 44-6, in their quarterfinal game Saturday, November 21. Salesianum scored five of its six touchdowns in the first h[...]
text:
The Salesianum offense lines up in the shotgun formation during their quarterfinal game against the Cape Henlopen Vikings on November 21. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Salesianum defeated Cape Henlopen, 44-6, to advance to the semifinal round of the 2026 DIAA Class 3A Football State Tournament. 
 
WILMINGTON, Del. — Salesianum football scored 37 points in the first half and defeated the Cape Henlopen Vikings, 44-6, in their quarterfinal game Saturday, November 21.
Salesianum scored five of its six touchdowns in the first half with four of them coming from the rushing ability of junior EJ Cotton. Cotton set the tone for the game on Sallies’ first offensive possession, breaking off a 70-yard run down the right sideline that put the Sals in the red zone. Cotton followed the long run with a 15-yard dash into the endzone and provided Sallies with their first lead of the game.
Cotton continued his massive first half with two more red zone touchdown runs, scoring from ten and five yards out. His fourth touchdown was scored on a 76-yard sprint down the left sideline that increased Salesianum’s lead to 30-0 more than four minutes into the second quarter. Cotton finished the first half with 246 rushing yards and four touchdowns.
“I came into the game knowing that they [were] a good team, we practiced hard all week. I just knew that they couldn’t stop me because I just train so hard,” Cotton said after the game.
The success of the run game allowed senior quarterback Brady Nabb and the Salesianum offense to be selective on when to attack through the air. Nabb threw four passes in the first half and completed two of them for 46 yards. Nabb’s second completion scored the Sals’ fifth touchdown on a 35-yard pass that ended with Tysir Jones catching the ball in the endzone with a little more than three minutes to play before halftime. 
Cape Henlopen leaned on the running game without starting quarterback Jameson Tingle and put together a couple strong drives in the half. The Vikings made it into Salesianum territory on half of their first half offensive possessions, but the Salesianum defense stopped those possessions before the ball could get within the ten-yard line and didn’t allow a score. Sallies entered halftime with a 37-0 advantage.
Following the halftime break, each team gained possession one more time. Salesianum scored its final touchdown on a one-yard run by backup running back Michael Brock on a drive that took up the whole third quarter. The Vikings scored their lone touchdown in the fourth quarter on a pass from freshman quarterback Robbie Myers to senior receiver Stephen Sivels. The Vikings’ score was the final play of the game.
Salesianum is moving on to the semifinal round for the fourth consecutive season and are set for a semifinal matchup against the Smyrna Eagles. The Sals defeated Smyrna in the semifinal round last season and defeated the Eagles in the regular season this year. The last time Smyrna beat Salesianum was in 2022.
“We’re going to keep the same momentum, it’s never good enough,” Cotton said. “We’re going to keep practicing hard over and over again until we make it to the championship.”  
Cape Henlopen’s 2026 season concludes with a 7-4 overall record and a sixth consecutive appearance in the DIAA State Tournament.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Army plans to go ahead with detonation by Nov. 24, according to DOJ filing
description: The U.S. Army intends to invoke an emergency exclusion to skirt a court-issued pause and intentionally detonate nearly 5 tons of lead-containing explosive material in southeast Iowa by Tuesday.  A federal court issued a stay on the detonation permit but the U.S. Department of Justice said, in a response to the lawsuit filed late Saturday, […]
text:
Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. (Photo via Google Earth) The U.S. Army intends to invoke an emergency exclusion to skirt a court-issued pause and intentionally detonate nearly 5 tons of lead-containing explosive material in southeast Iowa by Tuesday. 
A federal court issued a stay on the detonation permit but the U.S. Department of Justice said, in a response to the lawsuit filed late Saturday, that the Army intends to operate without the permit, citing the “immediate risk” that the degraded lead azide “will explode” when temperatures drop in the next several days. 
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” the DOJ response said. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
The DOJ filing also includes a deposition from an Army explosives expert, dated Nov. 21 in Middletown, who details the state of the lead azide and its volatility to temperature changes. Lead azide is an explosive material used in detonators such as blasting caps.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The detonation, which is anticipated to release “some lead-containing particles” into the air, was initially scheduled for Nov. 20 but following significant public concern, a lawsuit from environmentalists and criticism from public officials, Army officials postponed the detonation to Monday, Nov. 23. 
Since the postponement was announced, the Army has not released details such as the time for the rescheduled detonation, nor updated predictive maps showing areas that could be impacted with lead particles in the air or settling on surfaces. 
The City of Fort Madison posted publicly Saturday that it was informed the detonation would take place either Monday or Tuesday and shared a document with modeling from the National Weather Service that showed the plume was anticipated to travel southwest of Middletown, if detonated on Monday.
This is a change, due to weather patterns, from the Army’s original models for the Nov. 20 detonation which showed the lead could travel nearly 100 miles northeast of the site. 


Safety precautions
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has a page dedicated to safety measures Iowans can take. Some actions include:
— Staying indoors and keeping windows and doors closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation if you are in a potentially impacted area
— Turning off heating and cooling systems, or placing on recirculation mode
— Using a portable air purifier
— Washing outdoor surfaces with visible dust using soap and water
— Washing hands before eating; taking shoes off at the entrance of homes
Additionally, Iowans in the impacted areas can gather soil samples before and after the detonation and get them tested independently for lead. Households can also give the Army or University of Iowa researchers permission to take samples on their property.


Public outcry over the intended detonation, which many — including state officials — only found out about less than a week before it was slated to occur, has centered on concerns of lead exposure. Lead is toxic to humans and animals, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and is especially dangerous to children and pregnant persons as it can damage the brain and nervous system. 
The Army has held that intentionally detonating the 68 drums of lead azide is the best way to contain the explosive, which it says is at risk of spontaneously detonating due to its deteriorated state. 
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the DOJ said in its filing with the U.S. Appellate Court for the Eighth Circuit. 
Environmental groups are suing EPA over the emergency permit it granted the Army to allow the intentional detonation. The permit also required the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant to notify the public about the plans and collect baseline and subsequent soil and wipe samples to determine the impact of the detonation. 
Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice, in the lawsuit, alleged EPA did not adequately consider alternative containment methods, like chemical neutralization or transporting the material elsewhere to be detonated. 
In a letter to Gov. Kim Reynolds Friday, EPA addressed the alternative containment options the Army considered and ultimately deemed were more dangerous than intentional detonation. Chemical treatment, according to the letter, was ruled out because removing the lids on the barrels to administer the chemical could be enough disturbance to cause a detonation.
Reporting from The New York Times Saturday revealed the Army contracted with MuniRem Environmental, shortly after discovering the crystallization of the lead azide, to treat the material with chemicals. But the contract was canceled around two months later. 
The DOJ notice of the Army’s plan to detonate argues that the court’s stay on the permit does not “prohibit the Army from acting under a separate legal authority.” 



Quotation







“The environmental and health interests Petitioners seek to protect plainly are better served by a controlled detonation than by an uncontrolled explosion.”


– A filing from the U.S. Department of Justice in response to a lawsuit from environmental groups.


The filing holds that the condition of the lead azide and the approaching change in temperature constitute an immediate risk that allows the Army to operate under an exclusion of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. 
The act says its standards don’t apply to treatment or containment issues when there is an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment, as determined by an explosives or munitions response specialist. 
Environmental groups did not immediately respond to a request for comment early Sunday. But when asked Friday about the possibility of the Army acting thus, Thien Chau with Earthjustice said the exclusion to the law had “an incredibly high bar, and we strongly urge the army not to rely on it.”
Army explosives specialist says state of lead azide presents ‘immediate threat’
The DOJ notice includes a declaration of support from Col. Aaron Teller, a commander of an Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal group, who said the 68 drums of lead azide “pose an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property or the environment.” 
Teller said the Army’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit  inspected the barrels of lead azide in April 2026 and determined there was crystallization in all but 10 of the barrels. 
According to Teller’s account, Iowa Army Ammunition Plant contracts with American Ordnance to visually inspect the drums monthly and to open the drums on an annual basis to check levels and refill the ethanol/water mixture which helps “sustain stability.”
Teller said the lids have not been safe to remove since the crystallization was discovered. This means September 2025 was the last time American Ordnance refilled the ethanol-water solution in the drums. Teller said the lower ethanol concentrations of the drum makes them more susceptible to freezing, which in turn can “increase sensitivity of the crystals and cause an uncontrolled detonation.” 
“Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction,” Teller wrote. 
The bunker where the lead azide drums are stored is surrounded by a sand bag barrier nearly two stories tall in preparation for the detonation. Teller said an uncontrolled detonation would lack the safety precautions the Army has planned for the intentional detonation, including alerting the public ahead of time and wetting the material around and on top of the detonation area, to limit the spread of lead. 
Further, Teller said an uncontrolled detonation would not guarantee all of the material is destroyed, meaning potential secondary detonations could be necessary.
The account from Teller, the DOJ said in the filing, is the “requisite determination” allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide without the EPA permit. 
“An uncontrolled detonation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast—harm that cannot be undone,” the lawsuit said. “The environmental and health interests Petitioners seek to protect plainly are better served by a controlled detonation than by an uncontrolled explosion.” 
DOJ said that while the Army intends to operate without the permit, it will “remain consistent” with the terms of the EPA emergency permit and its mitigation measures.
Part of the EPA permit required the Army to distribute plume impact estimates 48 hours before detonation, again 6 hours before and then every hour up until the detonation. Per this alert schedule, the Army should have issued new maps Saturday if it planned to detonate on Monday. 
As of early Sunday, the Army had not provided updated maps nor the official time it plans to detonate.
The DOJ is expected to file a response in opposition to environmental groups’ lawsuit before noon on Sunday, per a request of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Coloradans would be left to live with the wreckage of permitting bill
description: In the wake of an election in which Americans voted overwhelmingly to rein in President Donald Trump’s agenda, Congress is considering a bill that would remove legal guardrails on a president that has repeatedly shown his cards. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — which recently passed in the Senate — would […]
text:
Oil and gas infrastructure is seen on the Roan Plateau in far western Colorado. (Courtesy of EcoFlight)In the wake of an election in which Americans voted overwhelmingly to rein in President Donald Trump’s agenda, Congress is considering a bill that would remove legal guardrails on a president that has repeatedly shown his cards.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — which recently passed in the Senate — would allow the Trump administration to fast-track permits for activities like oil and gas development, mining, pipelines, data centers, transmission lines and ICE detention centers while significantly weakening bedrock environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The bill also includes “certainty” provisions that would make it more difficult — if not impossible — for future presidents to rescind or even modify unlawfully issued permits, no matter how harmful they are. If the bill passes, we could very well be stuck with the fallout from the Trump administration’s two-year-long smash-and-grab of our public lands, wildlife habitat and resources, all to benefit the fossil fuel and tech industries.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ordinary citizens in Colorado and the wider West would be left to live with the wreckage. For example, the administration is already planning to sell oil and gas leases and allow mining on vast swaths of our national forests, Bureau of Land Management lands, and national monuments (putting Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante at risk), followed by fast-tracked permitting for the ensuing extraction. The Roan Plateau, public lands in northern Colorado’s Routt County, and thousands of acres of land with historic, cultural and religious importance to Indigenous peoples are all at risk. Drilling could occur with minimal, if any, analysis of its effects on Tribes, wildlife and habitat, clean water or recreation, and all without public comment.
Data centers could sprout on lands sold or leased by the Interior Department, something it has already started to do. Just this month, the Interior Department revealed in its strategic plan that it wants to “decrease the size of the federal estate” by offering public lands for sale. We could also be stuck with ICE detention centers like the one that the Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition and GreenLatinos have challenged in Hudson, a suit that is based on National Environmental Policy Act violations. These permitted projects could proceed, even if the court rules the project is unlawful.
Not surprisingly, many Americans haven’t heard of BAAJA. It was released on Sept. 30 during the barrage of wall-to-wall election coverage. Congress is trying to jam this bill through without a single hearing and with no public debate. That’s nothing short of astounding for a bill this consequential. When voters learn more about the bill’s impacts, they oppose it.
Many of BAAJA’s supporters assert that it will unleash development of clean energy resources like wind and solar, and it’s true that the provisions facilitating construction of new transmission lines to serve those sources are important. But let’s not forget who we’re dealing with here: Trump said just recently that he would not permit wind projects, dubbing them “losers.” As long as this administration oversees the permitting process, the fossil fuel, pipeline and tech industries that have been lobbying intensely for this dog of a bill will unleash destructive oil and gas drilling, pipelines and data centers. Why would we put trust in an administration famous for the enrichment of itself and its allies, and for its hostility to clean energy?
Finally, one of the most egregious aspects of the bill is the way it excludes the voices of Tribes that will suffer devastating impacts to lands and cultural sites that are central to their way of life. The bill rolls back decades of progress, albeit imperfect, we have made in respecting Tribal interests and traditional knowledge.
There are examples of the federal permitting process taking too long, and the need to address that is legitimate. So let’s fix that problem, without sacrificing the environmental laws that have kept our lands, our waters and our communities safe in the process. Sen. John Hickenlooper was 1 of only 15 Democrats to support passage in the Senate, despite these significant blows to environmental protection. When the House votes, Colorado’s members should defend — not give away — the special places that their constituents value so highly.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Calls mount to shutter Osborn Correctional, one of CT’s oldest prisons
description: Current and former officials say Osborn has outlived its usefulness, but the state says it has no plans to close the prison.
text:
Dallas Bailey said his body hasn’t felt the same since the years he spent incarcerated at Osborn Correctional Institution.
Roughly a year after arriving at the prison, Bailey reported significant gastrointestinal bleeding, medical records obtained by The Connecticut Mirror show. A physician recommended a colonoscopy or an at-home test, but it would take another 10 months — and a trip to the emergency room as the symptoms resurfaced — before he’d get the necessary testing.
Doctors eventually diagnosed Bailey with an H. pylori infection, a bacterial stomach infection that can spread through contaminated food or water, among other avenues. Bailey believes he contracted the infection from Osborn’s drinking water, a claim also made by plaintiffs’ lawyers in an eventually settled 2016 class action against the state over conditions at the prison. 
“When you first get there, you realize, ‘Oh, this water is crazy.’ You can smell it. Then, after a while, you just have to drink the water,” Bailey said. “It’s sad, but you come to accept the fact that don’t nobody care.”
Osborn is among the oldest Department of Correction facilities. People incarcerated there describe living conditions like discolored, foul-smelling drinking water, extreme heat and delayed medical care. Current and former officials say the prison is past its useful life.

Supporters of efforts to close Osborn Correctional Institution held an October rally outside the Central Office of the state Department of Correction in Wethersfield.

Criminal justice reform organizers are now pushing for the state to shut it down. The “Close Osborn Coalition,” made up of multiple advocacy groups, plans to petition state officials for a phased-in closure of Osborn during the upcoming General Assembly session.
The timing is strategic — an effort to capitalize on momentum from near-unanimous support for measures passed in 2026 to improve prison healthcare, said Alicia Strong, one of the organizers leading the effort. Strong also serves as co-director of the advocacy organization CT People’s Survival Programs.
“This is not a place that anybody should live or work,” Strong said. “It seems like something that could bring a lot of different people who have a lot of different views about the prison system together under the banner of public health.”
But the effort will face an uphill battle. 
DOC has no plans to close Osborn, according to spokesperson Andrius Banevicius. Even those who believe the prison should close say that doing so would require navigating a host of complicated logistics, including where to house the men currently incarcerated there.
Closing a prison
Osborn, located in Somers, is one of Connecticut’s oldest and largest prisons. Opened in 1963 as the Connecticut Correctional Institution-Somers, it originally served as the state’s maximum-security prison. In 1994, it was reorganized into a medium security institution and renamed Osborn Correctional Institution. 
Today, Osborn houses roughly 1,100 individuals, down from a peak population of over 2,000 between late 2007 and early 2008. The prison includes an inpatient medical hospital and one of the main hubs of the Correctional Enterprises of Connecticut, the state’s prison industry program that manufactures goods like clothing, furniture and signs.
“The facility has run its course,” said Abraham Santiago, acting head of the Office of the Correction Ombuds, a state agency charged with overseeing DOC. “Department of Correction has buildings that have been closed that are in far better condition than Osborn.”
Banevicius said DOC is “committed to maintaining the condition of all its facilities including the Osborn Correctional Institution, to ensure a safe and functional environment for staff and incarcerated individuals alike.” A $120 million infrastructure improvement project is currently underway to bring new energy efficient windows and doors to Osborn, Banevicius added.
Santiago does not consider the major expenditure a mark of success.
“You’re basically borrowing money and throwing it at a building that should have been closed decades ago,” Santiago said. “Imagine what $100 million would do for communities.”
Closing a prison requires the coordination of several state agencies, including DOC, the Office of Policy and Management, as well as the governor’s office. Connecticut has closed a handful of facilities in the last decade, including Willard Correctional Institution in 2023 and Northern Correctional Institution in 2021. In both cases, the state cited the declining prison population and cost savings opportunities as reasons for closure.
Criminal justice advocate Barbara Fair said that years of sustained organizing efforts helped to bring about the closure of Northern. Fair led the campaign, working with organizations like Yale Law School and regularly publishing op-eds, holding public hearings and hosting press conferences over the course of a “couple of years.”
“Hopefully we won’t need that [long] with Osborn,” Fair said. 

Denise Paley sits in her home in Guilford on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Paley serves as the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) Shoreline co-president. Credit: Connor Sharp / CT Mirror

Denise Paley, whose son is incarcerated at Osborn, said she supports calls to close the prison but would like to see it done in such a way that doesn’t exacerbate issues at other facilities. 
“Osborn needs to close. It does,” Paley said. “But if they’re going to close Osborn and relocate everybody to another horrible facility, I don’t advocate for that.”
Paley said that ideally she’d like to see a new facility built. As of now, the Close Osborn Coalition is proposing to reopen certain facilities previously closed by DOC that they believe are in better shape than Osborn, including Gates, Bergin and Enfield Correctional Institutions.
Former DOC Commissioner Scott Semple said he doesn’t disagree that Osborn has outlived its usefulness, but reopening DOC’s shuttered facilities would require all kinds of fortification. And replacing a facility of Osborn’s size and complexity could cost the state upwards of $1 billion, he said. 
Prison labor
Some people, like Santiago and Bailey, believe the effort to close Osborn will face additional challenges because of the goods produced by men working in its shops. 
The facility is one of the main production hubs for the Correctional Enterprises of Connecticut, or CEC, which produces furniture, chairs, laser engraving and clothing available for purchase by state agencies, municipalities, the federal government and certain nonprofit entities.
“They’re never going to shut Osborn down,” Bailey said. “It makes too much money. That’s where the factories are.”

Dallas Bailey at the Waterbury barber shop where he works on Dec. 18, 2025. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror

Roughly 200 men incarcerated at Osborn work making mattresses and clothing used by the correctional system. People incarcerated in Connecticut producing such goods make hourly wages of $0.90 to $1.50, according to a 2018 report by the Office of Legislative Research.
“The real reason the state has been slow at closing down Osborn is because of the infrastructure in place. The 13th Amendment allows for a lot of this — the fact that we pay people slave wages to do this work,” Santiago said.
DOC spokesperson Banevicius said the program provides incarcerated individuals with valuable vocational training, leading to better employment opportunities as they transition back to the community. Strong said she, too, has heard feedback that the jobs are important to the people who do them, and any plans to close Osborn would need to consider how to maintain those opportunities.
Former DOC commissioner Semple said both points have some truth.
“There is an argument that we use inmate labor to produce stuff at a low cost in terms of what they’re paid. But at the same time, you want some kind of structured activities and responsibilities,” he said.
Public health concerns
Public health concerns at Osborn are not new. Most recently, people formerly and currently incarcerated at the facility have voiced dissatisfaction with the water quality and episodes of extreme heat.
Banevicius said the water is tested monthly by an independent contractor and consistently meets all applicable Connecticut Department of Public Health safety standards.
A 2018 complaint filed against DOC in federal court by current and former individuals incarcerated at Osborn alleged they were exposed to toxic substances in several now-closed housing buildings and forced to drink and shower in contaminated water. 
The complaint described the facility’s water as “brown, cloudy or opaque, with a strong, acrid and offensive odor and taste” and alleged it caused skin rashes and gastrointestinal distress. It also alleged that at least 10 individuals had reported H. pylori infections while at Osborn, the same stomach infection Bailey contracted. But a plaintiffs’ expert said there was no accepted testing method to establish that Osborn’s water caused the infections.
A plaintiff’s expert also tested the water and found it was potable and met all federal and state standards. The case settled in 2024, with the state paying $5,000 to each plaintiff without admitting liability, according to a settlement agreement provided by the state Attorney General’s office.
But Bailey said the water issues were widely acknowledged during the four years he spent at Osborn — part of his eight-year sentence for assault and attempted robbery charges. Correctional officers bring their own water, and even therapy dogs drink bottled water, he said — a point also alleged in the 2018 complaint.
“It’s not something that’s swept under the rug,” Bailey said of the water quality. “Everybody knows.”
Bailey said his digestive issues have improved since his release from DOC custody in 2025, but he still experiences frequent stomach pain and sudden urges to use the bathroom immediately after eating.

Former Correction Ombuds DeVaughn Ward testifies at a hearing of the Correction Advisory Committee in July 2026. Credit: Katy Golvala / CT Mirror

Osborn is also one of just three DOC facilities that isn’t fully equipped with air conditioning, leading to sweltering temperatures during the summer months. 
A $25 million project is underway to install HVAC systems at Hartford and Bridgeport Correctional Centers, the other two facilities lacking AC. But the state does not have plans to bring facility-wide AC to Osborn.
A January 2024 Department of Administrative Services feasibility study estimated that a “full facility retrofit” would cost between $76 million and $85 million. DOC estimated the actual project cost — including DAS fees, contingency fees and construction management — would be closer to $120 million.
Instead, the state has spent $2.4 million over the last two years to bring 18 “industrial grade air conditioners” to Osborn, DOC spokesperson Banevicius said. 
Former Correction Ombuds DeVaughn Ward visited Osborn on July 1, during a multi-day heat wave that swept the East Coast. 
Using a temperature gun, Ward clocked a temperature of 85.6 degrees in the mess hall and kitchen. A cell in the C block registered a temperature of 81.5 degrees. The portable units DOC installed mostly provided cooling to the housing units, Ward said, but not in other areas, like the corridors, mess hall or kitchen.
“Even though they’re pumping in AC, there are really questions about the efficacy of whether it’s really working in some housing units,” Ward said at the time. “I have long said, and I’ll continue to say, that [Osborn] is a facility beyond its useful life. That’s as a whole, not just with respect to the air conditioning.”
One person incarcerated at Osborn wrote in testimony to the state’s Correction Advisory Committee in January that the extreme heat in the summer months makes him feel like he’s being suffocated.
“The cell is so hot it literally feels like there is no air in the cell to breathe, throughout the night I have to constantly get up to drink water from my sink and wet a towel to lay across my stomach and chest in order to fall asleep for a few hours before my cellmate and I would have to repeat the process.” 
Paths to closure
Organizers zeroed in on this moment to rally for Osborn’s closure in order to capitalize on momentum following legislative successes during the 2026 session, Strong said.
A law passed nearly unanimously contained several measures related to prison healthcare reform, including the elimination of medical copays for people in DOC custody as well as the expansion of the correction ombuds’ health oversight capabilities. 
The Close Osborn Coalition is still gaining momentum. Organizers meet regulary and have hosted a few rallies. But it’s unclear whether organizers can build a sustained campaign that could ultimately lead to the prison’s closure.
Mike Lawlor, professor of criminal justice at the University of New Haven and former House chair of the state Judiciary Committee from 1997 to 2011, said closing Osborn would not be easy.
“Is Osborn a facility that really should be shut down based on the facility? Yes. Is there a way to actually do it? Maybe, but it’s complicated,” he said. 
Lawlor expects advocates will raise proposals this session that could decrease the overall DOC population, which could make space for people currently residing at Osborn. These include bail reform, which could reduce the pretrial DOC population, and parole eligibility for people who committed crimes when they were young.

Denise Paley holds of her son Ellis Tibere in Guilford on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. The photo of Tibere was taken before his high school homecoming just months before his incarceration. Credit: Connor Sharp / CT Mirror

Both Fair and Paley say they also have faith in the possibility of reform under the agency’s new commissioner, Sharonda Carlos, who took over the post in May. 
“Her mind and heart are both in the right place,” Paley said. “She’s leading with compassion and I think she has really good ideas about what needs to be improved.”
DOC declined to make Carlos available for an interview.
Bailey isn’t holding out much hope. He said he thinks Osborn shouldn’t exist but he doubts the state will take the financial hit of closing the production shops. In general, though, he doesn’t believe in abolishing prisons. He just thinks incarceration should look different from what he experienced at Osborn.
“I’m not against prisons,” Bailey said. “It should be humane.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Remember that time when technology was a boon to humanity? Yeah, I miss it, too.
description: The word of the year is “human.” That’s according to the Cambridge Dictionary, which each November chooses a word to suit the year. In 2025, the online dictionary gave us a real clunker of a word, “parasocial.” What the hell does that even mean? It apparently describes a one-sided (read: fictional) relationship people have with […]
text:
Plaques affixed to the side of the Pioneer 10 and 11 space probes, launched in 1972 and 1973, display images of a nude woman and a nude man with a hand upraised in greeting, along with a diagram of the solar system and our position in the galaxy. (Photo by NASA)The word of the year is “human.”
That’s according to the Cambridge Dictionary, which each November chooses a word to suit the year. In 2025, the online dictionary gave us a real clunker of a word, “parasocial.” What the hell does that even mean? It apparently describes a one-sided (read: fictional) relationship people have with celebrities, fictional characters or chatbots. Think of Chiefs fans and Taylor Swift. Or me and every song on Neil Young’s 1972 album, “Harvest.” Yep, that’s parasocial.
Despite a few misses like “parasocial,” the dictionary gets it right some years. For 2020, they nailed it with “quarantine.” Another winner was 2016’s “paranoid.” But we were right.
The dictionary, which is associated with the University of Cambridge, England, chooses the word for the year based on how often it is looked up by users and taking into account the prevailing cultural zeitgeist, the spirit of the age.
“The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines,” the dictionary declared in the announcement for 2026. The word, derived from Latin, as the dictionary notes, is from the 1450s, and relates to the qualities possessed by people “as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
Fair enough, but to that I would add background from Eric Partridge’s 1958 dictionary of word origins, that notes “human” is related to the word “humus,” or “of the ground,” and is also associated with “humility.”
My copy of the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary generally agrees with Cambridge. The “shorter” OED is in two volumes with a combined 3,472 pages. I say my copy because my wife, Kim, also has the two-volume dictionary. We wound up with multiple copies of books, including “The Crying of Lot 49″ and various translations of “The Odyssey,” because we merged separate but similar personal libraries when we married in 2011.
There are a plethora of gods, animals and machines in our combined library. My side of the collection has more machines, and there are more animals in Kim’s, but it is a celebration of difference and not a sign of disagreement. And, I must add in this age of blurred boundaries, every damn book we own was written by a bona fide human.
If you are unclear about the nature of humanity, please refer to images of the gold-anodized aluminum plaques affixed to the side of the Pioneer 10 and 11 space probes, launched in 1972 and 1973. Each has an image of a nude woman and a nude man with a hand upraised in greeting, along with a diagram of the solar system and our position in the galaxy defined by the position of our sun relative to 14 pulsars. These craft were the first man-made objects to leave the solar system. Pioneer 10 is on a trajectory that will take it to the vicinity of the star Aldebaran, while Pioneer 11 is headed to the constellation Aquila. Their journeys will take several million years.
This rumination on words and libraries and humanity is a necessary preface for what follows. I have written about artificial intelligence and its data center creches often over the past several months, but I could not drag myself again to the fray without a reminder of the joy of human accomplishment. I would argue with editors of the Cambridge Dictionary about their description of AI blurring the boundaries between humans and machines, because in my view the debate has sharpened, not softened, the lines.
This year has witnessed a groundswell of resistance to AI and data centers. Of at least 40 ballot initiatives across the country on data centers, only one locality — tiny Harwood, North Dakota — gave its approval.
The big tech backlash has been driven by factors that include the fear of higher utility prices, a desire to protect the environment, and concerns about the threat AI poses to human welfare and creativity.
A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters described concerns about data centers as crucial or major factors in their decisions. This was similar to the number of respondents in the recent Kansas Speaks public opinion survey who said they had concerns about energy and water usage connected to data center construction.
Kansans in three cities voted Nov. 3 to adopt data center bans.
In Ottawa and El Dorado, voters overwhelmingly approved 10-year moratoriums on data centers. In both of those towns, the bans passed by landslides, with more than 70% of the vote.
In my town of Emporia, voters also approved a decade-long ban on data centers and battery energy storage systems. In the days leading up to the Nov. 3 election, Emporia (and Ottawa) voters were showered with mailers attempting to persuade them to vote against the ban, partially paid for by the Defend US PAC, which is aligned with Republican causes.
“The activist group pushing to ban technology jobs in Emporia is working straight from the Bernie Sanders-Mamdani Playbook,” claims one of the mailers. “Don’t be fooled. If we pass their ban, they won’t stop there. Which jobs will they try to ban next?”
On the other side:
“If we follow their plan, EMPORIA WON’T HAVE ANY JOBS AT ALL.”
But Emporians weren’t buying it. The data center ban was adopted, with about 60% of residents in favor.
The ban might be rendered moot by a pending court case. The city sued to have the measure, which was placed on the ballot by petitions circulated by Emporia Neighbors United, deemed administrative in nature rather than legislative. If a judge finds the measure to be administrative, meaning that it was already or more properly addressed by city policies or regulations, the Emporia ban would be nullified.
The data center issue had roiled Emporia since it was announced June 2, creating a rift between business and civic leaders and average citizens concerned about what the project would do to utility rates, the environment and the character of the town. Public relations surrounding the project was a disaster from the beginning.
The legal entity behind the proposal, Kanza Park Place LLC, identified the “master developer” as Gary Pinkston, a West Coast businessman who had filed a massive personal and business Chapter 11 bankruptcy case in May 2026. Pinkston later swore in a bankruptcy proceeding that he had no personal interest in the Emporia data center project, just days before he received a $3 million wire transfer from Kanza Park Place.
The mystery surrounding ownership of Kanza Park Place has been a cause of citizen concern about the project, which seeks to turn about 1,000 acres on the west side of Emporia into a “digital campus.” The end user of the proposed data center has not yet been chosen, according to a Kanza Park Place spokesman.
Although Kanza Park Place is a cipher, that hasn’t stopped it from attempting to exert its influence on the legal challenge filed by the city. Just two days after the election, the company filed a motion to intervene in the case.
“Kanza has a substantial interest in the subject matter of Emporia’s litigation,” the motion stated. “Kanza has already taken substantial steps towards constructing what the proposed ordinance would prohibit as a ‘high-impact data center’ by optioning the necessary land, having said land rezoned and having the DI-O (digital infrastructure overlay) applied, and paying Evergy for an energy study.”
The amount Kanza paid the utility is not cited. The document, filed on behalf of Kanza by a trio of Topeka lawyers, contains no hint as to the actual owner of Kanza Park Place.
An election postmortem, conducted recently by the Regional Development Association, a group wholly funded by the city and which touted the data center as Emporia’s economic savior, was a bitter exercise in attempting to prove the association right about the claimed negative effects a ban would have. The Emporia Main Street director said one investor unrelated to data centers had already walked away from the city, while others were delaying decisions.
If any of the association members attributed the economic handicap to a loss of trust in community leaders, it was not reported by the local news media. The implicit message sent to the public by the RDA was to blame voters and to complain, this is why we can’t have nice things.
Instead of coming to terms with voter anger about data centers, city leaders — and Kanza Park Place — are doubling down on a widely hated project that has been poorly described and whose ownership remains cloaked in mystery. They appear oblivious to the fact that the midterms represented a referendum on AI in general, and that big tech was on the losing side.
Harwood, North Dakota, was the exception, but its 845 residents at least knew who the owner and operator of the $3 billion data center would be: Applied Digital, a Texas firm.
The lack of transparency with the proposed Emporia data center is symptomatic of similar projects across rural America, where the identity of developers is a tightly held secret. A new study accelerated environmental concerns, because it found the largest U.S. data centers spew carbon emissions on a par with entire countries the size of Bolivia or Denmark. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps the heat from sunlight, driving global warming. America’s largest data centers also consume about 2% of the nation’s electricity, the study said, which is more power than New York and Los Angeles combined.
Add to this the events of the past week or so, in which security patches and routine updates appear to have crippled the very systems they were supposed to fix. From the Friday the 13th “ground stop” of the nation’s airports to outages that hit Microsoft and many major banks, the transition to new systems has been a hellscape for consumers.
Wall Street suffered a “correction” as of Nov. 20, in which stocks dropped 10% from their peak, despite a historic initial public offering of AI company Anthropic. “The wheels are coming off the AI trade,” wryly noted the Wall Street Journal.
The AI reckoning is here.
The battle between tech oligarchs and average Americans will continue, and it will be waged on devices from Main Street to Wall Street. It’s not just the frustration and loss of control that many of us feel when attempting to make a doctor’s appointment, check a bank balance or make a simple purchase. It goes to a fundamental question: At what point does artificial intelligence make us less human?
It’s easy to blame our devices.
But it’s not the machine’s fault, or the fault of machine learning. It’s the human beings pushing the technology who should be held accountable, the tech masters who treat us as pawns and the lawmakers who regard us as so much electoral fodder. If we’d had the kind of regulation and safeguards for AI instituted for the commercial use of nuclear power, we wouldn’t be having conversations about threats, existential and otherwise.
From Emporia to Washington, D.C., our leaders have failed us.
About 1 in 5 Americans can’t pay their utility bills in full, and with winter coming on, many will face a choice of heat, food or medicine. Meanwhile, our largest data centers are using enough electricity to power Denmark.
There’s a word to describe that.
It’s inhuman.
Technology isn’t the problem. It’s the hand that wields it.
In 1972, the creators of the Pioneer 10 plaque — Carl Sagan, Linda Salzman Sagan and Frank Drake — wrote a piece for the journal “Science” in which they explained the intent of the Pioneer 10 plaque. Titled “A Message from Earth,” they wrote that the visual intergalactic postcard “should carry some indication of the locale, epoch, and nature of its builders.”
It is a remarkable testament to what can be achieved when cutting-edge technology serves the human spirit. Sadly, those roles seem now to be reversed.
Their interstellar Adam and Eve pictograph likely will never be found by an extraterrestrial intelligence. The spacecraft is about the size of a small car and the universe in unimaginably vast. But the message was really meant for ourselves all along. It is, as the creators put it in 1972, a “hopeful symbol of a vigorous civilization.”
We need some of that human hope now.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Home for the holidays? Maybe not this year
description: For the first time in years, Thanksgiving travel won’t set a record.  The culprit?  Higher fuel prices.
text:
Heading home for the holidays next week?  Maybe not. 
For the first time in years, Thanksgiving travel won’t set a record.  Mom’s turkey is still free. Getting to it is not.  The culprit?  Higher fuel prices.



Gasoline prices are up… way up.  An average gallon in Connecticut cost $3.94 last week, down a bit from the $4.30 we were paying a month ago, but still up 27% over last Thanksgiving. 
And domestic airfares are also soaring… by one estimate, up 31% over last year.  And that’s for a middle-seat and $50 bag fee (thanks, JetBlue).  And we all know how much fun (and how unreliable) our airlines have been of late, suffering under FAA ground halts and tech-woes.
Frankly, I’ve always wondered why Americans spend so much money for so little vacation time at Thanksgiving, basically a four-day long weekend with hugely concentrated travel on Wednesday and Sunday.  We pay peak prices to spend 30 hours in transit for 48 hours of family time to argue about politics and then head home.
But if you can’t afford to drive or fly and you really want to get to Mom’s, there are options.  Just don’t take them for granted without pre-planning.
AMTRAK: Here in the Northeast Amtrak trains are also expensive and with limited, if slightly increased, capacity.  And Thanksgiving week is the busiest all year for the railroad.  Last year’s Thanksgiving ridership was 1.2 million, up nearly 6% over 2024.  This year Amtrak is adding two extra round trips… but just between Washington and New York.  Up here, we’ll get a few extra cars tacked on to their already busy trains.
On a typical Wednesday a ride from Stamford to Boston costs as little as $39 (coach) one way.  But the same trains on Wednesday November 25 cost $260 (also in coach).  Ouch!  That’s less a fare than a ransom note with pricey AmFood.  And it’s all about supply (limited) and demand (stretched).
Except for the uber-costly Acela, Amtrak trains between Washington and Boston offer reserved (but unassigned) seating.  So don’t expect to stroll to the station and climb onboard without a ticket.  And unless you paid extra for a Flex fare, your ticket can’t be changed to a different train.
HARTFORD LINE: Here you’ll find both Amtrak and CTrail trains, so check your timetable.  Some of the Amtrak trains are all-reserved (like the Vermonter) but others are first-come, first-served.  CTrail honors all tickets but holiday ridership can lead to standing-room-only conditions. 
Confusing, right?  That’s two railroads, one track, three sets of rules and minimal signs at the station explaining any of it.  Welcome to Connecticut visitors!
METRO-NORTH: Extra trains will be added but others dropped.  Grab a magnifying glass and study this timetable closely as it’s confusing even to this veteran rider.  The TrainTime app is a better choice for planning your journey.
Of course there are no reservations on Metro-North, so it’s something of a free-for-all.  Kind of like Black Friday at Walmart, with baggage.  Metro-North’s busiest day of the year is the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and it’s the one day of the holiday stretch when you will still get charged peak fares.
Always buy (and activate) your e-ticket before boarding or your holiday travels will be soured with an on-board penalty, up to $8.  Seniors can catch a break as they can buy tickets onboard without a penalty.  Finally, a perk for getting old.
My advice? Book now, pay up, pack light and lower your expectations.  Or do what smart families do: let the kids come to you.  More Zoom stuffing anyone?

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Boston’s old lessons for a new era of urban politics
description: What many observers call a resurgence of progressive urban politics is, in many respects, a revival of one of the oldest traditions in American city governance: the belief that economic growth and social inclusion are not competing objectives, but mutually dependent goals.
text:
AS HOUSING COSTS rise, new development reshapes neighborhoods, and elected officials face mounting pressure to address inequality, Boston is once again grappling with a familiar question: Can economic growth be reconciled with social justice? The debate often appears new. It is anything but. 
What many observers call a resurgence of progressive urban politics is, in many respects, a revival of one of the oldest traditions in American city governance: the belief that economic growth and social inclusion are not competing objectives, but mutually dependent goals. 
Boston has wrestled with that tension for decades. Each generation confronts it in different forms—through debates over housing affordability, neighborhood change, downtown development, public investment, and economic opportunity. The language evolves, coalitions shift, and political labels change. Yet the underlying question remains remarkably consistent: Who benefits from growth? 
That question is reshaping urban politics once again. Across Boston and other major cities, voters are demanding answers. In New York City—the global financial capital where the contrast between those flying high and those barely able to get by is especially stark—that frustration helped propel a 34-year-old democratic socialist into City Hall one year ago. And earlier this month, voters in the nation’s second-largest city, Los Angeles, delivered another victory for the democratic socialist left with the election of Nithya Raman as mayor. 
In Greater Boston, where housing cost increases have outpaced income growth for many residents, these concerns are especially urgent. Can working families afford to remain in the communities they helped build? Can economic growth coexist with affordability? Can neighborhoods accommodate change without sacrificing stability? Can prosperity be shared broadly enough to sustain civic trust? 
Supporters often call these leaders progressives, while critics call them ideologues. Both labels can obscure what is actually happening. Successful urban leaders rarely prevail because they fit neatly into an ideological category; they succeed because they connect broader civic goals to the practical realities of everyday life. 
American cities have long produced reform movements that sought to balance growth with inclusion. Settlement house reformers, labor organizers, civil rights leaders, neighborhood activists, and urban mayors have repeatedly confronted the same challenge: ensuring that prosperity served democratic purposes rather than merely private interests. 
One of the clearest modern examples emerged in Boston during the 1980s and 1990s. Mayor Ray Flynn took office as investment reshaped the city following decades of post-World War II economic malaise. Boston’s skyline was changing, downtown growth was accelerating, and economic opportunities were expanding. Yet Flynn recognized that prosperity alone could not resolve the city’s deeper divisions. 
He believed economic growth and social justice were inseparable. A city that generated wealth while excluding large segments of its population from opportunity could not sustain civic trust. Likewise, a city committed to fairness yet indifferent to economic growth would undermine its ability to deliver progress. As Flynn saw it, the challenge was not choosing between growth and justice but achieving both. 
That perspective shaped the major policy debates of his administration. Disputes over affordable housing, neighborhood participation, local hiring, homelessness, race, and economic development were often treated as separate issues, yet Flynn saw them as interconnected. 
He rejected the idea that cities should measure success solely by cranes, towers, investment totals, or rising property values. Economic development was necessary, but not sufficient; a city also had to ask whether working families were gaining opportunities or losing ground. 
To that end, his administration launched the groundbreaking Parcel 18 initiative in Roxbury—part of Boston’s first-in-the-nation parcel-to-parcel linkage program, designed to build equity and create wealth for communities of color—while granting the Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative unprecedented eminent domain authority to assemble land for permanently affordable housing and open space. Those policies—established nearly 40 years ago—continue to guide urban development today, alongside the institutionalization and expansion of affordable housing and job-training linkage. 
Were neighborhoods benefiting from investment or facing displacement? Were minority communities sharing in prosperity or watching its rewards flow elsewhere? 
Those questions have grown even more pressing in today’s Boston. Median rent now exceeds $2,400 per month, among the nation’s highest, while median home prices approach $850,000 citywide and surpass $1 million in many surrounding communities.  
At the heart of Boston’s current housing debate is how much affordable housing the city should require in major private developments—and whether overly aggressive mandates risk stalling construction altogether.  
Amid high interest rates and soaring building costs, housing starts across Boston have slowed sharply. Critics of the city’s 2024 expansion of inclusionary zoning rules, which raised the affordability requirement in larger projects to 20 percent of units, argue that such mandates make projects financially unviable, choke off overall housing supply, and ultimately hurt everyone. Some contend that the city should slash or eliminate those requirements to jump-start construction. 
Yet building only luxury housing will never advance equity or long-term affordability for most Boston residents—and residents will not support growth unless they are sure they can remain in the neighborhoods where it occurs.  
Mayor Michelle Wu’s recently proposed adjustments offer a pragmatic middle path: preserving Boston’s core 20 percent affordability mandate while relaxing some payment timelines and other rules so stalled projects can pencil out and get “cranes back in the sky.” As Boston showed in the 1980s and 1990s, smart urban policy requires both unyielding equity guardrails and the flexibility to adapt to capital-market realities. 
Flynn’s influence endures because the central dilemma he confronted remains unresolved. Rising housing costs, widening inequality, and fears of displacement have fostered the perception that growth primarily benefits investors and developers, leaving working residents behind. 
Whether that perception is always justified is less important than the political reality it has created—a reality underscored nationally in this month’s midterm elections. Across the country, voters who feel disconnected from economic growth have grown increasingly skeptical of institutions and leaders who celebrate aggregate prosperity while households struggle to afford the basics. 
Urban voters increasingly want evidence that government can shape market outcomes rather than merely react to them. That is why debates over political labels often miss the point. The future of urban politics will be determined not by whether elected officials adopt the language of progressivism, liberalism, moderation, or socialism, but by their ability to translate moral aspirations into practical results. 
As I wrote in The Battle for Boston, which chronicles the struggle for racial, social, and economic justice under Flynn, Boston’s experience teaches us that cities need not choose between economic development and social justice; ignoring either is perilous. At a moment when public confidence in democratic institutions remains fragile, that lesson extends well beyond Boston—with national demands to address “affordability” shorthand for how many Americans feel squeezed and left behind by today’s economy. 
Citizens support growth when they see tangible benefits in their own lives and neighborhoods. Economic development creates opportunity, but only when residents believe they can share in it. What appears to be a new political movement is, in many respects, a rediscovery of an old civic truth: Cities thrive when economic growth and social inclusion advance together. 
Don Gillis is an urban sociologist and the author of The Battle for Boston: How Mayor Ray Flynn and Community Organizers Fought Racism and Downtown Power Brokers. He served as director of Neighborhood Services and Economic Development under Flynn from 1984 to 1993.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Retiring Deputy House Leader Larry Springer reflects on legacy, warns Democrats on spending
description: After 22 years in the Washington House, retiring Deputy Majority Leader Larry Springer is closing a legislative career marked by advocacy for small businesses, charter schools and wildfire prevention, alongside pointed criticism of his own Democratic colleagues. The Kirkland Democrat, who took office in 2005, describes himself as a socially progressive, fisc[...]
text:
Deputy Majority Leader Rep. Larry Springer on the set of Inside Olympia with Austin Jenkins. (TVW)After 22 years in the Washington House, retiring Deputy Majority Leader Larry Springer is closing a legislative career marked by advocacy for small businesses, charter schools and wildfire prevention, alongside pointed criticism of his own Democratic colleagues.
The Kirkland Democrat, who took office in 2005, describes himself as a socially progressive, fiscally conservative pragmatist shaped by four decades as a small-business owner.
On TVW’s Inside Olympia, Springer told host Austin Jenkins about his two signature accomplishments: negotiating legislation that preserved Washington’s public charter schools despite Democratic opposition, and partnering with Republican Rep. Joel Kretz on landmark wildfire prevention legislation in 2021.
Springer also served as a liaison between House Democrats and the business community, frequently challenging regulations he considered burdensome for small employers.
He estimates the number of consistently business-friendly House Democrats has fallen from 15 early in his career to five today. The House Democratic Caucus is scheduled to elect a deputy majority leader during House committee days. A caucus spokesperson says Springer’s successor as a designated liaison with the business community will be decided then.
Springer supported Washington’s new tax on salaries above $1 million despite criticizing its design and backing unsuccessful amendments. He said the measure failed to deliver meaningful tax reform but could lay the groundwork for broader changes. Voters rejected an initiative to repeal the tax in November, although a constitutional challenge remains pending. Springer predicted the tax would eventually extend to lower incomes, despite Gov. Bob Ferguson’s pledge to veto such an expansion.
Springer’s sharpest criticism concerned state spending. He agreed with former Govs. Gary Locke and Chris Gregoire that spending has become misaligned with priorities.
After successive tax increases and recurring deficits, Springer urged Democrats to exercise fiscal restraint, even when it means disappointing political allies, including organized labor.
“We need to say no to some of our friends. We really do,” he said.
