title: Appoquinimink Boys Soccer Ends Five Year State Championship Drought with Upset Victory over Salesianum
description: Appoquinimink boys soccer defeated Salesianum, 1-0, in the 2026 DIAA Division One State Championship Game for the program’s first state championship title since 2020.   FREDERICA, Del. — Appoquinimink senior, Lincoln Neubauer, stood in goal and watched as Salesianum’s offense passed the ball around in the game’s final minutes. The Sals trailed by a goal with[...]
text:
The Appoquinimink boys soccer team poses for a picture after winning the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Appoquinimink boys soccer defeated Salesianum, 1-0, in the 2026 DIAA Division One State Championship Game for the program’s first state championship title since 2020.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — Appoquinimink senior, Lincoln Neubauer, stood in goal and watched as Salesianum’s offense passed the ball around in the game’s final minutes. The Sals trailed by a goal with the seconds trickling away in extra time when senior Nico Rossi served a pass into the box.
Rossi’s pass hit the head of an Appoquinimink defender and rolled to the feet of sophomore Caden Walpole. Walpole settled the ball and fired a fast shot toward the net where Neubauer stood ready. Neubauer deflected the ball into the air and secured the catch, turning away Salesianum’s chance at an equalizer.
Neubauer and the Appoquinimink defense held the Sals scoreless for just the second time this season, winning the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game, 1-0.
“Our defense is definitely the best in the state and we proved that tonight,” Neubauer said. “We played against the best offense in the state I’d say, but like our coach said I have my dogs over theirs.”
Neubauer’s night wasn’t over yet after making the save on Walpole’s goal attempt. Salesianum got possession right back and earned a corner kick opportunity soon after. The corner kick was headed by a Jaguar defender, but the header ended up being received by a Salesianum player. The ball eventually made its way to Sallies senior, Foster Myers, who lofted a pass toward the net in hopes of generating a game tying goal. The ball was headed away by an Appoquinmink defender and after a foul on Sallies, the Jaguars regained possession. 
Neubauer jogged over near the right corner to take the free kick, but the whistles blew as he was preparing to launch the ball down the field. Appoquinimink boys soccer were division one champions.
Neubauer finished the game with over five saves in goal against a Salesianum team that outscored Delaware competition, 58-5, this season. The senior goalkeeper — and the Appoquinimink football team’s kicker — almost didn’t play soccer this season. Jaguar head coach, Lance Berry, said Neubauer was going to focus on his place kicking duties, but a call in the week before preseason started convinced the senior to return for one final run. 
Neubauer said he’s happy he decided to run it back one last time.
“Oh you don’t even understand how happy I am,” Neubauer said after the game. “I’m like speechless. I came here thinking like alright I’m just gonna finish up my senior year and call it a day, but then no we ended up being state champs.” 
The Jaguars defense was stout all game and earned a program record 13 shutouts this season. Appoquinimink won all three of its 2026 tournament games, 1-0, with the first two wins coming in overtime games. The Jaguars didn’t need an overtime period this time, scoring in the fourth minute on a goal from Freshman Caiden Stone. Stone’s goal was a low kick to the right side of the net that scooted under the dive of Salesianum goalkeeper, Thomas DeRosa. 
The Jaguars finish the season with their first state championship win since 2020 and the program’s second overall. This championship game appearance was Appoquinimink’s sixth since 2013 all of which against Salesianum. 
“It feels great,” Berry said about winning the state championship. “The past week and half, two weeks we’ve been talking about playing for the guy next to you, play for the guy that came before you and play for the guy that comes after you. And these boys really did that today, so I’m at a loss for words.”
Sallies’ season ends with a 15-3 overall record and their 17th consecutive state championship game appearance.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Democrats demand answers from Oz after delay in $50B rural health awards
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble, KFF Health News
description: Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans. Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator of the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks alongside other members of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud during a press conference discussing advancements in what the department calls the War on Fraud Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in St. Cloud, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Congressional Democrats are demanding answers and more transparency from the Trump administration after a nine-day delay of annual awards from a $50 billion fund meant to improve healthcare for rural Americans.
Saying rural care is “in an acute state of crisis,” 18 members of Congress sent a letter to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz late Thursday. The letter pointed to what it called “an alarming lack of public transparency” and said the fund “lacks sufficient guardrails to protect rural hospitals at greatest risk of closure.”
Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski said her state “got no explanation from CMS as to why” it got $3 million less in its second-year Rural Health Transformation Program allocation. It was a roughly 1.5% reduction from its $193.4 million first-year award. State leaders have not received information about an appeals process, she said.
Any delay in knowing how much they received and any reduction in their base funding is significant, Budzinski said, because states need to plan for an “acute impact” from the loss of other federal funding.
In the first year, states competed for their initial share of the $50 billion, which is handed out at $10 billion a year for five years. They won awards ranging from $147 million to $281 million. Most of the lawmakers who signed the letter were from states that lost funding this year. Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama, which got $4.1 million less, along with Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, which saw a nearly $3 million drop, also spearheaded the letter along with Budzinski.

One concern, Budzinski said, is “making sure that the money isn’t going to consultants, that it’s actually getting to the rural providers that it is supposed to be getting to.” The lawmakers asked Oz for a response to detailed questions by Nov. 25. They also requested a briefing about the delays to the funding announcement, which was first reported by KFF Health News, and the impact on states.
The second-year awards were due to be announced by Oct. 31, but an Oct. 30 letter from CMS stated officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.” Instead, second-year funding was announced Nov. 9.
“Those kind of delays prevent a state to fully prepare for what’s to come,” Budzinski said.
CMS oversees the fund and its newly formed Office of Rural Health Transformation. Agency officials did not respond to questions for this article before the given deadline.
Republicans passed the Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to offset other ramifications of President Donald Trump’s signature budget law, including an estimated $137 billion in Medicaid spending cuts for rural America over 10 years.
That rural money is “retail therapy for Congress,” said Cara James, president and chief executive of Grantmakers in Health, while speaking at a Milken Institute event this month.
Because the same tax law cut Medicaid spending, which rural hospitals and people disproportionately use, as well as supplemental food assistance and other government grants, the short-term money would not “help sustain people” in rural America, James said.
Then, she posed a persistent fear about the fund: “If it’s even getting to the communities.”
Five rural hospitals have closed or been converted into lower-level facilities since the rural fund was created, including one in Michigan that shuttered beds and switched to providing only emergency services to survive, according to a list curated by the Cecil G. Sheps Center for Health Services Research at the University of North Carolina.
The letter stated lawmakers’ concerns that too much of the rural fund “could flow to large consulting and technology firms rather than supporting providers and communities on the ground.”
After the law passed last year, state leaders had just over seven weeks to write applications as they competed for the first-year funds. All 50 states won funding with allocations determined by a federal scoring process. Each year, officials are to revisit the funding allotments.
Most states saw their funding change by less than 2%. North Dakota and Iowa won the largest gains; New Jersey, Florida, and Vermont saw the biggest reductions.
Although federal officials have created state data maps, released a slew of press announcements, and led sessions on the complicated scoring of state applications, it’s not enough, said Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association.
The association, which represents hospitals and community clinics nationwide, sent its own letter to federal officials Nov. 9. Morgan said that the way states win money needs “to be articulated in a way that success can be replicated by all states going forward.”
Morgan said his association’s analysis found that state leaders are sending the federal money to local hospitals and clinics because communities and individuals are “relying on rural hospitals to be there to deliver care.” But it’s unclear, he said, how much of the overall rural fund local hospitals are actually receiving versus how much is benefiting other entities, such as consultants.
In their letter, Budzinski and the other Democrats asked if CMS would establish a searchable database that tracks spending. They also asked for an explanation of how federal officials will evaluate state performance and allocate awards.
It was just the latest congressional letter to federal health officials on this issue.
In August 2025, a month after the law passed, Democrats sent a letter about the program’s rollout to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. And last November, Budzinski reached out to Oz on behalf of Illinois. Bennet, along with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and others, signed a letter in June asking that the funds be targeted to rescue rural hospitals and clinics.
“We haven’t gotten full responses to any of these inquiries,” said Budzinski, who will become chair of the House’s largest Democratic caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.



KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Auditor Hunt represented car wreck clients against a West Virginia city he audits
description: While serving as state auditor, Mark Hunt tried to extract settlements for clients who had been in car wrecks involving the city of Charleston, West Virginia.
text:
Charleston City Hall in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)While serving as state auditor, Mark Hunt tried to extract settlements for clients who had been in car wrecks involving the city of Charleston, West Virginia. 
Charleston city officials have called it a “conflict of interest” since the state Auditor’s Office is responsible for reviewing its financial records every year. It’s another installment in controversies coming to light involving the recently indicted auditor. 
Hunt is a personal injury attorney with more than 30 years practice in the Kanawha Valley. He was indicted Monday on federal charges on multiple counts related to nine delinquent tax deeds he signed for Robert L. Johns. 
Federal prosecutors said Hunt, 66, of Charleston, overruled career employees at the Auditor’s Office and issued the deeds after they found Johns had not complied with the law. 
Hunt sent the city letters between March and July 2026, declaring he was representing a woman injured in a car crash and the estate of a woman who had died in one, according to documents West Virginia Watch received from a public records request. 
Hunt asked for settlements ranging from $11,000 to $15,000 to resolve one case, the documents showed.
“We believe it is a conflict of interest and any negotiation involving public funds with the state auditor in a legal matter would not be in the best interest of the taxpayers of the City of Charleston,” said Matt Sutton, chief of staff for Charleston Mayor Amy Goodwin, wrote in a statement to West Virginia Watch. 
The state auditor is in a unique position in regards to the state’s 232 municipalities. Every year, his office analyzes their books to find accounting errors, improper use of funds and to check if they’re solvent. The auditor also oversees how cities use their purchasing cards, too. 
While there’s nothing in state law barring the auditor from moonlighting as a private practicing attorney, West Virginia state code is clear that public officials cannot use their office for private gain. 
Hunt, in a response to emailed questions, said he got two opinions from the state Ethics Commission stating it was legal to work as a part-time lawyer and to represent cases against the city of Charleston.  
“Have 2 State Ethics opinions that say OK to be full time Auditor and part time lawyer,” Hunt wrote. 
West Virginia Watch reached out to the state Ethics Commission, but did not receive a response. 
One March email exchange about a client Hunt would represent shows the official seal of the state Auditor’s Office on it.
“Private email, don’t know how they got it?” Hunt wrote on Thursday in an email. “I only use it between friends. It’s a free outlook email. I did not correspond with them on it other than 2 words. ‘Thank you.’” 
A couple weeks later, the Auditor’s Office sent a letter to the Kanawha County prosecutor about the city’s latest audit. Audits typically are not completely clean and have findings. 
Though the letter said the office didn’t believe there was anything warranting civil or criminal action, they wanted to bring it to the prosecutor’s attention, citing state code that requires notification if they believe a law may have been violated. 
The city hadn’t received such a letter since at least 2019, according to a records request. 
Hunt said he has nothing to do with the chief inspector, the division within his office that oversees municipal audits. 
“Chief inspector runs own ship,” Hunt wrote. “I am not informed on minor audit findings.” 
The city eventually raised its concerns to Attorney General JB McCuskey regarding Hunt.  
“We reached out and provided information to the attorney general, and others, to determine the best course of action to move forward,” Sutton said. “Based on that guidance, we took the appropriate steps until the parties notified us of new legal representation.”
Hunt confirmed that he no longer represents the plaintiffs in the case. Neither case has resulted in a lawsuit. McCuskey declined to comment on the concerns raised by the city. 
The Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a D.C.-based watchdog group that examines conflict of interest in government, called the situation questionable in light of the indictment. 
“Hunt has already violated the public’s trust by apparently abusing the power of his office, giving them reason to question whether there was any impropriety in the overlap between his private personal injury practice and official duties,” said Cynthia Brown, the organization’s senior ethics counsel.
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, has been leading the charge against Hunt. He said the situation adds a new layer to a pile of problems Hunt is facing. 
“West Virginia has ethics laws directly addressing this issue and they would undoubtedly factor into House impeachment proceedings if Mark Hunt doesn’t resign,” Leavitt said. 
Hunt has remained steadfast that he committed no wrongdoing, issuing a statement Monday that he would focus on the work of the Auditor’s Office while defending himself against the federal indictment. 
On Thursday, he had this to say to the more than 480,000 West Virginians who voted for him 2024. 
“Office running smoothly, up $23 million this year alone,” Hunt wrote. “Once again I checked with all appropriate officials before doing anything.”

name: California
title: Thousands of mixed-status California families to lose housing under Trump HUD rule
description: A new rule barring mixed immigration status families from federally funded housing will hit California harder than any other state.
text:
In summary
A new rule barring mixed immigration status families from federally funded housing will hit California harder than any other state. 


Housing authorities across the state are scrambling to prevent their clients from ending up homeless as they brace for a new Trump administration rule that could pull federal subsidies from 7,000 California households.
Starting next month, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development plans to bar all families with a “mixed” immigration status from federally funded housing. The upheaval is expected to hit California, with its large immigrant population, harder than any other state.
“This is a very big deal,” said Sanford Riggs, director of operations for the Santa Barbara County Housing Authority. “This is a huge change.”
The agencies that administer housing vouchers are trying to make emergency plans for their mixed-status families, attempting to move them from federally funded programs into ones that are paid for with city, county, state or philanthropic dollars. But how successful that effort will be will vary greatly county by county, depending on what resources each has available.
The Trump administration has framed this as a way to remove subsidies from undocumented immigrants and give them to homeless veterans and disabled or elderly citizens. “President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement.
But the change could hurt even U.S. citizens who don’t live in mixed-status households. That’s because in some counties, due to a technicality, the vouchers freed up when mixed-status families leave for any reason go away entirely rather than be reissued to other applicants.
Other counties say they’ll be able to serve fewer people overall because mixed-status families pay more in rent and receive a lower subsidy than U.S. citizens. If HUD forces them out and replaces them with citizen households, there will be less funding to go around, and fewer families will get housed.
How does HUD’s new rule change things?
Federal housing funds have always been reserved only for U.S. citizens, or people with an eligible immigration status, such as a green card. But historically, mixed-status families could receive prorated aid – meaning a family of four with two members who are eligible citizens, and two members who are undocumented immigrants, would be paid the same rate as a family of two. 
Under the new rule, set to go into effect Dec. 14, those families would receive nothing. U.S. citizens living with undocumented family members would have to separate from those family members or lose their housing, too.
An analysis of 2024 data by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities found 7,190 mixed-status households receiving federal housing aid in California. The only other state that comes close is Texas, with 4,500. 
HUD proposed this rule change once before during President Donald Trump’s first term in 2019, but rolled it back after a public outcry. This time, lawsuits attempting to block the rule from taking effect have already started, including one from a group of Los Angeles-based families and tenant rights advocates. 
The Santa Clara County Housing Authority has 157 mixed-status households in its program, including 290 children, who will be affected by the new rule. In many cases, the children are the only members of a family who are eligible for federal aid – so there’s no option for the family to separate in order for eligible members to remain housed, said Angie Garcia-Nguyen, deputy executive director of the county’s housing authority. 
The county saw this change coming, and prepared for the cutoff. The community has a contingency plan to help families at risk of being displaced, Garcia-Nguyen said. She wouldn’t disclose how much money has been raised, or where the funds came from, to avoid putting a “target on anyone’s back.” But, she said, whatever nonfederal aid they can provide is only temporary, meaning those families still need a long-term plan.
“I think families are going to have to make some pretty tough choices,” Garcia-Nguyen said. “Santa Clara County is not the most affordable place to live without a subsidy. Some households will need to make decisions about whether or not they’re going to stay.”
After the rule takes effect, it could be more than a year before people are evicted. Housing authorities have the option to grant deferrals for up to 18 months.
Seniors asked to verify immigration status
In Santa Clara County, the ripple effect of the new rule could extend beyond even the 157 mixed-status families. 
HUD also will require some people who were previously exempt to submit documentation that proves their citizenship or immigration status. The housing authority is assisting 12,000 seniors and almost 9,000 children who have not verified their immigration status. Now, those people will be required to do so or lose their housing subsidies. It’s not clear how many of them will be able to, Garcia-Nguyen said. 
In Santa Barbara County, Riggs said he’s not aware of any city, county or state funds that can help the 131 mixed-status families who receive federal subsidies through his agency. 
“It’s quite possible that some could end up homeless,” he said. “There’s no question about it.”
Many of the vouchers freed up when mixed-status families move out won’t be re-issued to U.S. citizens, or anyone at all, Riggs said. The cost of housing in Santa Barbara County, for example, is so expensive that HUD provides extra funding, on top of the regular housing vouchers, to cover people’s cost of rent. But there’s a catch. In exchange, once someone gives up a voucher (whether they die, are evicted or something else) HUD doesn’t let the housing authority re-issue it to someone else. 
The Housing Authority of the City of Los Angeles serves 1,709 mixed-status families who would be affected by the new rule. Those families pay more out of pocket and receive smaller subsidies than households where every member has an eligible immigration status. 
The housing authority said that removing all mixed-status families from the program would force it to cut at least 800 Section 8 housing vouchers in order to cover the increased costs – meaning 800 fewer families would benefit.

name: VTDigger
title: Pedestrian auditor walks the walk in South Burlington
description:
It’s not sexy work, taking a walk in the rain, measuring pothole after pothole, but it can make a big difference.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pedestrian auditor walks the walk in South Burlington.
text:
Pedestrian auditor Matt Van Wagner is assisted by Net Zero Vermont’s Elise Deuel and Deb Sachs in measuring a pothole.Photo by Briana Brady/The Other Paper

This story by Briana Brady was first published in The Other Paper on Nov. 19, 2026.
In the cold November rain Nov. 14, Matt Van Wagner, clad in reflective vest, led a small group of walkers along the sidewalk on Dorset Street headed north. Occasionally, the party would stop, bending over cracks in the sidewalk or small potholes, Van Wagner using a measuring stick or tape measure and taking notes on size and depth.
This was the fourth official community walk audit Van Wagner led as part of a grant the South Burlington City Center Collaborative received from AARP. The goal was to walk stretches of sidewalk connecting to the city’s new downtown center, checking for some of the most common walking or rolling hazards: high lips, broken crossing signals, deep potholes or general deterioration.
It’s not sexy work, taking a walk in the rain, measuring pothole after pothole, but it can make a big difference.
“We’re actually making reports to the city Department of Public Works, and I’m kind of astounded because I thought, you know, we’ll make a report and then we’ll hear about it in two years or something. The things we reported were fixed within three days,” Van Wagner said.
So far, along with the walk from Ann Roche Furniture up to Market Street on Nov. 14, Van Wagner has led groups from Market Street to the University Mall, from Aspen Drive to City Center, and along Williston Road from Hinesburg to Dorset Street. He’s also done “mini” walk audits in between during the week for shorter stretches.
There are some measurable defects that immediately necessitate city intervention, Van Wagner said. Federal accessibility standards dictate that a ramp or a bevel must be used when a change in rise is over half an inch. As a quick measurement, Van Wagner carried a stick, marked with yellow, orange and red tape down at the very bottom, to quickly note whether something might be a problem site.
For a lot of the defects that Van Wagner has been finding with the walk audit groups, an easy patch job will fix it up. For small lips or tiny potholes that might pose a tripping hazard, public works can quickly fill those in or grind down the edges.
But while many of these issues might be easy fixes, they aren’t necessarily problems the city would notice without someone to bring it to attention.
For example, Van Wagner said, on one of the previous walk audits, the group found a crossing signal at Aspen Drive where the speaking feature, which accommodates people with low vision, wasn’t working, nor was the walk signal on one side of the road. Once the Department of Public Works knew about it, he said, the department fixed it in a couple of days.
While part of the work is assessing the general walkability of the streets stretching out from Market Street, Van Wanger is planning to put together a more formal report from his findings. He wants to do more education in the community to help people find and report these, sometimes seemingly small, issues.
“You can now maybe schedule some different sort of preventative maintenance stuff, and just do patching here and there, so that in between the big capital projects that need to be done, you still can keep people safe. And so that’s really kind of the focus,” he said.
That kind of citizen participation might take an effort from people of all walks of life and abilities — and some education. Someone who doesn’t often move with the assistance of wheels or a walker might not notice the steep cross gradation on a sidewalk, but for someone in a wheelchair or using a motorized scooter, Van Wagner said, that could easily make someone feel as if they’re about to tip over, and it should be noted.
For now, Van Wagner has become a bit of a sidewalk expert himself.
“Doing good stuff that’s simple and you check in for an hour, check out for an hour. It’s good for the soul,” he said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pedestrian auditor walks the walk in South Burlington.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: South Dakota can’t recruit its way out of a workforce problem
description: South Dakota is facing a workforce challenge that won’t be solved by filling more job openings. And I wonder whether we’re spending enough time talking about why. Recent reporting by South Dakota Searchlight highlighted a troubling trend: the state’s labor force participation rate fell from 68.2% in September 2025 to 66.3% in September 2026. Meanwhile, […]
text:
A sign advertises for potential employees. South Dakota's workforce challenges include a declining labor force participation rate. (Photo by Mint Images/via Getty Images)South Dakota is facing a workforce challenge that won’t be solved by filling more job openings. And I wonder whether we’re spending enough time talking about why.
Recent reporting by South Dakota Searchlight highlighted a troubling trend: the state’s labor force participation rate fell from 68.2% in September 2025 to 66.3% in September 2026. Meanwhile, South Dakota has approximately three job openings for every unemployed person.
Those numbers deserve attention. So does the question of what we intend to do about them.
Much of the workforce conversation understandably centers on attracting workers, expanding training programs, improving wages, and addressing barriers such as housing and childcare. These are legitimate concerns, and they require serious attention.
But there’s another dimension to this challenge that receives far less discussion.
Are we preparing our organizations for the workforce we’ll actually have, or are we still planning around the workforce we wish we had?
Discussion of economic ‘headwinds’ in South Dakota includes falling labor force participation

For decades, many organizations have operated on a familiar assumption: When demand increases, add employees. When vacancies occur, recruit replacements. When skills become scarce, invest in training or compete harder for talent.
That approach becomes increasingly difficult when the available workforce isn’t growing fast enough to meet demand.
And it raises an uncomfortable question. What happens when everyone is competing for workers who simply aren’t available?
We can recruit employees from neighboring communities or other states, but that doesn’t necessarily increase the overall supply of labor. Sometimes we’re simply moving the same limited workforce from one employer to another.
We need to expand the conversation from workforce availability to organizational capacity.
Workforce availability tells us something about the people who can participate in the labor market. Organizational capacity asks a different question: How effectively can an organization deliver its products, services, and mission with the resources available?
A healthcare organization may struggle to recruit nurses while overlooking workflows that consume valuable clinical time. A manufacturer may face hiring challenges while continuing to rely on outdated processes. A nonprofit may pursue additional funding and programs without examining whether its operating structure can sustain the work.
In each case, recruiting more people may help. But it may not address the underlying constraints.
I’ve spent much of my career working with organizations confronting workforce shortages, financial pressures and operational challenges. One lesson has remained remarkably consistent: Adding people to an inefficient system doesn’t automatically make the system more effective.
Sometimes the better question isn’t how many additional employees we need. It’s what prevents the people we already have from doing their best work.
That requires looking beyond job vacancies and headcount.
It means examining how work is organized, whether responsibilities are appropriately distributed, where processes create unnecessary demands, and whether technology genuinely improves productivity.
It also means considering different staffing models, stronger partnerships, better workforce forecasting and opportunities to redesign jobs around changing needs.
Importantly, organizational redesign shouldn’t become an excuse to demand more from already exhausted employees. The objective is to remove unnecessary work, strengthen performance, improve the employee experience, and create sustainable capacity.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
South Dakota’s economic development leaders are already discussing automation and productivity as part of the state’s response to demographic changes. That’s an encouraging direction.
But technology alone isn’t an organizational strategy. Neither is recruitment.
The next challenge is translating workforce and economic development efforts into sustainable organizational performance. That means understanding not only which skills employers need, but how changing workforce realities affect their ability to deliver services, maintain quality, remain financially viable and grow.
We need to know whether our workforce investments are actually improving organizational performance, not simply whether vacancies are being filled. That requires understanding where capacity is being lost, what’s getting in the way of productivity, and whether our operating models are keeping pace with economic and demographic change.
South Dakota has an opportunity to approach its workforce challenges differently. We can continue investing in people while also helping organizations adapt to changing workforce realities.
That isn’t an either-or choice. It’s how we build a more sustainable economic future.
The question is no longer simply where South Dakota will find more workers. It’s whether we’re preparing our organizations to succeed with the workforce we have and the workforce we’ll have tomorrow.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Can Nebraska learn from Kansas’ mistakes?
description: We Nebraskans had better learn from what happened in Kansas under Gov. Sam Brownback and a state legislature dominated by Republican politicians beginning just 14 short years ago. And we better do it quick. In 2012, Brownback and the Kansas Legislature enacted significant tax cuts that soon produced unsustainable revenue shortfalls, budget deficits, credit r[...]
text:
A budget book for Nebraska's fiscal years between 2025 and 2027 sits on a lawmaker's desk. April 29, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)We Nebraskans had better learn from what happened in Kansas under Gov. Sam Brownback and a state legislature dominated by Republican politicians beginning just 14 short years ago. And we better do it quick.
In 2012, Brownback and the Kansas Legislature enacted significant tax cuts that soon produced unsustainable revenue shortfalls, budget deficits, credit rating downgrades and deep cuts to vital governmental services like public education and roads. Is any of this sounding familiar? 
In 2012, legislation was passed that cut Kansas’ top state personal income tax rate from 6.45% to 4.9%. That was done so Kansas could “compete” with neighboring states with lower state income tax rates. The same law eliminated state income taxes on pass-through entities, prompting the creation of hundreds of thousands of small businesses that paid their owners pass-through “profits” rather than “wages,” allowing them to pay zero state income tax on those earnings. 
Kansas’ revenue dropped $700 million in the first year alone. Ultimately, the state Supreme Court ordered the state to increase state funding of public K-12 education in 2017 and 2018 by $293 million in order to meet the state constitutional requirement that the state provide public education. Is any of this sounding familiar? 
Brownback and his Republican cronies insisted that the tax cuts would pay for themselves through an explosion of economic growth. That did not happen, to put it mildly. 
Instead, the Kansas economy grew at near average annual rates, and the loss of revenue from the tax cuts produced multimillion-dollar budgetary deficits and deep cuts to needed services like those to public education that the Supreme Court’s order attempted to remedy. Brownback’s approval rating fell to 25%, and Republicans lost seats in the Kansas Legislature in the 2016 election that elevated Donald Trump to the White House. In 2017, the Kansas Legislature repealed the 2012 tax cuts over Brownback’s veto. 
Here in Nebraska, the state budget was bulging with a $1 billion surplus in 2021 and 2022, largely from receipt of one-time federal relief dollars in the wake of the COVID economic downturn. That surplus was offered as rationale for cutting the state income tax rate so Nebraska could “compete” with lower-taxing neighboring states. 
In 2023, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed into law LB 754, passed by a Republican-dominated Unicameral that implemented, starting for the 2024 tax year, a phased-in reduction of the state income tax rate from 6.84% to 3.99% for the 2027 tax year. Ever since, we here in the Cornhusker State have watched our governor and state legislators scramble to repeatedly fill hundreds-of-millions-of-dollars holes in the state’s budget — holes caused by the reduction in revenue resulting from the income tax rate cuts.
Pillen directed state agencies to implement across-the-board spending cuts of 8%. Money was pulled from specifically designated funds such as the State Veterans Aid Fund, which provides for the needs of our state’s citizens who served in our nation’s armed forces, and the Environmental Trust, the funding for which is a portion of state lottery revenues as voters mandated when the lottery was approved by them in 1992. The clamber goes on to patch a deficit of approximately $300 million in the current budget, and projections are for a $1.2 billion deficit for the next two-year state budget that senators will be confronted with in the upcoming session. 
In our Big Red state, registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats by at least 20 percentage points. After being reelected two weeks ago by a margin of 7% over Democrat candidate Lynn Walz, Republican Gov. Pillen claimed a “mandate” for his policy of tax cuts and spending reductions, the policies that have produced the deficits, directives for cuts and raids on state funds. 
Pillen insists that his approach of capping local government spending, the state paying the operational expenses of public education and cutting property taxes is the “fix” voters demand. Noticeably, Pillen fails to explain where the state — which has already exhausted the underside of every couch cushion to pay past bills and is still facing a $1.2 billion shortfall in the next biennial budget — is going to come up with anything near the $3.3 billion in local property taxes spent annually on public education.  
Perhaps we can learn Kansas’ lesson? If the economic and societal damage sustained by our neighbors to the south is insufficient disincentive for following the path Pillen advocates, maybe the loss of elective office by the Kansas politicians who went along with an irresponsible fiscal fantasy will be.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Missouri livestock farmers face environmental regulations. The CAFO debate should reflect that.
description: A recent commentary in the Missouri Independent by Rural Crisis Center member Darvin Bentlage paints a misleading picture of Missouri’s livestock industry and the environmental safeguards that govern it. Missouri’s livestock producers supply affordable, domestically produced protein while operating under state and federal environmental regulations designed t[...]
text:
(Scott Olson/Getty Images)A recent commentary in the Missouri Independent by Rural Crisis Center member Darvin Bentlage paints a misleading picture of Missouri’s livestock industry and the environmental safeguards that govern it.
Missouri’s livestock producers supply affordable, domestically produced protein while operating under state and federal environmental regulations designed to protect our natural resources. Those safeguards deserve to be part of the discussion.
The suggestion that Missouri livestock producers operate with virtually no environmental oversight overlooks important requirements already in place. Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are subject to extensive state and federal environmental requirements governing facility construction, manure storage, nutrient management, land application and water quality. Requirements vary by the size and type of operation.
Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it

These are not voluntary suggestions. They are enforceable regulations, and producers must comply or face penalties.
Start with the numbers. The commentary claims Missouri’s impaired waters list grew from 24 in 2002 to 549 today.But those figures do not provide a straightforward comparison of water quality over time. The state’s current list includes 24 impairments first identified in 2002, not a total of just 24 impairments that year.
The commentary also points to 215 listings added since 2020. An important part of the explanation is a change in how Missouri evaluates water quality. Missouri adopted numeric nutrient criteria for lakes in 2018, and the 2020 list was the first to be measured against those criteria.The new standards led to additional lakes being identified as impaired.
That is not evidence that livestock farms are driving a surge in pollution. Rather, as standards become more protective, more waters may be added to the impaired waters list. In fact, none of the 549 listings identifies a CAFO or livestock farm as its source.
The commentary also suggests that Missouri has no meaningful setback requirements. While Missouri does not require minimum spacing between separate CAFOs, other siting protections exist. Missouri regulations establish minimum separation distances. For example, CAFOs must be more than facilities generally must be at least 100 feet from human water supply lakes, losing streams or sinkholes. Larger operations are also subject to substantial buffer distances (in some cases, more than half a mile) from neighboring residences and public buildings, along with advance neighbor notification requirements. These safeguards exist for a reason: to protect neighboring landowners and natural resources while allowing responsible agricultural operations to continue.
Missouri’s approach to CAFO regulation recognizes that responsible facility siting involves far more than the distance between neighboring operations. Livestock operations must account for their surroundings, comply with established applicable engineering standards and meet environmental requirements.
Missouri’s regulatory framework includes setbacks from waterways and residences, though it does not establish minimum distances between separate CAFOs. Those existing safeguards are an important part of evaluating whether additional requirements are warranted.
The commentary also misleads you about manure storage and handling. Modern livestock facilities are engineered with environmental protection in mind. All Missouri CAFOs must be designed and operated to prevent discharges. This means they must be designed, constructed, operated and maintained to prevent the discharge of manure, litter and process wastewater into state waters, subject to limited regulatory exceptions. Even smaller animal feeding operations that do not require permits are prohibited from polluting state waters.
For example, swine operations commonly use enclosed barns with manure stored in pits beneath the buildings. These pits are designed to prevent leakage. Poultry operations likewise often house animals indoors, with litter managed within the production facility and protected from the elements until it is applied to farmland as fertilizer. These systems are fundamentally different from the open, uncontrolled waste operations the commentary suggests exist. No one in Missouri, including farmers and ranchers, is permitted to pollute state or federal waters.
Manure management also is subject to strict regulations governing how and where waste may be applied. Permitted operations must follow nutrient management requirements for land under their control, and manure and litter must be applied at rates that account for appropriate agricultural use of nutrients. Setback distances also apply to manure and litter applications. For example, manure application must maintain a 300-foot setback from a public or private drinking water structure, sinkhole or losing stream.
There is another important fact missing from the discussion: Farmers are economical people. Manure is a valuable, natural source of nutrients that can reduce the need for commercial fertilizer and improve soil productivity. No responsible farmer has an economic incentive to oversaturate fields with manure. Proper manure application is both good environmental stewardship and good business.
None of this means agricultural operations are incapable of making mistakes or that environmental violations never occur. If violations happen, they should be addressed and producers should be held accountable. But using isolated concerns and broad generalizations to suggest that Missouri’s entire livestock industry is inherently irresponsible does a disservice to the thousands of farm families who take their environmental responsibilities seriously.
Animal agriculture is essential to Missouri’s economy. It supports our communities and puts protein on our plates. It also provides livestock production opportunities for young and beginning farmers to enter agriculture, build equity and establish viable farming operations without having to acquire thousands of acres of land.
Missouri farmers deserve a discussion grounded in facts, not one that unfairly characterizes an entire industry. Debates about environmental protections should recognize both the need to safeguard our water and the regulations farmers already follow.
Scott Hays, executive director of the Missouri Pork Association; Alfred Brandt, executive director of Missouri Dairy; Blake Rollins, president of the Poultry Federation; Mike Deering, executive vice president of Missouri Cattlemen’s Association; Bradley Schad, CEO ofthe Missouri Corn Growers Association; and Casey Waster, CEO of Missouri Soybean Association, contributed to this commentary.

name: Delaware
title: St. Mark’s Boys Soccer Repeats as State Champions, Defeat St. Andrews in 2026 DIAA Division Two Boys Soccer State Championship Game
description: The St. Mark’s Spartans defeated the St. Andrews Saints, 2-0, winning back-to-back state championships for the first time in over two decades.   FREDERICA, Del. — St. Mark’s senior, Brayden Wrinn, stood behind a pair of St. Andrews defenders and just in front of a third watching as striker Justin Baxley tapped a pass back to midfielder Caleb Nelson. Nelson .[...]
text:
The St. Mark’s Spartans pose with the 2026 DIAA Division Two State Championship trophy after repeating as state champions. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The St. Mark’s Spartans defeated the St. Andrews Saints, 2-0, winning back-to-back state championships for the first time in over two decades.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — St. Mark’s senior, Brayden Wrinn, stood behind a pair of St. Andrews defenders and just in front of a third watching as striker Justin Baxley tapped a pass back to midfielder Caleb Nelson. Nelson took the pass and booted the ball past everyone. Once the ball left Nelson’s foot, Wrinn took off.
Wrinn got behind the lone defender placed behind him and sprinted to the ball. Wrinn got to the ball right before it entered the box and now had only one person to beat for a score, St. Andrews goal keeper, Liam Wilson. Wilson ran out to make a play on the ball, but his sprint out of the net left the goal exposed. Wrinn took one touch then fired just out of the reach of Wilson and to the center of the net.
Wrinn scored the game’s first goal in the 51st minute and another less than a minute later, helping the Spartans defeat St. Andrews, 2-0. 
“I mean we didn’t really look great during the first half,” Wrinn said. “We knew we had to make a change because its all we had left in the season and [Nelson] plays me a perfect ball, just tap in. It’s great.”
Wrinn’s second goal was set up by a clearing kick from the Spartans defense off the initial restart. Wrinn tracked down the long kick and faced a pair of two Saints defenders in front of him. Wrinn settled the ball, dribbled a few steps to his right and rocketed a right legged kick to the left post. The ball snuck in between the dive of Wilson in goal and the left post, doubling the Spartans lead about thirty seconds after they claimed it.
The Saints generated a couple scoring opportunities as the second half progressed, but those attempts were either saved in goal by junior Thomas Swasey or curtailed by the Spartans defensemen, especially the junior duo of Dylan Solomon and Declan O’Connor. The pair contributed throughout the night with key stops along the edges of the field and helped the Spartans earn their tenth shutout in the biggest game of the season. 
“Dylan stepped up,” Swasey said after the win. “[Branden] Kemp our centerback, [one] of our leaders went out [at] Brandywine and I mean Dylan filled his place.” 
Swasey added that Solomon was banged up a little bit during the week but powered through to help the team when it mattered most. Swasey himself stepped up with multiple saves throughout the first half which helped keep the Spartans in the game despite the offense’s first half struggles.
“The first half our guys didn’t have it,” Swasey said. “I gotta keep us in the game when our guys don’t have it. I know they’re going to score one or two and if I keep it to zero I know we’re going to win because they’re going to score one or two every game.” 
The Saints started the game aggressive on the offensive end and held possession in that area of the field for the majority of the opening half. The Spartans defense made key stops in that time and turned some of those stops into quick counter attack opportunities, but those were turned away by the strong defensive play of the Saints defensive unit, including seniors Steele Malkin and Lucas Sturges-Moyne. The two teams went into halftime without a score.
“I actually thought the first half, credit to St. Andrews, I thought they took it to us. They had a great gameplan, they wanted it, they were being a little bit more physical then we were,” Head coach Dan Swasey said. “We got to halftime and I think we made some adjustments that worked for us and I think our boys came out a little bit more juiced, a little bit more fire. And then once we got that goal I think it opened up and gave us a little bit more confidence we could do it.”
The Spartans exited halftime and found the spark they needed in the form of Wrinn’s two goals to win back-to-back division two state championships for the first time since 2000-2001. Those St. Mark’s teams were coached by Tom DeMatteis who led the program to six straight state championship titles between 1996 and 2001. This win increases the program’s total to 13.
St. Mark’s finished the season with an overall record of 14-4 and outscored its opponents, 11-2, throughout the 2026 state tournament. 
The Saints finished the season with their first state championship appearance in two seasons and an overall record of 14-4.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Democratic Party changes leaders after successful blue-wave election
description: Just weeks after a blue-wave election swept Maryland, and a little more than a year after the last change in leadership, the Maryland Democratic Party will be getting a new chair, with Steuart PIttman leaving and First Vice Chair Charlene Dukes positioned to take over.
text:
Maryland Democratic Party Chair Steuart Pittman points to 1st Vice Chair Charlene Dukes during the party's gala at Maryland Live! in June. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Just weeks after a blue-wave election swept Maryland, and a little more than a year after the last change in leadership, the Maryland Democratic Party will be getting a new chair.
Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman assumed chairmanship of the party in June 2025, but his term is up on Dec. 12. He said Friday that he was supporting First Vice Chair Charlene Dukes for the job when the State Central Committee meets to elect new officers next month.
“None of the success that we have achieved over the last 18 months, or during the two years that preceded it, would have been possible without the strength, the wisdom, and the support of First Vice Chair Dr. Charlene Dukes,” Pittman said in a statement released by the party.
That was seconded by Gov. Wes Moore (D), who said there is “no one better” for the job than Dukes, who he called a “proven community leader.”
“As our next Maryland Democratic Party chair, she will bring that same commitment to organizing in every community, developing new leaders, and turning our shared values into action,” Moore said in a prepared statement. “I look forward to working alongside her to build on our victories and move Maryland forward.”
Dukes was first vice chair last summer when then-Chair Ken Ulman stepped down from the position, but she said at the time she did not want the chairman’s job, opening the door to Pittman.
Maryland Democrats celebrate election victories at state, county levels

In the year since, he has mounted a listening tour of Democrats in all 24 of the state’s jurisdictions that resulted in the publication of a report on the findings of the so-called Talk Back Tour. For the first time since 1974, the party fielded candidates in every district race in the state.
Democrats came closer than ever before, but were not able to knock off their No. 1 target, Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), who beat Democratic challenger Dan Schwartz by a 52-48 margin in a year in which Democrats regained control of the U.S. House and Senate, with seats to spare.
Otherwise, Democrats rolled. Besides rolling up overwhelming, and expected, wins in the races for governor, comptroller and attorney general, the party notched a surprisingly easy victory on Question 3, the constitutional amendment that will lift restrictions on drawing congressional maps — making it easier to target Harris in the future.
The party said it flipped a total of 27 seats, at the state and county level, from red to blue this year. Those included gaining a seat in the state Senate, four seats in the House, and unseating the Republican county executive in Wicomico County, among other races.
“We went to work training organizers, recruiting candidates in red areas, preparing those candidates, and supporting their campaigns with a massive field operation that knocked on 340,000 doors, made 966,000 phone calls, and sent 1.6 million personal text messages,” Pittman said Friday. “We created the grassroots infrastructure to meet the political moment, and flipped 27 seats across the state from red to blue.”
Pittman said that serving as party chair has been “both a thrill and an honor.”
“I want to thank Gov. Wes Moore for believing that a political party is built from the bottom up and supporting a truly statewide strategy in every way possible,” said Pittman, who also thanked party staff and party Executive Director Karen Darkes.
Moore thanked Pittman for his service.
“In a moment when we needed moral leadership more than ever, Steuart Pittman stepped up to not only lead Anne Arundel County, but to usher in a new wave of Democratic leaders across the state as the Chairman of the Maryland Democratic Party,” Moore said. “I couldn’t be more thankful for his friendship, his tireless work, and the dedication he has shown to the entire state to building a Maryland that leaves no one behind.”
And he said he is confident Dukes can carry those “historic” wins forward.
“Through her leadership at Prince George’s Community College and her service on the Maryland State Board of Education and the Maryland Higher Education Commission, she has opened doors of opportunity and brought people together to deliver real results,” he said.
“The victories we saw this year in Maryland were historic, but we can’t stop there — and there is no one better to carry that work forward than Dr. Charlene Dukes,” his statement said.

title: Commentary: Analysis: The towns and legislative districts hit hardest by MaineCare cuts
description: Recent analysis by Maine Center for Economic Policy finds Mainers in the state’s most rural towns and legislative districts are among those most affected by the cuts to Medicaid, known as MaineCare,  in President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill.” Building on prior county-level analysis, MECEP projected healthcare losses for each state House of Represe[...]
text:
MaineHealth Franklin Hospital in Farmington, Maine. (Photo courtesy of MaineHealth)Recent analysis by Maine Center for Economic Policy finds Mainers in the state’s most rural towns and legislative districts are among those most affected by the cuts to Medicaid, known as MaineCare,  in President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Building on prior county-level analysis, MECEP projected healthcare losses for each state House of Representatives and Senate district, as well as at the ZIP code level. Because the cuts are a consequence of new work reporting requirements, the areas hardest hit include the parts of Maine where steady year-round work is hardest to find. In addition, because wages in these areas are lower than the rest of the state, a larger share of the population is enrolled in MaineCare to begin with.
For example, some of the legislative districts where Mainers are most likely to lose their MaineCare are Senate District 6, which covers Downeast Maine, and House District 3, which includes Fort Fairfield and the surrounding towns.
One important exception, however, is Portland, where the labor market’s strength does not do enough to insulate the large number of Portlanders using MaineCare. This is partly because despite meeting the requirements, thousands of Mainers will lose coverage when they’re unable to prove it or to navigate the new layers of red tape. Thus, Portland’s Senate District 28 and House Districts 118 and 119 have the most Medicaid losses of any part of the state.
By contrast, the areas of Maine least at risk from the changes in OBBB are the wealthy Portland suburbs, where employment is readily available, and relatively few people rely on MaineCare. In Senate District 25, which includes Falmouth, Yarmouth, and Cumberland, just under 400 Mainers are expected to lose their health care coverage, compared to almost 1,300 in District 6, and almost 1,600 in neighboring District 28.
It’s worth noting how damaging these cuts will be for some communities. Statewide, around one in three Mainers in the expanded MaineCare program could lose access to healthcare, but this number ranges from one in four to almost half, depending on which part of the state people live in. And in several communities, more than one in 10 of all adults under age 65 will lose their health care.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Alsobrooks-Van Hollen fallout, county executives scramble, freshmen postings, in political notes
description: Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks still get along, but the same can't be said of everyone, the clock is ticking on the five new county executives trying to set up their administrations and House freshmen get their committee assignments, in political notes.
text:
Sen Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) endorsed then-Prince George's County Executive Angela Alsobrooks (D) in 2023 in the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate seat Alsobrooks now holds. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)Maryland Democratic Sens. Angela Alsobrooks and Chris Van Hollen remain professional and cordial with one another, despite Alsobrooks’ announcement this week that she will support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) over Van Hollen in the race to lead the Democrats in that chamber in January.
Not everyone is being as cordial.
Groups including Progressive Maryland, Charm City Indivisible and CAIR (Council on American-Islamic Relations) Action Maryland plan to hold rallies Monday afternoon outside of three Alsobrooks’ district offices in Prince George’s and Montgomery counties and in Baltimore City.
“Rally organizers say her endorsement should be guided by the needs and demands of Maryland voters – not agreements made in Washington,” according to a statement released Friday.
A representative with Alsobrooks’ office declined to comment Friday.
Since Alsobrooks’ went public Wednesday in backing Schumer, criticism of her decision has spread on social media. Some voiced their disdain at Elizabeth Booker Houston, a lawyer and one of the biggest Democratic influencers, when she said people who back Van Hollen (like her) need to stop spreading disinformation “about Black women in politics.”
“Even though I disagree with Sen. Alsbrooks and her support of Chuck Schumer, threatening and harassing her and her staff is not the way to go,” Booker Houston said in her Instagram post Thursday.
Van Hollen released a statement Thursday and said he respects Alsobrooks’ decision, and called for people to lower the temperature.
Alsobrooks backing Schumer over Van Hollen in race for Senate majority leader

“These discussions among our party are critical to move our democracy and our caucus forward. And above all, they must be based in mutual respect and civility – there is no space in this discussion for vitriol or hostility,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Regardless of the outcome, Senator Alsobrooks and I will continue to respect one another and work together on behalf of Marylanders every day.”
Clock’s ticking on transition
In a little more than two weeks, the state’s five new county executives will drop “-elect” from their titles at their swearings-in, which all take place on Dec. 7. Which means their transition teams, or new staff in some cases, have a lot to do and not much time to do it.
Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando announced his transition team a day after polls closed, and we haven’t hear from Democratic Wicomico County Executive-elect Ernest Davis. But two others named their teams this week and one started naming her administration. All were a mix of current and former state and local officials, educators, community leaders and more.
Anne Arundel
County Executive-elect Allison Pickard has already started assembling her administration, naming Emily Hollis, who worked as deputy chief of staff in the comptroller’s office, as the county’s deputy chief administrative officer for government operations.
Jordan Bellamy, a communications lead for Everytown for Gun Safety who often lobbied in Annapolis during the legislative session, will be Pickard’s director of communications and Lawrence Schultz will be the county’s new fire chief on Jan. 4, replacing Chief Trisha Wolford, who is leaving after eight years.
At least two Baltimore County government employees will move south: D’Andrea Walker as chief administrative officer, the role she had in Baltimore County; and Tucker Cavanagh as deputy chief administrative officer for land use and infrastructure. Cavanagh had a similar title for economic development and infrastructure in Baltimore County.
Current Anne Arundel County Police Chief Amal Awad will remain as head of the force.
Pickard said the appointees have “the range and depth of experience to hit the ground running on Day One. With a shared commitment to building a modern, responsive, and accountable County Government that delivers results, strengthens public services, and creates opportunities for residents in every community. We are ready to meet the moment.”
Baltimore County

County Executive-elect Julian Jones has three co-chairs for his transition team: Towson University President Mark Ginsberg; Craig Thompson, an attorney and chair of the Maryland Stadium Authority; and Sharonne Bonardi, executive director with the Federation of Tax Administrators. Freeman A. Hrabowski III, president emeritus of University of Maryland, Baltimore County, will serve as an honorary co-chair.
Topical groups will include Baltimore City State’s Attorney Ivan Bates leading a public safety committee and former Baltimore City Councilman Eric Costello, a vice chair on the Maryland Economic Development Corp., will lead a committee on technology and government innovation.
Former Maryland State Education Association President Cheryl Bost will lead a group dealing with education, while Stacey Rodgers, acting secretary for the Maryland Department of Human Services, will serve as leader on a committee focused on health and human services.
“The people of Baltimore County work hard for their families, and they deserve a government that works just as hard for them,” Jones wrote Monday on his X page. “That’s why I’ve invited these accomplished leaders to help lead my transition and inform how we deliver a standard of excellence in our public services.”
Howard County
Howard County Executive-elect Vanessa Atterbeary, the first Black woman elected to the position, will get some help from county government veterans as well as some folks from her three terms as a state delegate.
She tapped outgoing Howard County Council Chair Opel Jones and Ken Ulman, the former Howard County executive and former Maryland Democratic Party, as her transition team co-chairs. (It’s a busy time for Ulman, whom Gov. Wes Moore named chair of the Maryland Entertainment Industry Council last month.)
Sen. Guy Guzzone (D-Howard), the chair of the influential Senate Budget and Taxation Committee, will be an honorary co-chair. Guzzone and Ulman both served on outgoing Executive Calvin Ball’s transition team for his first term in 2018.
Committees include public safety, education and one labeled “students,” led by high school student Gavin Falcón. The environment committee will led by Environment Secretary Serena McIllwain, who is stepping down at the end of the year. A Planning and Infrastructure Committee will be led by Alex Hughes, then-chief of staff for former House Speakers Adrienne Jones and the late Michael Busch.
“Brainpower, strategic vision, a deep understanding of local and state government, strong relationships and a real commitment to getting things done is what this group brings to the table,” Atterbeary said in a statement.
New kids on the committee
House keeps most of leadership, committee posts intact for upcoming legislative session

As long as we’re looking at the calendar, the start of the 2027 General Assembly is a little more than seven weeks away and House and Senate leaders were busy this week setting up committees and filling leadership posts.
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk, who announced leadership posts and committee chairs Wednesday, continued that work Thursday with committee assignments for the incoming freshmen.Peña-Melnyk welcomed the new delegate, who she said “bring a wealth of experience, fresh perspectives, and a strong commitment to public service.”
“They are joining us at a consequential time for our state, with difficult decisions ahead and important work to be done,” she said in a statement released by her office. “I am confident that each of them will bring valuable insight and energy to the work ahead as we serve the people of Maryland,” Peña-Melnyk said.
The freshman assignments are:
The Appropriations Committee will get Dels.-elect Abena Affum-McAllister (D-Charles), Dan Duggan (R-Garrett and Allegany) and C.L. Marshall III (R-Lower Shore).
 Dels.-elect Spencer Dixon (D-Anne Arundel), Josh Hastings (D-Wicomico), Molly McKee-Seabrook (D-Prince George’s) and Matt Post (D-Montgomery) landed on the Economic Matters Committee.
The Environment and Transportation Committee will get Dels.-elect Chanel Branch (D-Baltimore City), Amy R. Brooks (D-Howard), Jerry D. Donald (D-Frederick), Robin Harvey (D-Baltimore County) and Steve Whisler (R-Frederick and Carroll).
Dels.-elect Chuck Cook (D-Anne Arundel), Tracy Gant (D-Prince George’s), Charles Murphy III (R-Baltimore County), Jake Taylor (R-Harford) and LaTasha Ward (D-Prince George’s) head to the Government, Labor and Elections Committee.
Dels.-elect Adrienne Mathis (D-St. Mary’s), Steve Patten (R-Carroll) and Tiffany Welch (D-Baltimore City) head to the Health Committee.
The Judiciary Committee gets Dels.-elect Derek Howell (R-Cecil), Mike Jacobs (R-Anne Arundel), Keenon James (D-Prince George’s) and Christa Tichy (D-Montgomery).
The Ways and Means Committee will get Dels.-elect Andrew Duck (D-Frederick) and Ryan Turner (D-Baltimore City).
Peña-Melnyk also thanked the departing delegates for their “dedication to public service, commitment to their constituents, and contributions to the institution. Their leadership and service have helped shape the House of Delegates and have left a lasting impact on the communities they represented,” according to the statement from her or===

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden — and a drag on productivity
description: By now, almost everyone has asked an AI agent a question, only to realize that the answer seems not quite right. Something might be missing or wrong or out of date. An executive assistant told me she uses AI tools for drafting itineraries and briefings, but she’s caught enough issues that she now builds time […]
text:
Productivity gains from AI can be wiped out by the extra time workers must spend verifying whether the output is accurate and appropriate. (Photo by Dragos Condrea/iStock via Getty Images)By now, almost everyone has asked an AI agent a question, only to realize that the answer seems not quite right. Something might be missing or wrong or out of date. An executive assistant told me she uses AI tools for drafting itineraries and briefings, but she’s caught enough issues that she now builds time into her workflow to thoroughly check for inaccuracies and biases.
Therein lies the catch: AI responses can improve productivity, but the gains are often countered by time and mental energy spent determining whether the output is accurate and appropriate. This is the verification burden.
At a deeper level, the burden is the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work that is partly delegated to a system, while retaining responsibility for the final product. Cognitive engineer David Woods described this problem back in 1985 as the responsibility-authority double bind: Automation exercises practical authority, yet responsibility remains with the human.
I am a cognitive engineer, and I study how people work with automated decision-support systems. Generative AI verification is the latest instance of a long-standing human-factors problem: a new kind of necessary work brought about by use of a new technology.
AI workers are exchanging some skills related to creating and transforming information for separate skills that resemble supervising an extraordinarily fast and polished intern. The difficulty is that this intern delivers both good and bad work in the same confident voice, provides few clues about where scrutiny is needed, and bears no responsibility for the consequences.
 
Verifying instead of creating
Research shows that verifying new information is a different task than creating it, and it’s not a simpler one. A meta-analyis of 86 studies revealed that people remember what they produced far better than anything they only read. The same is true for understanding information. Research also shows that material that is easy to read and understand seems more credible, and people therefore consider it more likely to be true.
But humans do not always vet AI responses. Instead, they tend to weigh their own internal costs and benefits to decide when to check. Overreliance on AI output is hard to stop, too. One research team found that adding simple explanations of the AI’s reasoning did not eliminate the quandary people felt in committing the time and energy needed to check. People tend to generalize agents as either capable or incapable and nothing in between.
Economics scholars have found real productivity improvements from using generative AI in office work. But a randomized trial of experienced software developers found no gains, and completion times increased when a verification step was included. Surprisingly, the developers believed they had been faster when using AI, yet their completion time increased by 19%.
And a large study of consulting teams found that using AI outside of a person’s area of expertise resulted in more people reaching the wrong conclusion.
These studies do not establish that there is a universal verification “tax,” but they show why the speed alone of generating output is an incomplete measure of productivity.
 
Why verification is hard
Verification can feel burdensome in terms of cognitive load, time spent and motivation.
People feel a cognitive burden because verification is fundamentally different from creation. You generally know when something you are creating is “done,” or is at least sufficient for the task. When to stop verification is less obvious. A worker must decide what to check and how; they do not know whether an error exists, where it might be or what form it might take.
This is similar to airport security screening, where an unusual threat gets missed more often than a common one because it is easy for inspectors to conclude that rare threats are not present. This burden is greater when AI helps someone generate work that exceeds their ability to evaluate it. A recent study found that AI reasoning helped people catch mistakes on easy questions but not hard ones, when help was needed most.
A time burden arises because instead of ending work, finding an error starts another cycle of correction and then rechecking. Research into how people evaluate AI-generated suggestions has found that the more work needed to fix an identified mistake, the less likely people are to actually fix it.
Finally, verification carries a motivational burden. Creation produces visible progress, but verification may find only that nothing was wrong. When automation usually performs well, checking can feel unproductive, and people may gradually become less vigilant. This pattern was found two decades ago in a study of people working with automated decision-making systems.
 
Skill swap
Together, these burdens result in a skill swap. In a recent survey, knowledge workers said their critical thinking was moving from production toward verification. Workers also need to learn how to recognize the capabilities and limits of a specific AI agent, including omissions and biases.
These skills are different, but they are not necessarily easier, and they might not even be in the skill set of workers who excel at creation. Companies and organizations therefore cannot treat verification as a natural step that carries no effort. If workers remain accountable for AI-assisted output, I believe that they must also be given the time, training and authority needed to verify it.
The measurement of productivity gains cannot include just how quickly AI produces a first draft. Instead, the measure is whether the entire human-AI workflow produces trustworthy work at a lower total cost.

Karen Feigh is the Daniel S. Lewis professor and associate chair for research at Georgia Tech’s Daniel Guggenheim School of Aerospace Engineering with a courtesy appointment in the School of Interactive Computing. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
