name: Maryland Matters
title: After months of roadblocks, Maryland Reparations Commission holds first meeting
description: More than 19 months after it was passed, vetoed and had that veto overridden, the Maryland Reparations Commission finally held its first meeeting Friday, with members focused on the "historic" nature of their charge.
text:
Del. Alethia McCaskill (D-Baltimore County) gets a hug from Del. Catherine Forbes (D-Baltimore County) in December 2025, when the House overrode Gov. Wes Moore's veto of a bill creating a reparations commission. That commission finally held its first meeting Friday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)If members of the Maryland Reparations Commission appeared eager to get to work at their first meeting Friday, it’s easy to understand why.
It’s taken them 19 months just to get to this point.
The commission, approved during the 2025 legislative session, had to overcome a series of hurdles, not the least of which was an unexpected veto by Gov. Wes Moore (D), the nation’s only Black governor at the time. But the more than two dozen members who met Friday were more focused on the importance of being part of a “historic commission.”
“This is very important work that is long overdue,” said Stephanie Franklin, a civil rights attorney and one of six people appointed to the commission by Moore.
The nearly 90-minute online meeting began with members introducing themselves and talking about the commission’s charge. Members of the volunteer commission include those with expertise in the history of slavery, members of the House and Senate, and community and faith leaders. The State Archives office will help staff the commission, with Archivist Elaine Rice Bachmann serving as one of three ex-officio commission members.
Emily Oland Squires, an assistant state archivist, led the first part of the meeting and read a summary of the commission’s mandate, part of which is “to study and make recommendations relating to appropriate benefits to be offered to individuals whose ancestors were enslaved in the State or were impacted by certain inequitable government policies.”
‘Nearly erased’ Black patriots of the Revolution now enshrined at State House

Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City and Baltimore County) recommended changing “benefits” to “restitution or something like that. I don’t want us to mischaracterize the nature and the harm and the intent of what we’re doing here.”
The word “benefits” is mentioned five times in the legislation sponsored last year by Sen. C. Anthony Muse (D-Prince George’s) and Del. Aletheia McCaskill (D-Baltimore County). While the Senate bill ultimately passed, McCaskill is seen by many as the lawmaker who led the yearslong fight to get a reparations commission established.
Both bills were among the top priorities for the Legislative Black Caucus last year. Maryland become of the few states in the nation with a statewide body to study the inequality endured by African descendants.
The bill passed the Senate 32-13 in March 2025 and passed the House by a comfortable 101-36 margin almost three weeks later, after a day of failed amendment attempts by Republicans. But it was vetoed on May 16, 2025, by Moore, who said in his veto message that it was time to move past studies of the issue and toward action. That veto was easily overridden in a special session last December, which allowed for the commission to be created.
At Friday’s meeting, commission members discussed for slightly more than 30 minutes part of the group’s mission and the appointment of a chair.
A few members in the virtual meeting said they needed more time to decide on choosing a chair, since many were just meeting for the first time.
“It would be difficult for me to vote for someone as chair for the commission, who I hadn’t had the pleasure of meeting,” said Lawrence Jackson, a professor of English and history at Johns Hopkins University, whose father’s grandfather was born into slavery in Virginia in 1855.
“It would be great to have an in-person meeting to make that final selection, or I hope that that could be a possibility,” Jackson said. “If a person is currently interested in being chair of the commission, it would be appropriate to let us know.”
One member did step up: Dayvon Love, director of public policy with Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle based in Baltimore City. The group agreed that Love, who was appointed to the commission by House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), would serve as interim chair until they convene again next month.
“I would like for us to go into 2027 with a work plan,” Love said.
No date was set on when and if the group would meet in person or virtually.
A preliminary report is due by Sept. 1, 2028, and a final report three months later by Dec. 1 of that year. The commission would sunset by June 30, 2029.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Henson appointment to Senate fiscal committee questioned
description: A member of the legislature's ethics panel questioned another lawmaker's appointment to the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee, noting that an ethics investigation of that lawmaker two years ago led to her being removed from a House fiscal committee.
text:
The appointment of Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) to the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee was questioned Friday in the Joint Legislative Ethics Committee, which recommended after an investigation two years ago that she not be allowed to serve on the House Appropriations Committee. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A member of the legislature’s ethics panel on Friday questioned another lawmaker’s appointment to the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee, noting that an ethics investigation of that lawmaker two years ago led to her being removed from a House fiscal committee.
Sen. Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) asked Friday whether the ethics committee’s 2024 recommendation that then-Del. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) be kept off the Appropriations Committee should also apply to Henson now that she’s in the Senate.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) appointed Henson to Budget and Taxation on Wednesday, along with other committee appointments for the 2027 General Assembly session.
“I’m concerned that a recommendation was made to one chamber,” Hershey asked during the brief public portion of Friday’s meeting of the Joint Committee on Legislative Ethics. “It appears that this other chamber now maybe has not fully recognized that recommendation and chosen to make a different decision than the joint ethics committee did.”
The brief public airing of Hershey’s concern is a rarity for a committee that does much of its work in secret.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) questioned whether Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) should be allowed to serve on a Senate budget committee in light of a 2024 rebuke. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
A spokesperson for Ferguson defended the appointment, saying a recommendation to the House speaker was not binding on the Senate president and that Henson has demonstrated “high ethical standards” since being appointed to the Senate in January 2025.
Henson, in an email Friday, thanked Ferguson for his confidence in her and took a swipe at Hershey, noting that the meeting came just weeks after “a contentious election in which the Maryland Senate Republican Caucus Committee, led by Senator Hershey, invested significant resources in an unsuccessful effort to defeat my reelection.”
As she has in the past, she questioned the previous Ethics Committee report, calling it “far more deserving of review than an appointment that falls squarely within the Senate President’s authority.”
“My experience navigating the Joint Committee’s investigative and disciplinary process raised serious concerns about conflicts of interest embedded in the process, questions of impartiality, and the independence of the legislative ethics process. Those issues deserve meaningful attention,” her statement said.
That 2o24 ethics rebuke followed an investigation of Henson’s role in sponsoring a bill for state funding to benefit Odenton-based Kingdom Kare, the nonprofit arm for the nondenominational Kingdom Celebration Center. Henson is a member of the church, as well as an attorney who represented the organization — facts she did not disclose, according to the ethics findings.
Then-House Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County) removed Henson from the House Appropriations Committee months before a final recommendation was released.
The panel found Henson’s relationship and actions created “at minimum, the appearance of a conflict of interest.” It also admonished her for an improper use of her official title in an advertisement for her law firm. The report cited “an ongoing practice by Delegate Henson to hide her relationship with Kingdom Kare as evidenced by her false responses to direct questions” from Jones and other lawmakers. It also cited a “lack of transparency with other colleagues,” and called on her to apologize to them.
Meet the new bosses, same as the old bosses: Senate reelects leaders for next session

The committee took the unusual step of making its 2024 report public. The vote of the committee was unanimous.
Hershey on Friday called Ferguson’s appointment of Henson to Budget and Taxation “in direct conflict” with the 2024 ethics report.
“I find it difficult to understand how that action was able to take place from the Senate President’s office … if this committee itself made the specific recommendation to not return her to the Appropriations Committee,” Hershey said. While he recognized that “they are two different chambers and there are two different committees,” Hershey said the appointment appears to have “ignored” the committee’s recommendation.
Henson was appointed to the Senate in 2025 to fill the vacancy created by Sarah Elfreth’s election to Congress, and served on the Judicial Proceedings Committee for her first two years in the Senate — even though Elfreth had been on Budget and Taxation. Henson was elected to a full term this month, becoming the first elected Black senator from Anne Arundel County.
When Henson first came to the Senate, Ferguson declined to say why she was appointed to Judicial Proceedings, but said at the time the she came to the Senate with a clean slate. For the latest appointment, Ferguson “carefully considered the 2024 report on then-Delegate Henson’s actions,” and her subsequent service in the Senate, his spokesperson said.
“She has been a productive, thoughtful, and communicative member of the Senate of Maryland,” the statement said. Besides, “An Ethics recommendation from a prior term to a former presiding officer from the opposite chamber is not considered binding in the next term, and certainly a recommendation regarding another chamber’s committee assignments is not directly applicable.
“He is confident that Senator Henson will abide by all State ethics statutes and rules and believes that past conduct should not automatically result in a permanent limitation on an individual in the future,” the statement said.
Hershey’s concerns were not addressed in public Friday. The committee moved to closed session after Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) asked if the matter should be discussed privately. By law, the committee’s work is confidential. Complaints, hearings and most outcomes are not released to the public.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State health officials jump at chance to delay Medicaid work requirements
description: Maryland Department of Health officials announced Friday that Medicaid recipients in the state will be able to keep their coverage under the federal healthcare program through June, even if they fail to keep up with new work requirements set to start in 2027.
text:
A six-month delay in the enforcement of new federal work requirements for Medicaid recipients could, temporarily, let thousands of low-income households in Maryland keep their healthcare coverage, at least for a few months. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)Maryland Department of Health officials announced Friday that Medicaid recipients in the state will be able to keep their coverage under the federal healthcare program through June, even if they fail to keep up with new work requirements that start in 2027.
State officials are taking advantage of a “hold harmless” period recently offered by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services that grants states and affected residents an additional six months to adjust to the new requirements to qualify for Medicaid.
Those requirements — that recipients prove they are working or in school at least 80 hours a month, among other changes — are expected to cost thousands of Marylanders their coverage under the joint federal-state health insurance plan for low-income families and households facing other challenges.
Healthcare advocates applauded the delay, even though they still worry about the impact to Medicaid coverage once the hold harmless period lifts in July.
Administration gives states 6 more months to implement Medicaid work requirement

“No Marylander should lose access to needed medical care simply because of paperwork or administrative barriers,” said Gene Ransom, CEO for MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society, in a written statement Friday. “This six-month period gives the state an important opportunity to get the implementation right, but it does not eliminate our concerns about the potential loss of coverage under HR 1.”
Ransom is referring to the budget reconciliation legislation Congress passed in August 2025, sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which imposed the new work requirement rules. The changes will also require that some Medicaid recipients prove eligibility twice a year, rather than annually.
Without an adequate runway to adopt those requirements, state officials and healthcare advocates warned that the new eligibility rules could lead to upwards of 100,000 people from Maryland losing coverage, as recipients struggled to keep up with the increased paperwork and state agencies rushed to adapt to the increased administrative burden.
Recognizing those concerns, officials with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced last week that states could have an optional “hold harmless” period to work out any challenges before kicking people from their healthcare coverage due to the work requirements.
“The delay in enforcement only applies to federal Medicaid work requirements. Other federal eligibility and enrollment changes scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027 will be implemented,” the state health department said in the Friday notice. “Maryland will continue implementing these requirements consistent with federal law while working to ensure eligible residents maintain access to health coverage.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Experts: Fuel Spill Could Swiftly Reach Oʻahu’s Fragile Coast
description: The fuel spill has already spread to a sanctuary for endangered native plants located next to H-Power.
text:
Reworld officials have asserted that a flat groundwater table along Oʻahu’s ʻEwa plain is helping keep the massive fuel spill at H-Power contained to the area right around the city incinerator plant. 
There’s no indication the contamination has reached the nearby shoreline, they said Thursday, and they expressed little concern that it would.
However, local hydrologists and community members say the situation there is far more complex and strong concerns remain that the fuel could eventually seep into West Oʻahu’s fragile coastal ecosystem.
Experts say there are strong concerns that the H-Power fuel spill at Campbell Industrial Park could reach the nearby shoreline.  (Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2017)
The water table there may be flat, University of Hawaiʻi Mānoa hydrologist Chris Shuler said, but the area’s underground caves, cracks and fissures might also give the polluted water faster pathways to the ocean.
Those formations are part of the mostly limestone subterranean landscape that connects that corner of West Oʻahu to the shoreline, said Shuler, who’s studied the hydrology there in recent years. 
“There’s a high potential for any fluid —  water or petroleum — to move through that kind of an aquifer quickly,” Shuler said Friday. The fuel-polluted water could move in ways that “are hard to understand,” Shuler said, without knowing all the potential underground pathways.
The Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, confirmed Friday that it has opened an investigation into the spill based on its proximity to the shoreline. An agency spokesman said it’s been helping the state Health Department since Aug. 21, when state officials first reached out to the federal agency.
Shuler’s comments came after Reworld Vice President Michael Van Brunt on Thursday compared the leak of an estimated 400,000 gallons of incinerator fuel from an underground pipe at H-Power earlier this year to spilling water on a flat table. 
“It will spread out, but it’ll stop,” Van Brunt said during a press conference held in Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi’s office. “It helps us keep it in that generalized area. We know where the material is. It’s sitting mostly below the site.”
Brunt displayed a map with the 22 monitoring wells Reworld has installed since its workers reported the spill in May. Several wells to the west of the H-Power facility have not detected the fuel, according to the Reworld map. The company, which contracts with the city to run H-Power, is still working to install monitoring wells south of the incinerator plant.
“It has stayed on site, it has not migrated to the coast,” Brunt said.
Shuler said the map offers an incomplete, two-dimensional picture. 
It’s possible, he said, for the fuel to move past the area and toward the shoreline at depths not monitored by the wells. Reworld, Shuler said, should release more data from the wells, including the depths at which they’re monitoring.
“When not a lot of information is shared, that doesn’t help with trust-building,” Shuler said. “I’d be happy to see all the information that’s available.” 
Groundwater discharges into coastal waters near the plant at various spots, he added.
‘More Than Just An Environmental Thing’
Board of Water Supply Manager and Chief Engineer Ernie Lau told Civil Beat Friday that the area’s 400-foot-thick “caprock” layer, made of limestone and muddy clay, will prompt the fuel to flow horizontally toward the coast, not vertically down into the ground.
That means there’s no risk to the island’s drinking water supply, but the coast is a different concern.
Community advocates and volunteers, meanwhile, fear the spill could jeopardize efforts to restore native, endangered ‘Ewa Hinahina plants at the Kīpuka o Kāhinahina plant sanctuary just west of the H-Power facility.
This map, first displayed by Reworld executives, shows how far the company believes the fuel spill has spread based on its monitoring wells. The dotted line, which includes part of the Kīpuka o Kāhinahina sanctuary, shows Reworld’s believed boundary. The black dots represent monitoring wells where the fuel has not been detected.  (Courtesy: City and County of Honolulu)
The plant once grew abundantly across the ʻEwa plain, said Ulukoa Duhaylonsod, cultural director and founder of the nonprofit Kauiki o Kapo. Decades of industrialization decimated the plant, prompting federal officials to place it on the endangered species list.
The Kipuka sanctuary is one of the last places to find ‘ewa hinahina on Oʻahu, Duhaylonsod said. His nonprofit has struggled to keep the plant alive on city-owned sanctuary land set between H-Power and an industrial yard.
Van Brunt’s map indicates the spill has already reached the sanctuary.
The plants at the sanctuary rely on the brackish groundwater there to survive, said Duhaylonsod, who’s from the area. The area’s aquifer used to have a top freshwater layer, he added, before heavy industrialization depleted it.
“This is more than just an environmental thing. This is our home,” Duhaylonsod said. “This is the place that we grew up, that we all love. So we malama because we care, because we love this place.”
He added that community-led plans are underway to test the groundwater at the sanctuary.
Civil Beat Reporters Matthew Leonard and Ben Angarone contributed.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Community looking for answers after DA declines to charge officer who shot Corey Ruiz
description: The decision Thursday by Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne not to charge Madison police officer Keil Baitinger-Peterson for fatally shooting 38-year-old Corey Ruiz in Madison in July drew passionate responses from the community and calls for systemic change.  Attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the Ruiz family, said video depicting the shooting[...]
text:
Protesters gather at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison on Thursday, Nov. 19, in remembrance of Corey Ruiz. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The decision Thursday by Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne not to charge Madison police officer Keil Baitinger-Peterson for fatally shooting 38-year-old Corey Ruiz in Madison in July drew passionate responses from the community and calls for systemic change. 
Attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the Ruiz family, said video depicting the shooting “cries out for a civil rights lawsuit.” But families bringing such cases in Wisconsin face an uphill battle in court. Meanwhile, local residents are navigating a crisis in trust in local government and in one another.
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Widely circulated video depicting the shooting was captured by bystanders using their phones in the early afternoon on July 22. Madison police officers do not have body cameras. Dash camera video from a Madison police car also shows Ruiz struggling with several officers in the middle of the intersection, causing a traffic backup. One of the officers used a taser on Ruiz. Then, while Ruiz was on the ground, Baitinger-Peterson fired three shots to Ruiz’s chest and head. Officers had pursued Ruiz after receiving reports of bicycle thefts and a burglary. 
Before firing, according to an investigative file by the Wisconsin DOJ’s Division of Criminal Investigation, Baitinger-Peterson claimed that he heard another officer tell Ruiz to “drop the knife or you’ll be shot in the head.” Baitinger-Peterson’s DCI interview was the only officer interview which described this warning.
Baitinger-Peterson and the other officers said that the knife made them fear for their own safety and that of their colleagues.
After Baintinger-Peterson fired, other officers immediately stepped away from Ruiz. One of the officers appeared to cover her mouth in shock. Baitinger-Peterson dropped to his knees and continued searching and restraining a motionless Ruiz. Baitinger-Peterson later said that Ruiz had a knife, which was photographed at the scene by investigator.
Use of force questioned
“There is nothing in the videos the district attorney showed us that justifies this officer stepping back, pulling his gun, and firing three shots at point-blank range at Corey Ruiz after he had been tased and was on the ground, hitting him once in the chest and with the kill shot to his head,” Crump said during a press conference after the charging decision was announced. “The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived. It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”
“The video of Corey’s killing is deeply troubling and raises serious questions about the force used against him,” Gov.-elect David Crowley said in a statement. “I recognize the pain and frustration many people are feeling following the District Attorney’s decision, especially in communities of color that have watched similar tragedies unfold for generations.” 
Signs at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison on Thursday, Nov. 19, (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“People have every right to be upset and to make their voices heard,” Crowley continued. “I encourage the community to continue speaking out and demanding answers, but to do so peacefully. More violence will not bring Corey back or change the District Attorney’s decision. It will only add to the pain of a community already carrying so much. As Wisconsin’s first Black governor-elect, I understand that these incidents are part of a much longer history that has left generations of Americans questioning whether our justice system values their lives equally and whether law enforcement officers are held to the same standards as everyone else.”
Other elected officials also released statements on the charging decision Thursday. “The death of Corey Ruiz this past summer has deeply affected our community, and I recognize the strong emotions surrounding the District Attorney’s decision,” said Dane County Executive Melissa Agard. “Corey’s life mattered, and my heart remains with his family and loved ones as they continue to grieve. They deserve our grace and compassion during this difficult time. We must continue working toward safer communities and a justice system that is effective and fair for all. I have faith in our community’s ability to express its emotions and convictions passionately and peacefully, while treating one another with respect.”
Protesters at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets  (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“The people calling for justice for Corey Ruiz know the truth: that he should still be alive today,” said Sen Dora Drake (D-Milwaukee), who will serve as the next president pro tempore of the state Senate and chair of the Legislative Black Caucus. “Since this summer, there were millions of views online of people watching multiple Madison Police Officers hold Mr. Ruiz down before one officer chose to shoot him from point-blank range. The Dane County District Attorney’s decision today is not only disturbing but continues to amplify the mistrust in our legal institutions. Continuing to deny victims of violence equal treatment under the law, regardless of who you are, will never allow our state to fully heal. Corey’s family was denied their day in court. Now, as elected leaders, it is our duty to reform this flawed system to ensure that the law is equally applied to everyone.” 
Rep. Sheila Stubbs (D-Madison) said in a statement, “I am shocked to have learned that there will be no criminal charges for the officer who took the life of a son, brother, father, and member of this community.” Stubbs, who joined the Ruiz family and Crump at the press conference Thursday, added that “this is not the decision this community was expecting, and it is one that will have lasting detrimental impacts on our city and the trust between residents of color and law enforcement.”
The challenges in bringing criminal charges against police 
Ozanne said in his decision that “a knife can be used as a dangerous weapon and may pose a grave danger of bodily harm and/or death to an individual.” Under Wisconsin law, he said, a person may threaten or use “force reasonably believed necessary” to stop a threat. “A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however, I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” said Ozanne. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
Steven Wright, a clinical professor at UW-Madison’s Law School and a former attorney for the U.S. Department of Justice, explained that police officers are afforded layers of legal protection that lawyers must overcome to bring a criminal charges. 
“The odds of making it to trial tend to be very, very slim,” Wright told the Wisconsin Examiner. Officers involved in shootings have qualified immunity, which often leads judges to dismiss lawsuits. “And so, lawyers spend a lot of time just trying to get over that immunity issue before anything else,” said Wright. “And many fail. The U.S. Supreme Court, I think it’s fair to say, keeps raising the bar for people to overcome qualified immunity. And so that’s why we see so few cases.”
Protesters gather at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Local officials might also want  to “put this in the rearview mirror as quickly as possible,” Wright said, and move towards a settlement. A small number of police shootings have also been reviewed under Wisconsin’s John Doe law, which allows a local judge to review a case where prosecutors declined to file changes and decide whether probable cause exists to appoint special prosecutors for a second look. 
The dynamics of police shooting investigations also present challenges. In Wisconsin, although police departments cannot lead investigations into their own shootings, the local district attorney who routinely relies on those same officers decides whether charges should be filed. “There is the argument that there is a conflict of interest here,” said Wright.
Additionally, police officers who fatally shoot civilians often refuse to allow their interviews to be recorded. This was the case with Baitinger-Peterson and the other Madison officers involved in Ruiz’s killing. 
Without a recorded statement, officers can more easily change or adjust their recollection of a shooting. Even just getting through the discovery and document obtaining phase takes time. “By that time, people’s memories fade, people’s stories change,” Wright said. “And so, because there’s not the original recording in the document, it’s very hard to compare, ‘Well you said this immediately after the shooting, now you’re saying this.” 
“Police unions tend to be pretty powerful in many jurisdictions,” said Wright. “And among the rules that they have are that — and they train their members when these types of shootings happen — [to] ask for your representative and these rights.” 
(Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“I don’t think that it comes as a giant surprise to many Americans that police investigations of police officers are often handled very differently and sometimes more kindly to other officers, as opposed to the rest of the community,” he added. “Those are things that can be fixed by legislation. Those are things that cities can choose to do, but again, you know, that’s a very tough political accomplishment, I think, to achieve these things.”
Crowley vowed that his office will “look beyond this one case and examine what we can do differently to prevent tragedies like this from happening again.”
 “That means reviewing how officer-involved deaths are investigated and how information is shared with families and the public,” he said. “It also means taking a hard look at use of force policies and training, while listening to communities most affected by these encounters.” 
Crowley added that he will work with lawmakers, law enforcement and community leaders “to identify meaningful changes that can make our justice system more transparent and help rebuild public trust.” 
“We cannot change what happened to Corey, but we can take responsibility for making sure his death leads to serious conversation about how we move forward so that every Wisconsinite can have confidence that they will be treated with dignity and fairness, regardless of their race or ZIP code. That is the standard our state must work toward, and I am committed to it,” Crowley said.
Community responds 
Community members gathered at the corner of Williamson and Baldwin on Thursday evening to protest the charging decision, chant and comfort each other.
Some in the crowd, distrusting media coverage of the shooting and its aftermath, confronted a group of television reporters and demanded that they leave. Overhead, two drones monitored the gathering for hours.
One participant was a combat veteran who said he was appalled by the behavior of officers. Another was a law student who argued that the laws regulating “reasonable” use of force  need to be changed. Yet another was an unhoused man who claimed to have known Ruiz, and said that although he was imperfect that he didn’t deserve what happened to him. 
A petition to recall  Ozanne as district attorney circulated through the group. Later in the evening a march was escorted by police. 
 (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
One young man named Kofi said he came out “to advocate against the consistent injustice that plagues our entire country, and that starts with taking out these cops, putting them in prison, giving them justice that families have been asking for, and that goes for countless Black victims.” 
Amanda Stein, an ordained elder in the United Methodist Church, said she joined the Ruiz family and others earlier Thursday to pray. “We just thought it was really important to be present throughout the day,” said Stein, “whether it was at the Center for Black Excellence, or at the church, or here on the street, for us to walk alongside, listen, be present, for people going through a lot of pain right now.” 
“This strikes really into the heart of the community when something like that happens in broad daylight, in front of passersby,” Stein said. “It’s unspeakable.” 
Stein said that she wants to hear more about the shooting and its aftermath from the candidates for  mayor of Madison. “I do think we need to be holding our elected officials to better accountability,” she said. “And I wouldn’t necessarily say even so much the legal aspect but coming as a person of faith: How is this affecting the heart and the lifeblood of our communities? Because there’s real pain and I think, often, our government and elected officials will lean into the legalities and the, for lack of a better term, just the formality of process and it would mean so much if we could actually have contact with one another in conversation rather than confrontation.”

title: North Slope Borough sues state to stop planned expansion of tax break for oil firms
description: The North Slope Borough sued the state of Alaska on Thursday, seeking to halt a proposed petroleum property tax change that could slash local tax revenue by more than 70%, leaving the North Slope unable to pay debts, operate schools and fund basic services. “A reduction of this magnitude would have devastating consequences for North […]
text:
ConocoPhillips' CD-5 drill site is one of the existing extensions to the company's major Alpine development on Alaska's North Slope. A new Alpine extension, CD-8, is provoking objections because of its proposed location: two miles from the Iñupiaq village of Nuiqsut. (ConocoPhillips)The North Slope Borough sued the state of Alaska on Thursday, seeking to halt a proposed petroleum property tax change that could slash local tax revenue by more than 70%, leaving the North Slope unable to pay debts, operate schools and fund basic services.
“A reduction of this magnitude would have devastating consequences for North Slope communities and severely impair the borough’s ability to sustain essential services and government operations,” borough attorneys wrote in a request for a preliminary injunction that would bar the state from making the change in the immediate future. 
The suit, filed in Anchorage Superior Court and assigned to Judge Yvonne Lamoureux, names the governor, lieutenant governor and other officials as defendants.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The state’s proposed change would affect local governments across Alaska and the state itself. Under state law, Alaska charges a 2% tax on qualifying oil and gas property, and local governments may take custody of some or all of the revenue generated from property within their borders. 
In a public notice Oct. 29, the Alaska Department of Revenue said it is planning to significantly increase a tax deduction for “intangible drilling expenses,” netting oil and gas companies a significantly smaller tax bill.
“I am concerned that the proposed methodology could place more than 70% of the Borough’s assessed property tax base at risk,” wrote the North Slope Borough’s finance director, Fadil Limani, in an affidavit submitted with the borough’s legal complaint.
On the North Slope, that tax accounts for the vast majority of local government revenue. While the Alaska Municipal League and the Kenai Peninsula Borough have submitted public comments against the proposed change, only the North Slope Borough is thus far named as a plaintiff.
Unusually, the state did not notify local governments or state legislators about the proposed tax change until Nov. 10, more than a week after the public notice was published. 
“As the representative of communities directly affected by North Slope oil and gas property taxation, I should not have to learn of a consequential proposed change through others rather than through the formal notice process established by the Legislature,” wrote Rep. Robyn Niayuq Frier, D-Utqiagvik, in a public comment requesting the state to halt the regulation change.    

Rep. Robyn Niayuq Frier, D-Utqiagvik, speaks on the House floor on the last day of the regular legislative session on May 20, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The proposed regulation change wasn’t signed by the director of the department’s tax division but by a political appointee, Deputy Commissioner Lee Cruise.
The reason for the change, listed by the state in an appendix, is to “streamline regulatory ambiguity” under an administrative order issued by Gov. Mike Dunleavy in August 2025.
In its request for preliminary injunction, the North Slope Borough suggests a different motive.
For years, the state and Oil Search Alaska LLC have been fighting a legal dispute over the proper value of that company’s oil and gas property on the North Slope.
This year, the Alaska Department of Revenue estimated the taxable value of Oil Search’s relevant Pikka Project property at $52.6 million for 2024, $128.5 million for 2025, and $197.8 million according to the North Slope Borough’s legal complaint.
Oil Search has said the taxable value should instead be $2 million, $7 million, and $1.9 million respectively, according to the North Slope Borough, according to the complaint.
Those values are almost identical to what would be collected if the new tax exemptions become final.
In its request for a preliminary injunction, the North Slope Borough says that “the new regulations appear to be the result of lobbying efforts by Oil Search based on the identical language in the proposed regulation and Oil Search’s internal documents.”
Under the standard regulatory timeline, the state’s proposed change would take effect Dec. 30, immediately before taxes are assessed on Jan. 1.
For that reason, the borough said in its filings, it is requesting a speedy hearing on the issue.
No court date had been set by the end of Friday.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Will Alaska’s blue wave become a blue waste?
description: The morning after the Nov. 3 election, I woke up mad. As a lifelong nonpartisan Alaska voter, I was mad because Democrats swept the nation. They won back the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House, and were on track to clinch the U.S. Senate. You’d think that would make me, a left-of-center guy, happy. I’ll […]
text:
Democrat Mary Peltola waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)The morning after the Nov. 3 election, I woke up mad.
As a lifelong nonpartisan Alaska voter, I was mad because Democrats swept the nation. They won back the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House, and were on track to clinch the U.S. Senate.
You’d think that would make me, a left-of-center guy, happy. I’ll admit I am delighted that Dan S. Sullivan, a senator whose office never seems to answer the phone, is on his way out, and I hope Peltola will actually try to represent all Alaskans. But as a student of history, I remember how often the Democratic Party has disappointed me and working-class Americans this century, and I fear it will repeat the same mistake with this win.
This is the era of whiplash politics for a reason: each party rides voters’ frustration with the other into power, then fails to deliver. Yet Americans, Alaskans included, need help now more than ever. I just don’t think it’s going to come.
 A lifetime of letdowns

A CNBC survey this July found that 63% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, with 71% of respondents saying a single one-week delay in pay would cause a major hardship or a critical emergency. In Alaska, about half of our neighbors are struggling. I’ve been one of them. Two years ago, I was an unhoused teacher in Anchorage. After my apartment flooded, I rotated between friends’ couches, Planet Fitness and my Anchorage School District classroom. It’s not what the American Dream promised me, a straight white male with a masters degree, and it’s not something either party seems interested in fixing.
Call me a “double hater.” I’m one of the 21% of voters who view both parties unfavorably, according to a Wall Street Journal poll this fall, up from 13% in the 2022 midterms.
That distrust comes from a lifetime of watching. In 2000, my Ryan Middle School history teacher, an Iñupiaq woman, taught me how the U.S. Supreme Court settled George W. Bush’s election, not voters. As a teenager, I watched the bombing of Baghdad on a friend’s TV, and later saw the richest country on Earth abandon its own citizens after Hurricane Katrina. In 2008, I watched how President Obama, elected on a platform of hope, continued bailing out the institutions that caused the Great Recession while my parents’ investments tanked.
Again and again, the two parties that have traded power since the 1850s have let me and lots of Americans down.
 Who decides “What’s Next”?

This week in Denver, Democratic party insiders gathered to decide what to do with the blue wave. The “What’s Next” conference, held Nov. 12-14, is a private, invitation-only gathering of about 2,000 guests hosted by a group called Majority Democrats. The name sounds harmless. But the group has been largely funded by Stephen and Sue Mandel of Greenwich, Connecticut, who have put $20 million into building the Democrat’s centrist faction. Stephen Mandel founded Lone Pine Capital, which is heavily invested in artificial intelligence. And according to the Colorado Times Recorder, Mandel spent tens of millions of dollars in this year’s Democratic primaries backing corporate-friendly candidates, many of whom lost to progressives.
So why am I upset about Nov. 3? Because people like the Mandels, who back losing candidates that refuse to empower the seven in 10 Americans opposing AI data center construction or the 44% of Americans struggling to pay for at least one basic necessity are claiming the majority. Public school taught me that seven out of 10 is a vast majority. Yet the needs of the many keep getting ignored for the benefit of the rich. We saw it when Trump promised to drain the swamp and make America great again, then cut SNAP benefits — with Sullivan’s support) and we’re seeing it now as the group Majority Democrats works to blunt the progressive Democrat wins that powered this wave.
 What it means for Alaska
To bring it home: Mary Peltola and our next governor, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, aren’t progressive Democrats. They won because Alaskans are tired of eight years of Trump-aligned leadership that pillaged this state, including a governor who became the first in state history to veto school funding below the level set in law. As a teacher, I felt every one of those vetoes.
 Alaska and America’s Democratic majority need to change how things are done. We live in a time of rampant corruption, record corporate profits built on post-Covid price hikes, off-the-charts climate chaos  — the worst coastal flooding on record in the Kuskokwim Delta and Juneau’s hottest August day ever — polluted water and dying wildlife  — a Western Arctic caribou herd at its lowest in nearly 50 years, Yukon king salmon runs too small to fish, and moose hunts canceled after a brutal winter hit calf survival.
If Peltola and Kreiss-Tomkins don’t take a stand and hold accountable the people who keep profiting off the actual majority, they will lose their next elections. Peltola, Blue Dog champion of the Willow Oil project, already lost once to Floridian Nick Begich, III, in 2024. I fear the new Democratic majorities in Congress will help see the blue wave become a blue waste like so many other Democratic hopes before.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: NU regents, Nebraska Medicine forge ahead with $2.748B ‘Project Health’ in new agreement
description: LINCOLN — The University of Nebraska and Nebraska Medicine approved a new agreement Friday to move forward with the $2.748 billion “Project Health” mission in Omaha. The regents unanimously approved the memorandum of understanding Friday morning, and the Nebraska Medicine Board of Directors, which includes three regents, unanimously approved it hours later. [...]
text:
A model detailing how the University of Nebraska Medical Center's footprint would grow in Omaha with the $2 billion "Project Health" endeavor sits in front of University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold. Oct. 3, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The University of Nebraska and Nebraska Medicine approved a new agreement Friday to move forward with the $2.748 billion “Project Health” mission in Omaha.
The regents unanimously approved the memorandum of understanding Friday morning, and the Nebraska Medicine Board of Directors, which includes three regents, unanimously approved it hours later. The document lays out an assumption that Nebraska Medicine will invest at least $800 million more into the project, leaving a funding gap of about $856.4 million.
The Omaha Community Foundation, which came on to lead the nonprofit alongside NU this summer, has agreed to help raise the final funds.
Regent Paul Kenney of Amherst, chair of the NU Board of Regents. April 23, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“We’re not quite to the finish line, but we’re getting really close. I can see the tape,” NU Regent Paul Kenney of Amherst, the chair of the board, said during the morning meeting.
“We’re close to that tape, and hopefully we can get through it.”
Project Health is a multi-year endeavor to build a new 1.54-million-square-foot building that includes a state-of-the-art teaching hospital and clinical learning facility.
‘Dedication of partnership’
Dr. Michael Ash, CEO of Nebraska Medicine, said after the regents meeting that the day really represented “partnership.” He said at the “heart” of the MOU was bringing Nebraska Medicine to the main decision-making tables on senior management and project management teams. The agreement also gives voting rights to the architect, Kiewit Building Group Inc., and contractor, HDR Architecture Inc., in certain project decisions or amendments.
“We have a shared mission, shared values, shared campus, and this really elevates that dedication of partnership to each other,” Ash said of NU and Nebraska Medicine.
Dr. Michael Ash, CEO of Nebraska Medicine, speaks at a forum with dozens of Nebraska state senators regarding a University of Nebraska proposal to buy out the share of Nebraska Medicine owned by Clarkson Regional Health Services. Jan. 14, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Kenney said the agreement “sets the roadmap for the future days coming.”
“We’re excited about the facility that will lead the central part of the United States on technology of healthcare,” Kenney said.
In addition to specifying fundraising responsibilities, Nebraska Medicine will also assume responsibility for legally defending any challenge to the funding model or ownership structure of Project Health. The regents agreed to sell certain property that Nebraska Medicine uses in Omaha and Bellevue to the nonprofit board for $310 million.
The project is expected to be completed in 2032. Nebraska Medicine is the clinical partner to NU’s University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha.
Regent Jack Stark of Omaha, who has taught across NU, including at UNMC, said he was proud the project would allow Nebraska Medicine to add more outpatient services.
UNMC Student Regent Allie Daro, a fourth-year medical student, said she was excited for the future of Nebraska Medicine and the healthcare it delivers but also for the academic opportunities for future students.
Forging ahead
Regents called the emergency meeting for the MOU late Thursday. Kenney, Ash and other regents said it was because they needed to move ahead with ordering iron for the project, which they’re eyeing from a European company. Ash said certain discounts will expire soon, so moving ahead now allows the project to remain closer to its estimated $2.748 billion price tag.
“We don’t have to pay for it or anything, but it’s the final day to order it,” Kenney said of the iron. “… If you don’t order the iron today, then you fall back behind.”
Speaker of the Nebraska Legislature John Arch, left, talks with former Speaker Jim Scheer of Norfolk. Scheer now serves on the University of Nebraska Board of Regents. June 6, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Regent Jim Scheer of Norfolk said Nebraska will be “lucky” to have what will soon be the “epitome of an educational medical facility that no one else will hold a candle to.”
“We take the doubt and the resistance away, and now it’s full steam ahead and looking for those opportunities and the economic growth that it’s going to spur along,” Scheer said.
In the spring, questions surrounded whether NU would be the sole parent organization of Nebraska Medicine after the exit of Clarkson Regional Health Services or if another philanthropic organization could take Clarkson’s place. By mid-2026, the Omaha Community Foundation stepped forward and joined the nonprofit structure.
Ash said he’s comfortable with the funding model and that “philanthropy allows things to happen that otherwise wouldn’t.”
“We’re really fortunate to be in a state that’s both investing in the future of education and research but also have a donor community, a philanthropic community, that is so committed to elevating education research but also the care of people,” Ash said.
Ending a ‘clan war’
Regent Rob Schafer of Beatrice told his colleagues he is generally not in favor of selling off real estate. However, in this case, he felt the opportunity was “so unique,” and given NU’s longstanding relationship with the Omaha Community Foundation and ongoing stake in Nebraska Medicine, it deserved his support.
President Jeffrey Gold of the University of Nebraska system, left, joins Regent Rob Schafer of Beatrice, NU Board of Regents chair, after being formally installed as the ninth system president of the University of Nebraska. Sept. 5, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Schafer said moving forward would also be good for NU’s future.
“There’s been a clan war going on here the last couple of years, and that needs to stop,” Schafer said during the meeting. “We need to get the whole state and all parties behind it and put the past in the past and move forward.”
Schafer explained after the meeting that there seemed to be a disconnect between Omaha philanthropists and NU “really for, in my opinion, for no good reason.”
“We acquired Clarkson’s half thinking we’re doing a good thing and kind of almost felt as if no good deed goes unpunished, and I’m not for sure what’s at the crux of that,” Schafer told the Nebraska Examiner. “Maybe at the end of the day it’s just lack of communication.”
‘Only in Nebraska, I’m very confident’
NU President Jeffrey Gold, who led UNMC as chancellor for 10 years before becoming president in July 2024, noted the idea for Project Health grew out of a meeting about a decade ago in his UNMC office with the then-speaker of the Legislature, Scheer. 
Interim University of Nebraska Medical Center Chancellor Dele Davies. Jan. 15, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Gold, a doctor, said that having dedicated his life to the delivery of healthcare, he knows the project will attract the “very best” students and healthcare professionals nationwide. He predicts it will also be a “major boost” for Nebraska’s economy.
“What this will do for the quality and safety of care that this facility not only provides to this region but provides on a national and global level is truly remarkable,” Gold said. “I’m really deeply honored to be sitting in my role as the president of the university at this time on this day.”
UNMC Chancellor H. Dele Davies offered one word to sum up his feelings to the board: “Gratitude.”
“I cannot speak clearly about how thankful I am and how thankful all our faculty, staff and students speaking to us are to see this project going forward,” Davies said.
Schafer said he hopes all of Nebraska can get behind and support the project, NU and Gold.
“He’s worked tirelessly on this, and this was his brainchild 10 years ago,” Schafer said. “We felt it was really important that we have the person whose dream and vision it was to come up with this, that that person’s got a strong, active leadership role in seeing it through.”
Asked about his confidence in reaching the finish line and running through the tape at the end, Ash said: “Only in Nebraska, I’m very confident.”

title: One last warm Saturday of the year?
description:
Saturday is forecasted to be the warmest Nov. 21 in Vermont this century.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  One last warm Saturday of the year?.
text:
A motorcyclist travels along the Notch Road in Cambridge during stick season on Thursday, October 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Keep the barbecue tongs out and sweaters tucked in the closet. Plan for a stroll through local farmers’ markets or a hike through November’s barren trees. Vermont has at least one more warm Saturday this year. 
Saturday is forecasted to be the warmest Nov. 21 in Vermont this century. The National Weather Service’s Burlington office predicts that the high will be 60 degrees with a low of 40. 
The 21st century’s previous hottest Nov. 21 in Vermont came in 2005, when the high, recorded in Berlin, was 55 degrees. The coolest Nov. 21 since 2000 was in 2014, with a high of 22 degrees.
This century, Vermont’s average Nov. 21 high temperature was 39.8 degrees, and the average low was 23. 
Countries across the world are seeing warmer-than-usual temperatures. Last month’s average global temperature was the hottest October in recorded history: 59.95 degrees.
That global average sent alarm bells to the United Nations, as it meant October was the third consecutive month to surpass a temperature limit set in the 2015 Paris Agreement. The treaty, signed by members of the UN, meant to hold warming temperatures steady. 
The UN’s climate negotiations, scheduled to conclude Friday, saw countries banding together seeking a solution.
For those who feel 60 degrees is too unseasonably warm for a Nov. 21 in Vermont, not to fret. Next week’s highs are expected to reach the 40s with lows in the far more familiar 20s and 30s.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Court further delays lead azide detonation at Middletown plant
description: The detonation of a lead-based explosive material planned for Monday in southeast Iowa will be held off until the court can rule on a lawsuit over the federal permit for the action, though the U.S. Department of Justice indicated the Army could skirt the permit requirement. The lawsuit, filed on behalf of Iowa environmental groups, […]
text:
A sign sits along the fence of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 20, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa where the Army intends to detonate a degraded explosive material. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)The detonation of a lead-based explosive material planned for Monday in southeast Iowa will be held off until the court can rule on a lawsuit over the federal permit for the action, though the U.S. Department of Justice indicated the Army could skirt the permit requirement.
The lawsuit, filed on behalf of Iowa environmental groups, alleged the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency did not adequately consider the human health or environmental outcomes of the detonation of 68 drums of lead azide, nor did it properly consider “less dangerous alternatives.”
The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. Appellate Court for the Eighth District, asked the court to either rule or issue an administrative stay on the permit before detonation, which was originally planned for Nov. 20 at noon. On Thursday evening, acting Secretary of the Army, Hon. Adam Telle announced the detonation would be postponed until Monday, Nov. 23. 
Following the postponement, Gov. Kim Reynolds said in a statement she had asked Telle to delay the detonation. On Friday evening, Reynolds activated a State Emergency Operations Center ahead of the planned detonation to coordinate state, federal and local operations.
Iowans, lawmakers, public officials and environmental groups began expressing concern about the potential effects from the detonation of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant after the Army released maps showing the potential spread of air and dust containing lead particles. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Some lawmakers were concerned by the short period of time between when the Army made the public announcement and informed the state and when the detonation was scheduled. They, like concerned Iowans and the petitioning environmental groups, questioned if the planned detonation and associated release of lead was the best course of action. 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy sent a letter to Reynolds Friday afternoon, detailing the collaboration between federal agencies to prioritize “health and safety” of all Americans living within the potentially impacted area. Depending on the weather, plume modeling has indicated the impacted area could stretch to parts of Illinois. 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy. (Photo courtesy of EPA)
In his letter to Reynolds, Macy said EPA was working with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the U.S. Department of Defense to “ensure” the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.” 
“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, which was sent to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.
Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice – the groups suing EPA over the permit – held a news conference Friday to discuss the lawsuit. 
Michael Schmidt with the Iowa Environmental Council said events leading up to the lawsuit have “demonstrated that we cannot rely on the federal government, including the Army and EPA, to adequately inform Iowans” about the risks posed by the planned detonation.
“As such, today we are calling on our state leaders, including Governor Reynolds, to take control of the communication regarding this potential detonation,” Schmidt said. “Iowans deserve a transparent, coordinated, and effective response to this unprecedented event.” 
The governor’s office did not respond to a request for comment Friday.
Considering the alternatives
The letter from Macy summarized the work between EPA and Army since March — when the Army identified the degraded state of the lead azide — which informed EPA’s decision to grant the permit.
Macy wrote that the Army “concluded the only viable option was a controlled detonation in place with extensive mitigation measures” after “considering and exhausting all other proposed alternatives.” 
The alternatives described in the letter include: treating the barrels with a chemical, using heavy earth-moving equipment to build a structure around the containers, moving the lead azide to IAAAP’s existing open detonation unit and leaving the 68 drums in place. 
Each alternative, according to Macy’s letter, presented “an unacceptable safety risk” with a high likelihood of accidental detonation of the explosive material due to the “advanced crystallization.” 
Environmental groups, in their lawsuit, allege EPA had an “arbitrary acceptance of the Army’s dismissal of treatment alternatives” that would have avoided a “blast plume.” 
Wally Taylor, legal chair of the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, said in the news conference Friday it was “discouraging that the EPA did not require those alternatives to be properly examined.” 
“We think that the Army has done the right thing, at least initially, in postponing the proposed detonation, but they still plan to do it,” Taylor said. “We are asking the court to send this whole process – the permit, the plan to detonate – back for further review, and let’s do it right.” 
In a post on X announcing the postponement, Telle said the Monday postponement was the “latest possible moment” for the detonation “prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.” 
Map from Nov. 18 showing the potential area that could have lead particles in the air following a now postponed detonation of lead azide in Middletown. (Photo via U.S. Army)
Asked Friday if the environmental groups worried that the explosive material would detonate on its own while the issue played out in the court, Taylor said “we need more assurance that there really is that danger and that immediacy that requires detonation right now.” 
“It seems to me that that’s a pretty lame excuse when that material has been there for years and years, and now they’re delaying another few days until Monday,” Taylor said. 
DOJ points to code allowing detonation without permit 
The administrative stay means that it would be unlawful for the Army to proceed with the detonation under the EPA permit questioned by the lawsuit, according to Thien Chau, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, until the court can consider the full motion. 
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a motion in the case on Friday telling the court it intends to file an opposition, on behalf of EPA, before Nov. 22. 
The motion acknowledges the administrative stay and the Army’s Nov. 23 detonation date, then says that “in qualifying emergency situations” EPA regulations authorize the Army “to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit” when there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”
Chau, said it wasn’t appropriate for him to speculate why the DOJ included that in their motion, but he said the regulation cited is “an extraordinary and extreme backstop for situations where there are truly no other things that could be done.” 
“It’s an incredibly high bar, and we strongly urge the army not to rely on it,” Chau said. 
A spokesperson with the Army Sustainment Command did not respond Friday to a message asking if the Army intended to proceed with the Monday detonation, even if the administrative stay were in place. 
The governor’s office did not immediately respond Friday when asked if the activation of the State Emergency Operations Center was an indication that the detonation would occur Monday. 
Communication
Part of the lawsuit, and public backlash over the planned detonation centered on a perceived lack of communication between the Army and relevant stakeholders. 
The letter from Macy to Reynolds included a timeline of actions between EPA and the Army, and with the public. 
Map from Nov. 18 showing the potential area that could have lead dust following a now postponed detonation of lead azide in Middletown. (Photo via U.S. Army)
Between April and September, EPA issued three emergency permits allowing Iowa Army Ammunition Plant to continue to store the material safely, while it evaluated potential treatment options. The letter to Reynolds shows that for each of these permits, notice was sent to the Iowa congressional delegation, state lawmakers, and local officials.
The same group of officials was notified Nov. 13 when EPA granted IAAAP the emergency treatment permit allowing the intentional detonation. 
State officials have said they were not aware of the planned detonation until the U.S. Army put out a public announcement with the original detonation schedule, air disbursement and dust deposition maps. 
Post detonation 
 The letter also explained the role EPA will play post detonation to monitor potential impacts.
According to the letter, and field team from EPA’s Region 7 has been in Middletown since Nov. 16 to conduct independent monitoring and sampling, in addition to the monitoring and sampling being collected by the Army. 
“Current modeling predicts that airborne lead levels may rise for a few hours as the plume passes,” Macy wrote in the letter. “The assessment is that this elevated, but low, level of lead will last for only a few hours.” 
EPA staff are also working to evaluate impacts from the plume to drinking water sources and surrounding watersheds. Macy wrote in the letter that if testing shows “potentially impacted water systems and waterbodies” the EPA and the Army will work to monitor drinking water and provide filters for homeowners on public water supply systems with elevated levels of lead.  
“My team is proudly committed to doing everything in our power to pursue clean, air, land, and water for all Americans,” Macy wrote in the letter to Reynolds. “We stand ready to provide additional support, and we will continue to engage with state and local officials and the public to provide additional updates in a timely manner.”
Reynolds’ office did not respond to a request for comment on the letter.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: As plans for a Carbon County data center and nuclear reactors advance, residents push to be heard
description: A group of neighbors frustrated with a company’s plan to bring nuclear reactors and a data center to their rural Utah county is pushing to be heard.
text:
The view from Elizabeth Trostle's front yard. The land is part of a broader area Valar Atomics is seeking permission to use as it plans to bring hundreds of small nuclear reactors and a data center to Utah's Carbon County. (Photo courtesy of Elizabeth Trostle) A group of neighbors frustrated with a California-based company’s plan to bring hundreds of small nuclear reactors and a data center to Carbon County made a longshot pitch Thursday, their latest in a growing battle. 
They urged members of the Utah’s Trust Lands Administration board to reconsider the lease they approved for Valar Atomics two months ago, arguing Valar should provide more details on what’s in store and calling attention to what they say is lacking transparency across multiple levels of government. 
“Why did our community have to learn about something of this magnitude through NPR?” said Elizabeth Trostle, whose family of seven lives near the small city of Wellington. “Is that what transparency looks like here in Utah?” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It was one of few opportunities Trostle and others in her rural community have had to weigh in on the project seeking to produce 9.6 gigawatts of power — more than double what the state of 3.5 million people consumes.
The project was not on the board’s Thursday agenda, and after two and a half minutes of comment via Zoom, Trostle was out of time. A board member thanked her and another critic for sharing their thoughts and moved on to a scheduled discussion. 
Later in the day, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed the residents’ request for a fresh review would not be granted. 
“When the lease was signed, it became a legally binding contract; reconsideration is not possible,” a spokesperson for the Trust Lands Administration said in an email. 
Trostle said she would have spoken up when the board considered the proposal earlier this year, but she didn’t hear about it until weeks later. 
In a statement to Utah News Dispatch that the Trust Lands Administration requested be used in full, spokesperson Marla Kennedy said: “TLA provided the public with two distinct opportunities to share their perspectives and provide input through open, public meetings held in August and September of this year.” 
A parcel of Utah trust lands Valar Atomics intends to use for its proposed Raceway Energy Campus in Utah’s Carbon County. (Utah Trust Lands Administration)
“At both meetings, the Board received and considered verbal and written comments from interested citizens before deciding to issue the ground lease.”
To add to some Carbon County residents’ dismay, when the county’s planning commission voted to approve a permit for Valar’s “Raceway Energy Campus” last week, it did not give members of the public an opportunity to be heard. 
At the meeting, Carbon County Attorney Christian Bryner told those in attendance the panel was not required to hold a public hearing to approve the application, The Salt Lake Tribune reported.
On Thursday, Trostle said she’s not against responsible development but feels the process is moving too quickly as she and others seek more information about possible environmental effects and the handling of radioactive waste from the proposed Valar campus. 
The company did not respond to an emailed request for comment Thursday, but told NPR in September that “this is home, and we’ve spent eighteen months answering our neighbors’ questions before being asked. We’ll keep earning that trust one answer at a time.” 
Valar has also applied for land use approval from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management for a project in the same area. Trostle said the stretch of federal land in question ends just across the street from her house. 
The federal agency is in the early stage of reviewing those materials and indicated in an unsigned statement to Utah News Dispatch that multiple layers of review lie ahead. If its managers decide to accept the application and deem it complete, they will start the process for an environmental analysis required under federal law, the statement said. 
In response to a question about concerns from homeowners in the area, the Trust Land Administration said in its statement to Utah News Dispatch: 
“It is important to clarify that TLA’s issuance of a ground lease is separate and distinct from the regulatory review and approval processes required by other governmental authorities. The ground lease does not grant, replace, or imply approval of any local, state, or federal permits, authorizations, or regulatory approvals the project may need. Those approvals are separate from TLA’s role and are subject to the review and authority of the applicable local, state, and federal regulatory agencies. The lessee remains responsible for obtaining all required permits and approvals before undertaking activities covered by the lease.”
