name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: A second SC GOP senator resigns, this time for health issues
description: Republican state Sen. Billy Garrett, of Greenwood, submitted his letter of resignation to Senate President Thomas Alexander, citing health issues.
text:
Sen. Ronnie Sabb and Sen. Billy Garrett, right, during a Senate Finance subcommittee meeting in Columbia, S.C. on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2025. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — Republican state Sen. Billy Garrett submitted his resignation Friday, setting up a second spring election for a seat in South Carolina’s upper chamber.
The 70-year-old senator from Greenwood cited “health-related issues” as the reason for his departure.
His “irrevocable resignation” takes effect April 6 to coincide with the special election to replace him. The timing also means voters will be choosing new senators in two parts of the state that day.
“This decision has not been an easy one,” Garrett wrote in a letter to Senate President Thomas Alexander. It followed “much prayer, careful consideration and consultation with my family and physicians.”
The district he represents includes all of Greenwood County and parts of Lexington and Saluda counties.
“Thank you for welcoming me into your churches, businesses, schools, farms, and homes,” he wrote in a letter addressed “To the People of Senate District 10” and provided to news outlets. “Thank you for your prayers, your encouragement, your friendship, and even your honest disagreements.”
The Greenwood Index-Journal reported Friday that Garrett is under a doctor’s care amid ongoing health concerns.
The senator also was previously hospitalized in March 2025 after experiencing chest pains and undergoing kidney and blood pressure tests, he posted on social media at the time.
“While I am saddened to see a friend depart this august body, I know that Senator Garrett is doing what he’s always done: seeking the best for South Carolina,” Alexander wrote in a statement.
Voters first elected Garrett, an attorney, to the Senate in 2020. He defeated 12-year incumbent Sen. Floyd Nicholson, the former longtime mayor of Greenwood, by 12 percentage points, flipping it red. At the time, the rural district spanned parts of Abbeville, Greenwood, McCormick and Saluda counties.
The district was heavily redrawn following the 2020 Census, and Garrett was re-elected in 2024 with nearly 70% of the vote, according to the state Election Commission.
The last Senate vote Garrett took, on May 26, was against the motion that officially stopped White House-driven efforts to redraw the state’s congressional lines ahead of the midterm. Garrett was among 18 Republicans voting not to kill the bill.
He was absent for special sessions in June and August, primarily to pass a state budget.
“South Carolina is better because Billy Garrett has served. He is a terrific gentleman with a wonderful family and a heart for helping people. Senator Garrett loves serving in the Senate and cares greatly for the people of Greenwood, Lexington, and Saluda,” Senate Majority Leader Shane Massey wrote in a statement. “I know he will miss the work, we in the Senate will miss his presence, and all of South Carolina will miss a dedicated public servant.”
While he will officially still represent District 10 until April 6, Garrett agreed to forgo all pay for Senate service for 2027, Senate leadership said.
SC gov-elect seeks public’s interest in openings; special election to fill Senate vacancy

The 2027 legislative session starts Jan. 12.
Florence County voters
Garrett is the second senator to turn in his resignation this week.
Sen. Mike Reichenbach, R-Florence, turned in his irrevocable resignation Monday.
It’s effective Jan. 13, the day he will sworn in as lieutenant governor alongside Gov.-elect Alan Wilson.
Voters will also choose Reichenbach’s replacement on April 6 for the district that includes most of Florence County.
Candidate filing for the seat doesn’t start until Dec. 4.
But at least four Republicans and one Democrat, the Rev. Jerrod Moultrie, have signaled their intention to run.
The Republicans intending to run, Florence attorney Hood Temple, county councilman William Schofield, former prosecutor John Holt and Dr. Mark Lawhon, a surgeon, all attended a voter forum this week.
Republicans hold supermajority control of the 46-member Senate.
Garrett and Reichenbach will remain among the chamber’s 33 Republicans until their resignations take effect.
A 34th Republican will soon join the caucus: James Burns won the York County seat vacated by Wes Climer, R-Rock Hill, who won his bid to represent South Carolina’s 5th Congressional District.

title: Idaho Legislature may clamp down on high powered e-motorbikes amid injuries
description: Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries. Rep. Brooke Green, a Boise Democrat, and Sen. Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries.
State Rep. Brooke Green, D-Boise, chats with fellow legislators on the House floor on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Rep. Brooke Green, a Boise Democrat, and Sen. Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which they say can reach over 30 mph but are often marketed as e-bikes — to be classified as motorcycles. That change would require riders of e-motos to have a driver’s license with a motorcycle endorsement to ride on public roads, and for the vehicles to meet certain requirements to be considered street legal, the lawmakers say.
Since the start of the year, Idaho emergency rooms have seen nearly 1,900 visits due to electric mobility devices, a category that also includes e-bikes and e-scooters, according to data from the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Young boys, between the ages of 11 and 15, accounted for 306 of the visits — the most of any demographic reported. An Idaho Statesman report published earlier Thursday highlighted the spike in injuries. 
Sen. Treg Bernt, R-Meridian, speaks from the Senate floor on Jan. 13, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Families are spending thousands of dollars on what they believe are bicycles, without realizing their 14-year-old cannot legally ride them down Eagle Road or on the Greenbelt,” Bernt and Green said in a joint statement. “Kids are getting seriously hurt, and we need to address this before more injuries occur.”
Ahead of the holiday season, the lawmakers urged parents to not buy e-motos for children who can’t legally drive motorcycles on public roads. 
The proposed statewide change seems similar to an action the city of Boise took earlier this year.
Other cities have taken notice, too. 
Meridian in July launched an education campaign focused on the use of e-bikes and e-motorcycles, BoiseDev reported. Nampa in September passed an ordinance adding local regulations, including barring e-motos from sidewalks and greenbelts if they can reach speeds in excess of 28 miles per hour, the Idaho Statesman reported. 
“There’s nothing wrong with enjoying these vehicles in the desert or on our public lands where motorized recreation is permitted, but motorcycles do not belong on the Greenbelt, sidewalks, or other pedestrian spaces,” the lawmakers added. “We want parents to have the facts before making expensive holiday purchases, and we’re working on bipartisan legislation to establish clear rules that keep our communities safe.”

title: Arkansas officials announce 5 probable measles cases in Lawrence County
description: Five unvaccinated Lawrence County residents likely contracted measles while traveling out of state, the Arkansas Department of Health announced Friday. The announcement comes three days after the Pan American Health Organization declared the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles. Elimination status refers to 12 months or longer wit[...]
text:
The number of confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year had crossed 5,400 by Nov. 12. (Photo by Getty Images Plus)Five unvaccinated Lawrence County residents likely contracted measles while traveling out of state, the Arkansas Department of Health announced Friday.
The announcement comes three days after the Pan American Health Organization declared the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles. Elimination status refers to 12 months or longer with no confirmed cases of a disease.
Measles is a highly contagious illness that can cause severe health complications. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and rash, according to the health department. Patients are infectious both four days before and after they develop a rash.
The number of confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year had crossed 5,400 as of last week, more than twice as many cases as last year. The five probable cases in Lawrence County are Arkansas’ first this year.
It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US

Arkansas recorded eight cases of measles linked to out-of-state travel last year. In April 2025, Faulkner County saw evidence of community spread when a child who was not fully vaccinated contracted measles and had not traveled out of state.
The Arkansas chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics said Tuesday that vaccinating children “remains our strongest tool for protecting children and preventing outbreaks.”
“Protecting children is a responsibility we all share, but the vaccination rates in much of Arkansas have dropped below levels that ensure community immunity,” the chapter said in a statement. “We encourage families to talk with their pediatrician about how to best protect their children, neighbors and communities.”
The chapter also emphasized that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are 97% effective against those diseases.
In August, President Donald Trump signed an executive order recommending three separate vaccinations for measles, mumps and rubella.
The executive order also called on federal programs and funding to “support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines.” Trump and U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have repeatedly made false statements connecting childhood vaccines to autism.
Trump and Kennedy reduced the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 in December 2025. Since then, 29 states and Washington D.C. no longer follow federal guidance regarding childhood vaccines.
Nationwide, vaccine hesitancy and misinformation has led to lower vaccination rates and a higher prevalence of several communicable diseases, including COVID-19 and whooping cough.
Since 2021, Arkansas has banned governmental entities from requiring employees to be vaccinated against COVID-19. 
The law, updated in 2023, allows entities to ask the Arkansas Legislative Council for exemptions from the ban if federal funding is at stake. This occurred on a handful of occasions following the 2021 law with agencies that receive reimbursements from Medicare and Medicaid.

text:
Protesters outside a campaign event for Supreme Court candidate Brad Schimel on March 31, 2025 in Green Bay, Wis., the day after Elon Musk handed out two checks at a rally that were later alleged to be illegal bribes for voting. A lawsuit accusing Musk of illegal election bribery was dismissed this week. (Photo by Jason Kerzinski for Wisconsin Examiner)A judge in Green Bay has dismissed a lawsuit that accused Elon Musk of election bribery and other offenses when he gave checks of $1 million described as rewards “for taking time to vote” to two people at a rally ahead of Wisconsin’s 2025 state Supreme Court election.
Brown County Circuit Judge Marc Hammer ruled late Wednesday that the lawsuit’s plaintiffs, two individual voters and the Wisconsin Democracy Campaign, lacked standing in the case.
The voters and the Democracy Campaign sued in June 2025 on the grounds that it is against the law to offer anyone more than $1 to induce them to go the polls, vote, or vote for a particular candidate. The Dane County court ordered the lawsuit moved to Brown County, where the events the suit referred to had taken place.
Law Forward, the Madison-based nonprofit law firm focused on democracy, voting rights and related issues, represented the plaintiffs along with the Democracy Defenders Fund in Washington, D.C., and the law firm of Hecker Fink.
“Wisconsin voters understand that doling out millions of dollars to induce people to vote is wrong,” Law Forward staff counsel Scott Thompson said after the judge handed down his ruling this week.
The dismissal “is a setback, but by no means the end of the road,” Thompson said. “We will press forward and continue to stand up for free and fair elections.”
Musk and his political action committee, America PAC, spent more than $20 million on the race between Dane County Judge Susan Crawford and Waukesha County Judge Brad Schimel. Crawford won what became the most expensive judicial campaign in American history.
Prior to the election, America PAC offered voters $100 if they signed a petition “in opposition to activist judges,” and another $100 if they referred another voter to sign the petition. Later, at a pre-election rally in Green Bay, Musk handed out two $1 million checks to voters, which had been advertised as awards “in appreciation for you taking the time to vote.”
In dismissing the lawsuit, Hammer wrote that standing in a lawsuit “restricts access to judicial remedies to those who have suffered some injury because of something that someone has either done or not done.”
The voters’ argument that Musk had “undermined Wisconsin’s democracy” by his actions “is not a concrete enough injury to give rise to standing,” the judge wrote.
In the same vein, the Democracy Campaign’s argument that Musk’s actions forced the organization to spend more time, effort and resources “ensuring elections are not tainted by corruption” and pursuing a “clean government, where people matter more than money” also fell short, the judge wrote, because the group didn’t say that it was blocked “from carrying out its mission of election advocacy, just that it had to use more effort and resources to do so.”
In a separate legal action earlier this year, the Wisconsin Elections Commission voted 5-1 to submit two complaints to the Brown County district attorney’s office alleging that Musk had violated the state law against election bribery.
That case was referred to a special prosecutor, La Crosse County DA Tim Gruenke, who concluded that the accusation was premised on “a poorly worded statement” Musk made on X and subsequently corrected. Gruenke declined to file charges, stating that a jury would be unlikely to convict Musk.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Commentary: Boredom, apathy work for North Dakota Republicans
description: In the aftermath of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the results in North Dakota seem troubling and boring. Boring because a near record-low turnout suggests eligible voters in a one-party state know the outcome before they vote. Troubling because voter non-participation might mean boredom is morphing into apathy, and that’s never a good thing in […]
text:
A voter enters the El Zagal Shrine Hall in Fargo, North Dakota, to vote in the midterm election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)In the aftermath of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the results in North Dakota seem troubling and boring. Boring because a near record-low turnout suggests eligible voters in a one-party state know the outcome before they vote. Troubling because voter non-participation might mean boredom is morphing into apathy, and that’s never a good thing in a representative democracy.
It is easy to conclude the North Dakota election was boring. But for two ballot measures that stirred some interest, there were no competitive races on the ballot to stimulate voter turnout. It’s harder to make the case that apathy afflicts the state’s voters. North Dakotans are more comfortable than apathetic. It’s more about being OK with the political status quo than it is about ballot laziness. A logical stance might be, no sense voting when the outcomes are foregone.  
The fact is, North Dakota is doing comparatively well by nearly all measures of voter contentment. A December 2025 poll by the North Dakota News Cooperative showed about two-thirds of those polled had not experienced any changes to their household financial situation. That sentiment likely is nurtured by the strength of the state’s energy sector and by expectations that no matter how Washington trade policies and tariffs hurt agriculture, the Trump administration will treat farmers like welfare recipients and mollify them with multi-billion dollar taxpayer-funded bailouts.
A solid majority of North Dakota farmers and ranchers vote Republican and have supported the president, even as he shredded international commodity markets and pursued policies that cost farmers dearly in record-high fuel, fertilizer and equipment prices. They have given him a pass because they expect he will again squeeze billions of dollars out of the U.S. treasury for “support” checks for farmers. Call it what you will: corporate welfare, ag welfare,  Republican food stamps for farmers. It certainly has the look and feel of a 21st century version of agrarian socialism. Ironically, it smells like something the North Dakota Democratic-NPL would advocate. But at this time in the state’s history, Trump’s river of taxpayer dollars cascading into farmers’ larders guarantee Republicans will win big in North Dakota. 
That being said, there were tentative signs that Democrats have a spark of life in their hitherto moribund party. The Republican supermajority in the Legislature is a skiff smaller because Democrats picked up a few seats. Also, Democratic U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer did better this time against one-term incumbent Republican Julie Fedorchak. Hammer got just short of 37% of the vote in a race that also included two independent candidates, compared to about 30% two years ago. That marginal improvement for the blue crowd in a deep red state might reflect creeping discontentment with the occupant of the White House, as was the case in several red states where Democrats won state and federal races, among them Mississippi, Alaska, Kansas, Texas and South Carolina. 
Also, in Fargo and Cass County, the most populous places in North Dakota (and among the youngest, most educated, fastest growing and most economically diverse populations in the state) several Democrats earned more votes than Republicans, bucking the GOP wave. Election results from the last few cycles show Republicans are losing – or already have lost – Fargo and Cass County. For example, while Fedorchak won in a blowout statewide, in Cass County she lost to Hammer 51% to 45%. Democrat Vern Thompson topped popular incumbent Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring 51% to 49% in Cass, while Goehring won in a statewide landslide. Cass County voters also preferred Democrats for two seats on the Public Service Commission, while Republican incumbents won easily statewide.
Whether from boredom or from the apathy that can come with the comfort of one-party dominance, a majority of eligible North Dakota voters sat out the Nov. 3 election. The result still was a Republican sweep in most places, but not in populous and growing Cass County and Fargo. If it’s the start of a blue trend (that’s a big “if”), voter apathy and boredom won’t be enough for Republicans to win in the future.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah lawmakers eye another attempt to repeal law allowing developers to form cities
description: Rep. Tiara Auxier narrowly lost reelection after a blue wave of Democrats swept the Utah House — but this week, Auxier teed up another attempt to repeal a controversial development law that was a contentious election issue this year, especially in Utah’s Wasatch Back.  Even though Auxier won’t be returning to Utah’s Capitol Hill next […]
text:
Homes in the Red Ledges private community in the Heber Valley, Utah are pictured on Sept. 19, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Rep. Tiara Auxier narrowly lost reelection after a blue wave of Democrats swept the Utah House — but this week, Auxier teed up another attempt to repeal a controversial development law that was a contentious election issue this year, especially in Utah’s Wasatch Back. 
Even though Auxier won’t be returning to Utah’s Capitol Hill next year, it’s likely the repeal will be carried forward by another legislator. 
Auxier on Wednesday presented draft legislation to the Political Subdivisions Interim Committee to fully repeal SB258, a law passed in 2024 that created a pilot program allowing up to three private landowners in mostly undeveloped, unincorporated areas to petition to create a “preliminary municipality,” which would be a first step toward the formation of a city or incorporation into a neighboring county. 
‘Threat’ to block state funds from Wasatch County stirs anger over ‘top down’ development pressure

Proponents of the law, which requires at least 10% of housing in the preliminary municipality to be affordable housing, have argued it’s meant to help ease Utah’s housing crisis. They have also argued it’s meant to bolster private property rights, allowing developers a new pathway to pursue projects in areas where county officials refuse to approve their proposals. 
Critics, including Wasatch and Summit county officials, have called on lawmakers to repeal the law. In their resolution calling for the repeal, Wasatch County leaders called it highly problematic, saying it allows developers to “entitle large-scale projects while sidestepping the infrastructure, housing, oversight and accountability standards every other community in Utah must meet.” 
Auxier on Wednesday said lawmakers need to reckon with the law’s problems, recognize it’s not fulfilling its intended purpose, and end the pilot program early. 
“We’ve taken governmental land use authority out of the hands of locally elected officials and placed it with a board controlled by people selected by the landowners seeking developmental approval,” she said. “I don’t think that’s local control, and I don’t think that it fits with our constitutional principles of representative government.”
It’s not the first time Auxier has tried to repeal or change the law. In 2025 she unsuccessfully sponsored a repeal, and in 2026 she ran a “compromise” bill to put more guardrails around the “preliminary municipality” process — both were unsuccessful.

Now, she’s trying again for a full repeal. But this time, as the legislation is currently written, it would also dissolve all preliminary municipalities created under the program, including those that have already been green lit by the lieutenant governor’s office. 
Seven preliminary municipalities have been attempted, most in Wasatch County, and most have either been rejected or are still under consideration. At least one has been approved: Echo Canyon in Grand County. 
“My intent would accomplish two things: it would end the preliminary municipality form of government entirely, and it would restore county land use authority going forward while protecting private rights that are actually valid and legally enforceable,” Auxier said. 
For two years, Auxier said “we’ve been trying to fix this process,” but she argued it’s beyond fixing. 
“What I’m asking us to do now is to consider whether the process itself is built on a government structure that never should have been created,” she said. 
Despite pushback from some lawmakers, the committee made up of both House and Senate legislators voted Wednesday to endorse Auxier’s proposed repeal as a committee bill, teeing it up to be prioritized during the Utah Legislature’s upcoming general session scheduled to begin in January. 
Though Auxier will be out of office by then, the repeal bill will likely be taken up by another legislator since it’s been endorsed by the committee. 
Last month, the House’s top Republican, House Speaker Mike Schultz, told Utah News Dispatch he’s open to making changes to or fully repealing the law. 
Utah House speaker says he’s open to repealing controversial development law

Chris Gamvroulas, president of Ivory Development (which is pursuing the Lost Creek preliminary municipality in Browns Canyon near Park City and Hideout), said the original law was meant to give property owners who had vested property rights an “off ramp” from “weaponized county government,” which he said happened in Grand County. 
“This isn’t just, like, a giveaway,” he said during Wednesday’s hearing. “No one in their right mind wants to use this tool. This is an off ramp when there’s weaponized county government. And you have to be cognizant of that and give a little bit of grace to that.” 
Gamvroulas said if there is a repeal of the bill, lawmakers should replace it in some way to better balance property rights. 
“The preliminary municipality is the second worst policy you could have,” he said. “The only worse policy you could have is the status quo of weaponized county government against property owners.” 
Several sitting lawmakers, incoming legislators and others spoke in favor of Auxier’s repeal. That included outgoing Rep. Mike Kohler, a Republican who didn’t run for reelection for House District 59, representing Wasatch and Summit counties. 
Tiara Auxier, R-Morgan, is pictured on the House floor at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 21, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Kohler’s Democratic successor Celeste Johnson, and Johnson’s unsuccessful Republican opponent Luke Searle both spoke in favor of the repeal during Wednesday’s committee hearing. 
“It’s flawed. … It creates chaos, and everybody up there is pretty concerned about it,” Kohler said. “It’s not fair. This needs (to be) repealed.” 
Another vocal critic, Jeff Pierce — a Park City investor who ran for the Republican nomination for Utah House District 59 earlier this year but narrowly lost to Searle — also called on lawmakers to support Auxier’s repeal. 
“You have the power to dissolve these cities. Please do it. Do the right thing. Take the voter’s side,” he said. “You just got wiped out in an election because of corrupt bills like this. Now get rid of it.” 
Some lawmakers including Sen. Don Ipson, R-St. George, and Sen. Calvin Musselman, R-West Haven, expressed misgivings about fully repealing the law and voted against endorsing it. And others, including Reps. Jordan Teuscher, R-South Jordan, and Jill Koford, R-Ogden — who both lost to Democrats this month — urged lawmakers to proceed cautiously to balance local control with private property rights. 
“I’m so tired of this issue. My head hurts,” Musselman said before voting against endorsing the bill. “I’ve already faced the reality that this is going to happen. A repeal is going to happen. Whether or not we have some kind of mechanism (to replace it) I don’t know.” 
Musselman encouraged legislators to talk to the Utah Attorney General’s Office and risk management officials to get a picture of potential liability to both the state and counties if they were to face lawsuits from landowners and developers if a repeal were to happen and if existing preliminary municipalities were to be dissolved.  
Ipson said in order for the bill to pass the full Legislature, it will likely need changes. 
“Whoever has this bill has to know that it has to have some work on it,” Ipson said. “It can’t go like it is.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Jackson mayor gets 37 months in prison for bribery scheme
description: Surrounded by family and friends, former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba, center, with wife Ebony, right, head to  the Thad Cochran United States Courthouse in Jackson for his sentencing hearing, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026.
text:
A federal judge on Friday sentenced Chokwe Antar Lumumba to 37 months in federal prison for receiving $50,000 in campaign contributions from undercover FBI agents posing as real estate developers seeking to build a hotel next to the downtown convention center. 
A solemn Lumumba told the judge that he had disappointed his community and placed an “unfair burden” on his wife and children, turning to face supporters in the courtroom dressed in white. 
Surrounded by family and friends, former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba, center, with wife Ebony, head into the   Thad Cochran United States Courthouse in Jackson for his sentencing hearing, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026.
“My failures have become unbearable,” he said. 
U.S. District Judge Daniel P. Jordan III said he admired many qualities possessed by Lumumba and that he thought the former mayor of Jackson was unlikely to commit future crimes. 
“I really think this case is a tragedy on a lot of different levels,” he said. 
But in levying a prison sentence, Jordan said he had to send a message to public servants in Mississippi’s capital city, who he said were engaging in corruption with no regard for past “convictions that have occurred in this state and in and around Jackson in the last 20 years.” 
“I am also required to consider general deterrence and the amount of corruption,” the judge said, before pausing. “Well, I’ll just say during this time period there were a lot of people with their hands out, and the level of corruption that’s reflected in this record is deeply disturbing.”
The FBI sting ensnared other Democratic politicians in Jackson, including former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens and former Jackson City Councilman Aaron Banks, who were each sentenced earlier this month to more than three years in state prison. 
The sentencing caps the Mississippi political career of Lumumba, who was once considered a rising star among young, Black elected officials in the Deep South.
“I want the people of Jackson to understand that they’re worth more than negative headlines, they’re worth more than all the negative things that we consider when we talk about the city of Jackson,” Lumumba said. “And hopefully I can demonstrate and hopefully the city of Jackson will see itself through my eyes, because I see a city and a community that is full of promise and hope.” 
A criminal defense attorney, Lumumba first ran for mayor in 2014 in a special election to replace his father, Chokwe Lumumba, who died eight months into office. He faltered against Tony Yarber before grabbing an overwhelming victory three years later.
At just 34 years old, Lumumba was the youngest mayor of Jackson – and among its most ambitious. He pledged to transform Jackson into “the most radical city on the planet,” promising to institute assemblies where residents could directly weigh in on routine city matters like budgeting and policing. 
“I can’t say how much I love this city,” he told the Clarion Ledger in 2017 during his victory party. “There’s a promise and an opportunity in this city that we don’t even quite comprehend ourselves just yet.”
Instead, Lumumba’s eight years in office were marked by parrying one emergency after another. Shortly into his first term, he fended off a state takeover of Jackson Public Schools. Then the coronavirus hit, followed by an ice storm in 2021 that froze pipes throughout the city and prompted a water crisis. In 2022, Jackson saw another water crisis that forced the state to declare an emergency, drawing national attention and scrutiny of the mayor’s management of the city’s water system. 
The following year, Jackson residents went without garbage pickup for two weeks amid a dispute between Lumumba and the Jackson City Council over the selection of a trash vendor. In the lead up to the dispute, Lumumba accused some members of the City Council of taking bribes. 
No charges ever arose from that matter, but it caught the eye of federal authorities, Mississippi Today previously reported. 
In 2024, a sweeping federal indictment alleged that in exchange for $50,000 in campaign donations, Lumumba directed a city employee to shorten a bid deadline to benefit a pair of out-of-town developers, who in reality were undercover FBI agents. 
When the indictment against Lumumba became public in 2024, he vowed to defend his innocence, calling the charges a “political prosecution.”
Until pleading guilty over the summer, Lumumba maintained that his actions didn’t constitute an “official act” – an element of bribery that federal prosecutors needed to demonstrate to prove Lumumba had agreed to a quid pro quo. 
Others involved in the scheme have also yet to be sentenced, including former Jackson City Councilmember Angelique Lee.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT nonprofits seek parity with union in funding for social services
description: Nonprofits that deliver most of CT's social services want the same pay raises awarded to members of the SEIU 1199 healthcare employees union.
text:
The hundreds of community-based nonprofits that deliver most of Connecticut’s social services insist they’ve been losing money for decades.
But the industry recently made a different funding pitch to Gov. Ned Lamont and the General Assembly’s Democratic super-majority: Give all nonprofits the same increases awarded to agencies that employ members of the state’s largest healthcare workers’ union.
“We recognize that it is not easy to choose between budget priorities,” Gian-Carl Casa, president and CEO of the CT Community Nonprofit Alliance, wrote this week to Lamont. “But federal changes will create problems we haven’t seen before, and this could be a last opportunity to keep some Connecticut residents from falling through the cracks.”
Casa is referring to the nearly $3 billion the state spends annually hiring private local agencies to assist people with intellectual disabilities or mental illness or addiction issues, along with victims of abuse and adults reentering society after incarceration. The alliance says those payments have lagged inflation for many years. It estimates contracts effectively make about $900 million less than they did almost two decades ago.
Casa also noted that nonprofits that provide skill-building, recreation and other day services for clients with intellectual disabilities received an extra 2% this fiscal year, and those running group homes for those clients got an additional 3.4%. Many agencies running programs in those two categories employ members of New England Health Care Employees Union, District 1199, SEIU.
Meanwhile, other nonprofits got a 2% bump in 2025, and that funding was held flat in 2026.
The alliance is seeking a funding increase of about 9% next fiscal year — for all social services agencies. This would cost the state $250 million to $300 million, Casa said, adding that represents just one-eighth of the surplus the current state budget is projected to have.
Programs that employ unionized members traditionally have enjoyed stronger support from Democrats in the General Assembly than non-union operations. Democrats control 116 of 151 seats in the new House and 33 of 36 in the Senate.
“We’re proud of the progress 1199 members have fought for in securing stronger wages, healthcare and paid time off for healthcare workers,” union President Rob Baril said Friday. “But the stakes go far beyond workers’ paychecks.”
Baril and other labor leaders have urged the governor and legislature for years to reform aggressive budget caps that have helped the state shrink pension debt aggressively since 2020 while siphoning nearly $2 billion annually away from many core programs and services.
“Despite the progress we’ve made, too many [healthcare] workers are still struggling to make ends meet, juggling multiple jobs and falling further behind as the cost of living continues to climb,” Baril said. “We must keep investing in this workforce and the services they provide, because both are essential to the well-being and dignity of the people who depend on them.”
Casa added in an interview with The Connecticut Mirror this week that he isn’t criticizing District 1199, which represents roughly 28,000 workers in various healthcare jobs statewide, nor suggesting its members don’t receive strong funding.
But all social service providers “have something to do with one another,” he added. “They all work together to make up what the safety net is.”
Many requests for more money
Lamont and the General Assembly, however, face a long list of financial requests when the regular 2027 legislative session convenes Jan. 6.
The state’s Medicaid program has faced sizeable cost overruns in each of the past three fiscal years, and new cuts in federal funding will add pressure to Connecticut’s budget.
Municipal school officials and other advocates say communities are struggling badly to cover surging special education costs. A citizens assembly convened by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities is seeking to redirect billions of expenses in this area off communities and onto the state budget.
Legislators also hope to expand major new investments to expand affordable childcare program slots statewide.
And fiscal analysts warn the Special Transportation Fund needs additional resources in the next few years or Connecticut will have to slow the rebuild of its aging highways, bridges and rail lines.
Rep. Toni E. Walker, D-New Haven, longtime co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, didn’t rule out any requests for aid Friday but noted Connecticut was struggling to keep up with these and other priorities when it enjoyed billions of dollars in federal pandemic aid between 2021 and 2025.
“The Band-Aid’s off,” she said, adding that since President Donald Trump’s second term began, Washington’s had a “gimme-back attitude” when it comes to funding for states.
Her Senate counterpart, Sprague Democrat Cathy Osten, said “all nonprofits should be receiving the same pay increases.”
But Osten also agreed that lawmakers and Lamont will be hard-pressed to meet all demands next year. “We do have to be willing to face a lot of things.”
Lamont’s budget spokesman, Chris Collibee, also was cautious in his assessment of the upcoming session.
“Community nonprofits do vital work every day to support Connecticut residents,” he said. “As the Lamont administration develops its next biennial budget proposal, we welcome ideas from advocates and the General Assembly that reinforce our commitment to a strong social safety net while keeping Connecticut on a responsible fiscal path.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA fines Longview mill $10M for tank rupture that killed 11
description: The company that runs a Longview paper mill must pay the state of Washington $10 million after failing to repair a tank before it imploded this spring and killed 11 people, state officials announced Friday. Nippon Dynawave Packaging’s G-tank, with about 900,000 gallons of caustic white liquor, ruptured the morning of May 26, killing eight […]
text:
Emergency tape reading "Caution: Sheriff Line - Do Not Cross" is seen in front of the Nippon Dynawave Packaging facility following a fatal chemical storage tank implosion on May 26, 2026 in Longview, Washington. (Photo by Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images)The company that runs a Longview paper mill must pay the state of Washington $10 million after failing to repair a tank before it imploded this spring and killed 11 people, state officials announced Friday.
Nippon Dynawave Packaging’s G-tank, with about 900,000 gallons of caustic white liquor, ruptured the morning of May 26, killing eight people in the mill’s electrical maintenance shop, two in the mechanical maintenance shop and one in the courtyard. Five maintenance workers and the foreman were able to escape, though two suffered serious chemical burns. 
Some of the liquid, which is used in paper manufacturing and can cause severe burns, flowed into the nearby Columbia River and a local diking system.  
The $10.1 million fine is for violations of both health and safety as well as environmental regulations. The state Department of Labor and Industries is citing Nippon for 75 violations, with fines totaling $9 million, after reviewing more than 40,000 documents and interviewing over 70 witnesses, said Joel Sacks, the agency director. 
“Our citations include egregious, willful, serious violations for keeping G-tank in operation despite repeated notice that it was not fit for service, not conducting sufficient inspections or addressing the problems their inspectors found at 13 other tanks, and exposing workers and first responders to more unnecessary dangers with their emergency response,” Sacks said in a press conference in Longview on Friday.
The $9 million fine is three times higher than the previous Labor and Industries record. The earlier record was for the 2010 Tesoro refinery disaster in Anacortes, which killed seven people.
Labor and Industries is referring the Longview case to prosecutors to consider criminal charges. Nippon has 15 days to appeal the citation.
“Our findings are both shocking and heartbreaking, and the resulting penalties should send a strong message to employers across the state of Washington,”  Sacks said. 
The state Department of Ecology found 34 violations of air, water and dangerous waste regulations. This led to a $296,500 penalty. Ecology is also requiring the company to pay $665,000 to the agency and the state Military Department for emergency response costs. The company could still face a damage assessment for the harm of the white liquor spill on natural resources. 
Labor and Industries also found Nippon’s emergency planning and response fell short of state requirements, putting workers and first responders in danger.
Nippon didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
In August, a preliminary federal investigation found Nippon knew the white liquor tank wasn’t fit for service and could fail nearly a year before it collapsed. The probe remains ongoing. Labor and Industries concluded three reports between August 2025 and February 2026 indicated the tank walls were significantly corroded, which the company knew but took no action to address. 
The result: 43 serious violations from Labor and Industries, one for each week Nippon kept the tank operating after the initial report of a problem.
“Nippon Dynawave had all of the information they needed to act, but they did not listen to the alarms of their consultants and their staff,” Sacks said.
The Labor and Industries fine will go into a workers’ compensation pension fund.
In the months and years before the implosion, a number of near misses at the Nippon mill piled up, according to Seattle Times reporting. The company put off other necessary repairs and appeared to put keeping the business running ahead of safety, while workers anonymously reported concerns to state investigators, according to the Times.
Since May, Labor and Industries has fined Nippon, which bought the mill in 2016, in multiple cases of workplace safety violations separate from the fatal tank collapse. In one case, the state agency fined the company more than $77,000 for a case where an employee fell into a sinkhole at the plant, was nearly covered in 145-degree pulp, and came close to being engulfed. Nippon appealed the fine.
In an earlier case, Nippon was cited for not documenting safety plans or keeping required records on an ammonia tank used to treat wastewater at the mill, leading to a small fine.

The company also faces multiple lawsuits from families of the victims, alleging Nippon violated state safety regulations. 
Pulp production at the mill remains shuttered. The company said this month it’s aiming to restart work next month. Other operations at the mill have reopened, with workers returning to the facility.
After the fatal rupture, Labor and Industries opened investigations into the state’s two other kraft pulp and paper mills, in Longview and Port Townsend.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Commentary: Landry can court Texas talent but also needs to show some homefield love
description: Gov. Jeff Landry said the state is “extending an open invitation to Texas companies and talent to take a look next door following recent elections that brought a significant shift in the state’s political leadership.”
text:
Louisiana officials have placed billboards along Interstate 10 in Houston to lure Texas workers and businesses. (Photo courtesy Louisiana Economic Development.Like other LSU fans, Gov. Jeff Landry and Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois probably suffered heartbreak last Saturday when University of Texas quarterback Arch Manning connected with receiver Raleek Brown for a touchdown in the closing seconds to escape Tiger Stadium with a win.
The governor is clearly invested in LSU football, having orchestrated the exit of coach Brian Kelly to make way for Lane Kiffin. Bourgeois earned her bachelor’s degree from the university.
But with the loss to the Longhorns still sinking in, you have to wonder if either official was having any “just you wait” thoughts in the back of their minds, knowing that Louisiana was about to launch a full frontal recruiting assault on the Lone Star State. Not for football talent but for its businesses and workforce.
The governor’s office announced Wednesday it was “extending an open invitation to Texas companies and talent to take a look next door following recent elections that brought a significant shift in the state’s political leadership.” 
The Nov. 3 vote in Texas saw the ouster of Republican Gov. Gregg Abbott in favor of Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and President Donald Trump’s endorsed U.S. Senate candidate, disgraced state Attorney General Ken Paxton, lost decisively to another Democrat, James Talarico.
Louisiana leaders are responding to the new landscape by placing billboards along Interstate 10 East in Houston. They feature a photo of Landry, with a beaming smile as he holds a welding torch and mask, and a frank message: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home” on one side of the governor, and “59,159 new jobs … and counting” on the other.
The campaign also includes a full-page ad in the Houston Business Journal “aimed at business leaders and corporate decision-makers.” The entire effort will cost $40,000 to $50,000 and will come from Louisiana Economic Development’s marketing budget, an agency spokesperson said.
Over the past two weeks, the governor has repeatedly referenced Texas’ election results as an economic development opportunity for Louisiana. 
“Elections have consequences, and business leaders pay attention to the direction a state is headed,” Landry said in a news release. 
His billboards were announced the day after Leaders for a Better Louisiana, a pro-business nonprofit, released a report saying the state will need 42,000 industrial construction workers to handle the peak workload for the 12 major industrial and technology projects planned statewide. The demand will be particularly acute in Lake Charles, Lafayette and Monroe, where the report says they will be roughly 19,000 workers short of what’s needed.
Richard Nelson, leader of the state’s community and technical college system, said in September the demand for trained personnel is so high that its 12 schools would have to double their enrollment for Louisiana residents to fill the available jobs. The system enrolls more than 100,000 students annually and awards 30,000 degrees and certificates each year.
Landry’s latest moves are certainly a shot across the bluebonnet bow of our neighbors to the west, but there are still major gaps that Louisiana isn’t likely to close in the immediate future. 
For starters, Texas has no corporate or personal income tax. 
Landry was behind efforts to establish flat income tax rates in Louisiana, and he said earlier this year he wants them to go away entirely. But doing so would likely require an increase in other state taxes, including a sales tax that’s already the highest in the country when combined with local levies.
Plus, Louisiana is one of the poorest states in the country. Even if lawmakers are willing to lean more into sales taxes (they aren’t), there’s simply not the ability or appetite to make up for the loss of income taxes with more consumption of taxable goods and services. Each 0.5% drop in the state income taxes eliminates roughly $500 million in government revenue annually, according to legislative calculations.
There are other reasons people move to another state besides work Landry also has to confront.
Louisiana is starting to see improvements in reading and math scores at the elementary level, but most overall public education rankings place Louisiana among the bottom five states. By comparison, Texas lands in the middle of the pack for its K-12 schools.
Healthcare is another area where Louisiana has been a consistent cellar dweller, with its substandard maternal and infant health being singled out again just this week. Texas doesn’t do much better, but it still outperforms Louisiana in a metric that’s important to the working-class families and business owners who Landry wants to pull up stakes and head east.
It’s understandable that the governor is getting creative to address a looming workforce shortage, but there are myriad matters here at home that, if improved, would go a long way toward building and retaining a homegrown talent pool to support an economic boom. Add affordable housing and insurance, clean air and better infrastructure to the concerns already mentioned.
Louisiana can and should lay out its welcome mat, but leaders can’t ignore why so many residents have departed — almost 237,000 over the past 10 years based on U.S. Census data.
Like New Orleans native Arch Manning, these departures have a way of coming back to bite us in the butt.

name: WyoFile
title: Rebecca Bextel, former governor candidate known for Checkgate, arrested for suspected drunk driving
description:
Police say they found empty mini bottles of vodka in the SUV driven by the conservative activist when they stopped her Thursday night.
The post Rebecca Bextel, former governor candidate known for Checkgate, arrested for suspected drunk driving appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Rebecca Bextel, a conservative activist who unsuccessfully ran for governor, was arrested Thursday night in Jackson on suspicion of driving drunk, police there said.
Bextel faces a driving under the influence charge along with three traffic citations including driving with an open container of alcohol, police told WyoFile. It was not immediately clear when she would make her first court appearance.
She did not respond to a text message seeking comment Friday morning.
After being stopped Thursday evening, Bextel told one Jackson police officer she’d consumed two shots of vodka before driving, and a second officer found a mini Tito’s Vodka bottle in the driver’s side door and two others in the front center console, according to her arrest affidavit, which Jackson Police Lt. Russ Ruschill read to WyoFile. Two of the bottles were empty, and a third had a small amount of liquid in it, the affidavit said.
“I would characterize this as a fairly common DUI for Jackson,” he said. “There’s nothing really outstanding about it from law enforcement’s perspective. It does support our mission of public safety by getting drunk drivers off the road.”
Jackson Police Officer Riley Williams stopped Bextel after police received a report of a possible drunk driver at 9:42 p.m. Thursday. Williams spotted an SUV matching the description traveling east on West Broadway near the intersection of Flat Creek Drive, the affidavit states.
In that report, Williams describes the SUV crossing into the oncoming lane of traffic before merging back into the correct lane. He turned on his lights and then sirens, and the SUV continued driving east and failed to completely stop at the intersection of Willow Street. Police say the SUV almost hit a truck driving south through the intersection at Willow Street before coming to a complete stop.
Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel laughs after taking a jab at Eric Barlow during the Wyoming PBS gubernatorial debate on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
A second officer, Kenton Kramer, also arrived at the scene, and both officers reported smelling alcohol on Bextel’s breath and hearing her slur her speech, according to the affidavit. Bextel agreed to perform field sobriety tests. 
“During all three batteries of tests, the officer observed signs of impairment,” Ruschill said.
Officers performed a breath test at the scene, which indicated Bextel had a blood alcohol concentration of .201%, according to the affidavit. In Wyoming, a person with a blood alcohol concentration of .08% is presumed too drunk to drive. 
After officers took Bextel to jail, they attempted to obtain the results from a breath test there, but were unable to get a sufficient sample, according to the affidavit. She “refused to do another chemical breath test and refused the options of blood or urine,” Ruschill said. Officers obtained a DUI search warrant, a nurse at the local hospital took a blood sample around midnight.
Ruschill said portable tests at the scene can be affected by the cold, and it would take four to six weeks before results from the blood sample come back.
“So I wouldn’t put any credence in the .201 until we got the result back from the blood test, but there was definitely alcohol on board,” he said.
Bextel describes herself as “the public face” of opposing Teton County’s mitigation fees designed to fund affordable housing. In 2025, she unsuccessfully ran for chairman of the Wyoming Republican Party. 
Rebecca Bextel testifies during the first meeting of the House Special Investigative Committee on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
She became more well known in February when she handed out campaign checks to Wyoming lawmakers on the House floor. The incident, known as Checkgate, dominated the 2026 legislative session and sparked multiple investigations, including an ongoing one by the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office. She denied any wrongdoing, and a legislative investigation determined the check passing did not amount to bribery. The panel also voted unanimously to adopt a report that admonished Bextel’s conduct.
Bextel earned roughly 17% of the vote in the general election — well short of Republican Eric Barlow, though enough to elevate the Constitution Party to major status. 
In May, Bextel announced she would leave the Republican party to run as a third-party candidate for governor if Republican voters nominated Gillette Sen. Eric Barlow in the primary election. She is now facing multiple complaints filed with the Wyoming Secretary of State’s office regarding her campaign finance reports. 
WyoFile staff writer Maggie Mullen contributed to this report.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Auburn University Board of Trustees approves new post-tenure review policy
description: The Auburn University Board of Trustees Friday voted to approve a new policy for post-tenure review that drew sharp criticism from faculty organizations. The change was authorized by HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April. The law also allowed boards of trustees to disband faculty senates […]
text:
Members of the Auburn University Board of Trustees as seen during its meeting on November 20, 2026. The board approved a new policy for post-tenure review, drawing criticism from faculty organizations. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Auburn University Board of Trustees Friday voted to approve a new policy for post-tenure review that drew sharp criticism from faculty organizations.
The change was authorized by HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April. The law also allowed boards of trustees to disband faculty senates and drew protests at Auburn.
The university will use a four-category scale for post-tenure reviews. The four categories are “exceeds expectations,” “meets expectations,” “does not meet expectations” and “unsatisfactory.” Under the policy, post-tenure review would occur at least once every six years. No faculty member can be reviewed more than once a year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Previously, the University Senate conducted the post-tenure review process and included an “exemplary” rating category which was removed from the policy approved by the board on Friday. 
Virginia Davis, the faculty advisor to the board, criticized the new system during the board’s meeting.
“Removing the exemplary rating from evaluations seems contradictory to the desire for excellence,” Davis said. “It undercuts the ability of faculty to continue to be recognized for the level of commitment that is distinctly offered.”
The policy states after the review is complete, the dean of the college will make a recommendation to the provost who can “seek advice from an appropriate faculty advisory body or other peer review body before making a final performance rating determination.” 
After the provost assigns a performance rating, the university president “shall exercise such review, approval, or oversight of post-tenure review determinations as provided by university procedures.”
Davis said “faculty are not afraid of evaluation.”
“We already have rigorous annual evaluations. Every proposal we write, every event we lead, every course we teach, every paper we publish is subject to review,” Davis said. “Any post-tenure review must carefully balance new requirements against real faculty and administrative time burdens.”
Heidi Hausse, a history professor at Auburn, said in an interview after the meeting the board’s passage of the post-tenure review policy “undermines protections of tenure, tenure safeguards and academic freedom.”
“My immediate reaction to the passage of this policy is deep concern for the future of Auburn University as a place of independent thought, as a place where students can trust they’re not going to have a censored education, as a place where cutting-edge research can be explored as a place where controversial ideas can be talked about and debated,” she said.
A petition started by United Campus Workers of Alabama, an organization that works to improve benefits, wages and working conditions for higher education employees, exceeded its goal of 500 signatures to maintain the current post-tenure review process. As of Friday afternoon, the petition had over 700 signatures.
Hausse, a member of UCW-AL, said the petition was emailed to all members of the board, except Ivey, Auburn Provost Vini Nathan and Board of Trustees Secretary Jon Waggoner at 4:30 p.m. on Thursday. The UCW-AL did not receive any response, according to Hausse.
Under the proposed policy change, professors who receive a rating of “does not meet expectations” will be referred to the provost to determine if a “Performance Improvement Plan” will be appropriate. Tenured professors who receive a rating of “unsatisfactory” could be dismissed without having a Performance Improvement Plan.
Tenured faculty members can be dismissed on performance-based, conduct and institutional grounds. Performance-based dismissal includes professional incompetence, failure to complete institutional evaluations and “serious or substantial neglect of professional or academic responsibilities,” among others.
Conduct-based dismissals include “conduct or unprofessional behavior that adversely affects the university or the faculty member’s performance of duties or fulfillment of professional responsibilities;” repeated or significant violation of the Auburn University policies, rules or regulations; and research misconduct, among others.
Institutional dismissals include institutional exigency, “discontinuance, reduction, reorganization, consolidation, or elimination of an academic program, department, unit, function, or position,” and other circumstances that are grounds for dismissal under board policy, university policy, or under applicable law.
“In describing the purpose of the post-tenure review in that policy they just passed, it includes one of its reasons to ensure that faculty work is in continued alignment with the university, and that is very concerning because it suggests the guiding question,” Hausse said. “One of the guiding questions of the post-tenure review isn’t: Are you doing well at your job? Are you doing well in the classroom? Are you doing well in your research? Are you doing well in service? One of the guiding questions in the wording of what they just passed is: Are you in alignment? And what that does is potentially turn faculty research into a tool for the interests of powerful people.”
HB 580 led Auburn and Jacksonville State University to abolish their faculty senates over protests from instructors at the schools. The University of Alabama and Troy University voted to maintain theirs.
The policy is effective immediately.

title: New Mexico’s outdoor recreation industry gains $200M in revenue, new federal data shows
description: New Mexico’s outdoor recreation industry grew by $200 million last year, according to federal data released Wednesday.
text:
New Mexico’s outdoor recreation industry brought in an additional $200 million in 2025 compared with the prior year, according to federal data released on Nov. 18, 2026. (Courtesy of Evan Green/Outdoor Recreation Division)New Mexico’s outdoor recreation industry grew by $200 million last year, according to federal data released Wednesday. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2025, outdoor recreation provided $3.8 billion to New Mexico’s economy, or 2.5% of the state’s gross domestic product, according to data from the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Economic Analysis, a $200 million increase from 2024. The industry’s overall contribution to the state’s economy makes New Mexico’s industry 24th nationally, according to the data.
“From our mountains and rivers to our trails and wide-open spaces, outdoor recreation is deeply connected to New Mexico’s identity and quality of life,” Rob Black, secretary of the New Mexico Economic Development Department, said in a statement. “The industry continues to create new opportunities for businesses and communities across the state while strengthening New Mexico’s economy for the future.”
The state’s top three revenue generators for recreation remained the same last year as the year prior: recreational vehicle use; boating and fishing; and snow activities — which netted $378 million combined, the BEA data showed. The activities with the largest revenue increases included recreational flying of aircraft, which rose 6.4%; and equestrian activities, which rose 3.3% from 2024 to 2025. “Other snow activities,” such as snowshoeing or snowmobiling, also grew by 10.4%. 
Compared to other states, New Mexico ranked 42nd in total outdoor recreation value added in 2025, but ranked 26th in revenue growth this year. The state logged a slight decline of less than 1% in outdoor-economy jobs. 
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham created the Outdoor Recreation Division under the Economic Development Department in 2019 with the stated purpose of growing the state’s outdoor recreation industry. Since then, the outdoor division has provided grants for outdoor infrastructure projects and for youth outdoor projects that are growing in demand. The agency cites a 36% increase in the sector’s inflation-adjusted contribution to New Mexico’s Gross Domestic Product.
ORD Director Karina Armijo said in a statement that the new data shows why investment in outdoor recreation matters: “Outdoor recreation is an important part of our economy, especially in rural areas,” she said, “supporting small businesses, creating jobs and bringing new opportunities to communities across the state.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The Latino vote and the community work that changed the electoral map in Kansas
description: This story was produced by Planeta Venus. After the Nov. 3 election, Kansas was left with a rare political setup: It elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932, kept the governorship in Democratic hands, and ousted Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach. The victories of Adam Hamilton, Cindy Holscher, and Chris Mann show […]
text:
Pictures of Latino voters from Kansas received by Planeta Venus during the 2026 general election. (Photo by Planeta Venus)This story was produced by Planeta Venus.
After the Nov. 3 election, Kansas was left with a rare political setup: It elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932, kept the governorship in Democratic hands, and ousted Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach. The victories of Adam Hamilton, Cindy Holscher, and Chris Mann show a coalition that united the strength of cities with gains in southwest communities, where immigration raids have become a major local issue.
The Latino vote was key in this story. In Ford, Finney, and Seward, post-election testimonies describe people who registered for the first time, voted again, or helped mobilize their neighbors after the September immigration crackdowns. Attributing the entire statewide result to that vote alone, however, would simplify an election also shaped by the suburbs, the cost of living, candidate profiles, and the support of some Republican voters.
 
The results: a historic rupture and a very close governorship
Hamilton’s victory over Sen. Roger Marshall ended nearly a century without Kansas electing a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist congregation in the Kansas City area, ran a campaign that reached beyond his party’s traditional strongholds. The AP notes that both strength in Johnson County and change in the southwest explain his victory.
The gubernatorial race was much closer. According to NPR’s tally updated on Nov. 13, Holscher had 552,328 votes (50.3%), and Ty Masterson had 545,128 (49.7%), a difference of about 7,200 votes. The AP declared Holscher the winner on Nov. 12, after several days of counting.
Holscher will replace Laura Kelly, who could not seek reelection. Her running mate, Wichita Congressman K.C. Ohaebosim, was elected lieutenant governor and will be the first African-American official to be elected to statewide office in Kansas since 1887.
In the Attorney General’s Office, Chris Mann beat Kobach in a rematch of the 2022 election. This result was important in the context of immigration, as Kobach has advised governments on restrictive immigration laws. However, that political relationship doesn’t let us determine exactly how much immigration influenced each vote for Mann.
 
Dodge City protesters gather on Sept. 25, 2026, outside U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann’s office, chanting “Tracey Mann, where are you? We need you?” They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
The key factors of the choice
1. The raids transformed a national debate into an everyday experience
In southwest Kansas, immigration wasn’t just a topic of speeches or campaign advertising. The late September raids targeted communities linked to feedlots, meatpacking plants, and other activities that rely on immigrant labor. The AP documented businesses closed, families afraid to leave home, and children who stopped attending school.
That closeness changed the political conversation. What once seemed like a distant dispute over the border began to involve co-workers, neighbors, family members, and how communities function.
The reaction was not limited to Democrats or Latino residents, either. The AP drew criticism from local Republican leaders for the intensity of the operations and the lack of coordination.
Marshall asked the federal government to consult local authorities before conducting raids.
There were also questions about the federal information. According to an investigation by The Wichita Eagle collected by AP, none of the five people presented by the government as examples of captured criminals were arrested during that operation: four had been deported months earlier, and the fifth was already in prison. The federal agency reported 104 arrests in the southwest, but local authorities quoted by the AP said they had not received a list. These are findings and journalistic statements, not a judicial resolution.
2. Community organizing turned anger into participation
Outrage doesn’t automatically produce votes. In Dodge City, community organizers worked to translate the protests into voter registration and voter turnout. AP describes how Amy Soberanes and others encouraged residents to channel their frustration into voting.
One testimony came from José del Real, an Army veteran who hadn’t voted for a decade. After the operations, he called on his neighbors to participate. His case illustrates an important mechanism: mobilization depended not only on new voters, but also on people who had abandoned electoral participation.
In Seward, a New York Times report found that during the three weeks after ICE arrived, about as many people registered to vote as in the previous nine months. The data shows an acceleration in registration, but it doesn’t let us assume those people voted for or supported the same candidate.
3. The suburbs contributed the volume of votes needed to win
The most striking change doesn’t always coincide with the largest numerical contribution. Johnson County was instrumental to Holscher’s victory: The scoreboard showed a Democratic lead of about 23 points in the gubernatorial race. The AP notes that Holscher won more than 60% of the county’s vote, offsetting wide Republican margins in rural areas.
Turnout was also elevated. According to KMBC, more than 300,000 people voted in Johnson County, the third-highest record in its history, behind only the 2020 and 2024 presidential years. As of Nov. 13, officials approved having approximately 5,000 additional provisional ballots.
The relationship between the two geographies is essential: the suburbs contributed many votes, while the southwest reduced Republican advantages or produced Democratic victories where there were normally none.
4. The economy and data centers also weighed
Immigration alone doesn’t explain the choice. Holscher made the cost of living a campaign linchpin and, after winning, said he heard the same concern across the state: that everything costs too much.
She also proposed a temporary moratorium on the opening of new data centers. Reuters identifies the rejection of those projects as a relevant factor in the contest. The issue strained alliances: labor organizations that supported data center development backed Masterson.
This dimension helps explain why it is insufficient to interpret each Democratic vote as a referendum only on immigration policy.
 
U.S. Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton gives a victory speech on Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park after he defeated Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in the 2026 midterm election. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
How the Latino vote influenced
The available evidence identifies three ways of influence: incorporating new voters, reactivating people who had not voted in a long time, and organizing communities around shared experiences. Latino presence is closely linked to the labor and demographic history of these communities.
But there is a difference between showing influence and accurately quantifying it.
Results for a county with a large Latino population do not automatically reveal how its Latino residents voted. Nor are the total population, voting-age citizen population, registered persons, and those who actually cast a ballot equivalent.
According to an AP Voter Poll, more than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapproved of the way ICE conducts its work. That figure reflects the general electorate in that election, not exclusively Latino voters.
Therefore, Latino mobilization was an important part of the change, but it worked alongside other sectors of the electorate. The sources verified for this article do not yet provide sufficiently detailed measures to establish Latino state participation, its distribution by candidate, or how many voters changed parties.
 
Which regions saw the most significant changes
To compare changes, you need to specify the reference. The following data contrasts the 2026 elections with the 2024 elections. They do not compare the same office or necessarily the same voters. They describe shifts in the party margin, not individual transfers of votes.
 
Seward and Liberal: The Most Pronounced Documented Change
The New York Times reported that Seward shifted 52 points toward the Democratic nominee in the Senate race compared to the 2024 presidential election, the biggest change on record in Kansas. That’s a cross-party variation: It doesn’t mean 52% of people have changed their vote.
The change also reached the governorship. Holscher won a county where Donald Trump had won 68% in 2024. According to KCUR, no Democrat had won the governorship in Seward since 1974.
Seward stands out, therefore, for two reasons: the magnitude of his displacement to the Senate and the historic rupture that his result for governor represented.
 
Sedgwick and Wichita: The Effort to Increase the Latino Vote
Organizers from Wichita and Lakin, Kansas, worked to register new Latino voters, mobilizing parents to encourage their U.S. citizen children to vote. The effort was nonpartisan and supported by The Voter Network, a nonprofit dedicated to strengthening Kansas communities through voter education and engagement. Their “Voter to Voter” tool, bilingual content, and interpretation support at polling locations in Wichita—in areas with a large Latino population—increased participation among new voters, most of whom are children of immigrants.


 
An election of coalitions, not a single bloc
Kansas in 2026 left two complementary images. In the suburbs, a broad electoral base largely offset Republican advantages in rural territory. In the southwest, immigrant and Latino communities, along with other residents, responded to the raids by organizing and participating politically.
The Latino vote matters not because it acted as a uniform bloc, but because it influenced competitive communities, narrowed margins, and helped change outcomes. The election showed that ability.
