name: Alaska Beacon
title: Under new rule, Trump administration greenlights Arctic winter drilling without public comment
description: Amid a flood of new investment in Alaska’s oil patch and an aggressive push by the Trump administration to speed up drilling, one of the state’s biggest producers is pushing west deeper into the Arctic. ConocoPhillips recently announced new plans to drill and conduct geologic studies this winter in search of oil beneath the western […]
text:
ConocoPhillips is planning to drill up to four wells and conduct seismic surveys across some 245 square miles of federal land in the western Arctic this winter. (ConocoPhillips)Amid a flood of new investment in Alaska’s oil patch and an aggressive push by the Trump administration to speed up drilling, one of the state’s biggest producers is pushing west deeper into the Arctic.
ConocoPhillips recently announced new plans to drill and conduct geologic studies this winter in search of oil beneath the western Arctic. It’s targeting federal land beyond the $9 billion Willow oil field the company is currently building at the western edge of existing roads and pipelines.
ConocoPhillips’ drilling campaign is the first one approved in the vast National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska since the Trump administration sold more than 1 million acres of oil and gas leases there in the spring. That huge sale reflected a resurgence of industry interest in the region after a string of new oil discoveries.
ConocoPhillips’ project is also the first in the reserve permitted under a new federal rule that speeds up reviews and effectively eliminates public comment periods for certain early-stage work there, including geologic testing and exploratory drilling — a policy change supported by the oil industry and opposed by environmental groups.
ConocoPhillips’ plans — which are similar in scope to work the company did last year in a different area — include drilling up to four exploration wells and conducting seismic studies across 245 square miles. The studies involve scanning for oil deposits by driving over the frozen tundra in trucks that shoot seismic waves deep underground.
Last year, the company did seismic surveys directly south of Willow, whereas this year the company is focused mostly to the west, according to maps in federal permitting documents.





Maps of ConocoPhillips’ planned winter exploratory drilling and seismic studies obtained from Bureau of Land Management permitting documents. The Willow oil field is in the area labeled Bear Tooth Unit.




Boosters say the project is part of an oil industry renaissance in Alaska that’s creating jobs and new income for the state government. And federal officials say they anticipate minimal environmental impact.
But environmental groups are worried about the implications for the largely undeveloped western Arctic. The Trump administration approved ConocoPhillips’ proposal with “no meaningful environmental review and with no opportunity for the public to weigh in,” said Ian Dooley, an Anchorage-based attorney with Earthjustice, a conservation-oriented law firm.
The petroleum reserve, also known as NPR-A, is an Indiana-sized expanse of federal land thought to hold billions of barrels of untapped oil and gas. Despite its name, the area also encompasses wetlands, caribou and migratory bird habitat and traditional hunting and fishing grounds of North Slope Iñupiaq residents.
In the past, oil exploration plans there were typically subject to federal environmental assessments and were posted for public comment prior to approval by regulators — adding to the time between a proposal’s submission and approval.
As part of a broader effort to accelerate permitting and development in Alaska, the Trump administration announced in October that environmental assessments would no longer be required for exploratory drilling and seismic surveys in the reserve.
Land managers approved ConocoPhillips’ permit for exploration work on Nov. 2. The drilling and seismic testing was highlighted last week by a ConocoPhillips executive at a conference in Anchorage.
No other companies have publicly disclosed plans for work in NPR-A this season. A few multinational oil companies that acquired leases there earlier this year — ExxonMobil, and Spanish company Repsol in partnership with Shell — are not expected to drill on their leases this season. (Analyzing existing geologic data, planning, and hiring contractors can take companies ample time; insiders say more projects are likely to be proposed in the reserve in future years.)



A spokesperson for the U.S. Bureau of Land Management, which manages NPR-A, said the agency has not received any other applications for exploration there this winter.
But ConocoPhillips’ project still could be a harbinger of things to come in the reserve – if not this year, then next.
ExxonMobil and Shell — which haven’t looked for new oil in Alaska in years — committed millions of dollars to acquire their new leases in NPR-A, and several small companies also have built up substantial interests there, including one led by the state’s most prolific wildcatter, Bill Armstrong.
Other companies, meanwhile, are moving ahead with projects this winter just outside the reserve. They include Santos, an Australian company that’s working to prove out earlier oil discoveries on state land — and a small Texas company called Narwhal Exploration that’s gearing up to drill through the ice into shallow state waters not far off the coast of the North Slope.
State officials hope the early-stage work will lead companies to commit much larger sums of money to building new fields and producing more oil. Industry boosters say the the increased investment and new drilling is likely to create jobs and generate revenue for the state government.
The federal government projects Alaska’s oil production to increase by 13% next year, driven mainly by an uptick in volume at the new Pikka oil field, which is operated by Santos and began producing this year.
But the push to develop the western Arctic also has fueled concerns among environmental groups and people in Nuiqsut.
The Iñupiaq village, at the eastern edge of the reserve, once sat beyond the western edge of the oil patch. Now, rigs dot the village’s horizon.
Nuiqsut residents hunt caribou in the area where ConocoPhillips plans to explore this winter, and caribou migrate through the area toward their calving grounds, said Rosemary Ahtuangaruak. She’s a former Nuiqsut mayor and current executive director of Grandmothers Growing Goodness, a small environmental group that’s suing the federal government over its oil and gas management in the region.
“The timing and location of this work will affect our families’ ability to bring food home,” Ahtuangaruak said in a statement shared with the Anchorage Press. She also expressed concerns about the new expedited permitting rule, known as a categorical exclusion.
“People who depend on this area deserve a chance to shape decisions before BLM approves them,” said Ahtuangaruak.
The Bureau of Land Management’s decision document says ConocoPhillips’ project “is not expected to result in any undue or unnecessary environmental degradation of the public lands.”
Representatives of the state’s oil and gas industry say the categorical exclusion provides more predictability for companies. They note that it doesn’t waive local or state regulations and draws on findings from dozens of past environmental assessments.
The challenging logistics of Arctic projects mean that companies must plan months in advance — and the new rule helps them coordinate, secure equipment and hire contractors, said Steve Wackowski, president of the Alaska Oil and Gas Association.
“Missing that window can mean waiting another year,” Wackowski said in an email. “Reducing that scheduling risk has real value.”
Wackowski described ConocoPhillips’ winter plans as “an encouraging commitment to the state’s future.”
The company’s exploration “underscores our commitment to Alaska and our ongoing investment in the state while supporting long-term U.S. energy security through the responsible development of domestic resources,” said Megan Olson, a ConocoPhillips spokesperson.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Supreme Court reinstates $562K verdict against Newark for bridge crash
description: Newark claimed it wasn't liable for a trucker's 2015 crash into an unmarked low-clearance railroad bridge, but NJ's top court ruled it is.
text:
Newark claimed it wasn't liable for a trucker's 2015 crash into a low railroad overpass, but the New Jersey Supreme Court ruled it is because officials failed to post the low-clearance signage state law requires. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey municipalities that fail to post signs warning motorists of low-clearance bridges can be held liable for damages and injuries when drivers collide with such overpasses, despite a state law that grants local governments immunity for more discretionary traffic signage, the New Jersey State Supreme Court said.
In a unanimous ruling Thursday, the justices reinstated a $562,500 jury verdict against Newark in the case of a trucker who followed a “truck route” sign in February 2015, only to crash into an unmarked low overpass while he had his eyes on the road below to dodge potholes. David B. Wilson’s 13-foot-6-inch tractor trailer got wedged under the 12-foot-2-inch railroad overpass on Avenue P near Foundry Street, leaving him with neck injuries, according to the ruling.
An appellate panel had overturned the verdict, agreeing with city and state lawyers who had argued that a provision in the state Tort Claims Act shields governments from liability for any failure to post ordinary traffic signals.
But state legislators in 1986 passed a law specifically to guard against the kinds of crashes Wilson had by requiring municipalities to warn motorists of bridges with less than 14 feet and 6 inches of clearance on or before the bridge, as well as at the last safe exit or detour before the bridge, wrote Justice Rachel Wainer Apter, who penned the decision.
Signs mandated by that 1986 law are not the “ordinary” signs exempted from liability under the Tort Claims Act, because public entities have no discretion over whether or not to post them, she added.
“As Wilson correctly points out: ‘The statute dictates what needs to be done. There is no discretion,’” she wrote.
The city not only failed to put the required maximum-clearance signs on the overpass and at the last safe exit before it, but also misled drivers by placing a “truck route” sign directing drivers toward the bridge, essentially assuring Wilson the route had no hazards, she added.
“The jury was thus entitled to conclude that the City created a dangerous condition by posting an ‘actively deceptive’ sign that ‘lulled [Wilson] into a false sense of security’ that he could safely make a right turn onto Avenue P without immediately crashing into an unmarked, low-clearance bridge,” Wainer Apter wrote, citing another 1994 state Supreme Court ruling.
Newark officials did not respond to a request for comment.
The case showed how the need for accurate signage to protect the driving public from known harms can conflict with the realities of local governments that struggle to keep up with changing road conditions.
A city worker had testified at trial that Newark’s road system spans about 350 miles, with just a three-person maintenance crew responsible for the tens of thousands of traffic signs on them. The worker said the city relied on reports from drivers and city employees’ own observations to learn of missing signs. In this case, a required sign had been replaced four times between 2011 and 2015, with workers reinstalling it again five weeks before Wilson’s crash, but just a bare pole stood by the time he hit the bridge, according to the ruling.
The city’s attorneys had argued “it is entirely possible that the sign went missing hours, minutes, or even seconds before Wilson’s accident, which is insufficient to show the City had notice.”
But Wainer Apter rejected that argument too, saying Wilson proved a provision of the Tort Claims Act that holds public entities liable if they create a dangerous condition through the negligence or omission of an employee.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ACLU-WV opposes attorney general’s motion to dismiss school funding lawsuit
description: Attorneys representing a Lincoln County student in a legal challenge over the state’s school funding formula have opposed a motion by the state Attorney General Office to dismiss the case.
text:
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia opposes a motion by the state Attorney General Office to dismiss a case on the state’s school funding formula. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Attorneys representing a Lincoln County student in a legal challenge over the state’s school funding formula have opposed a motion by the state Attorney General Office to dismiss the case. 
The attorney general’s argument in a motion last week should leave the Supreme Court and the state “deeply concerned,” the attorneys with the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia wrote in a response filed Thursday.  
“To avoid enforcement of one of West Virginia’s most firmly established rights, the State Officer Respondents propound a thoroughly undemocratic portrait of state government,” the attorneys wrote. “If the arguments of the State Officer Respondents prevail, the Legislature will have held itself to be the final arbiter of our Constitution, then used that self-proclaimed authority to  insulate itself from judicial review.”
They asked that the attorney general’s motion be denied. 
“The West Virginia Constitution, Not the Legislature, Defines This Court’s Jurisdiction,” they wrote in a 19-page filing. “The Constitution is the supreme law of West Virginia, and every branch of government is bound by it.”
ACLU-WV is representing M.D. and the student’s parent, Lakin Patten, in the legal challenge before the Supreme Court. It attempts to require state lawmakers to “correct the school funding formula.” 
Attorney General JB McCuskeyl — on behalf of the state officer respondents in the case — last week moved to dismiss a lawsuit, arguing that the state Supreme Court does not have authority over Senate President Randy Smith and House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, the two lawmakers named in the suit. It also argued the petitioner, a sixth grade student in Lincoln County, has not met the burden of showing standing to sue anyone.
The lawsuit lists as defendants Hanshaw, R-Clay; Smith, R-Preston; Auditor Mark Hunt; Tax Commissioner Matthew Irby; Treasurer Larry Pack; the state Department of Education; the state Board of Education, the School Building Authority, State School Superintendent Michelle Blatt, as as well as Lincoln County school board officials and county officials.
West Virginia public schools’ poor finances have prompted a wave of school closures across the state. The West Virginia Department of Education says it will take a $410 million increase in state aid for public schools to meet needs in special education, enrollment stabilization, personnel and more. 
State officials have asked the court to pause the case until April, giving lawmakers time to address the funding formula during the upcoming legislative session, when the formula is expected to be a focus. 
State school officials have agreed with the motion to delay the case. 
Attorneys with the ACLU, on behalf of M.D., have argued against delaying the case.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri education board selects Senate leader Cindy O’Laughlin as interim commissioner
description: Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, will lead Missouri’s Department of Elementary and Secondary Education as interim commissioner of education beginning Dec. 1. The State Board of Education voted 6-1 to appoint O’Laughlin in a closed meeting Friday morning. It will continue its search for a permanent commissioner, aiming to hire[...]
text:
Cindy O'Laughlin, pictured speaking to reporters in May 2024, will lead Missouri's education department as interim commissioner beginning Dec. 1 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, will lead Missouri’s Department of Elementary and Secondary Education as interim commissioner of education beginning Dec. 1.
The State Board of Education voted 6-1 to appoint O’Laughlin in a closed meeting Friday morning. It will continue its search for a permanent commissioner, aiming to hire a permanent commissioner by June.
O’Laughlin, who did not respond to a request for comment, will replace Lisa Sireno, who has served as interim commissioner since Oct. 21, following the resignation of Stacey Preis.
Missouri education chief resigns amid controversy over A-F ratings for public schools

The announcement came after months of rumors that O’Laughlin was being eyed for the position. As word circulated more widely in the past month, the state board’s inbox filled with angry emails and questions about her qualifications.
Wheaton school Superintendent Alyssa Kennedy was among those who opposed O’Laughlin’s possible appointment, sharing her letter to the board in a Facebook post.
“I respectfully urge the Board not to make this appointment based on political alignment or a predetermined outcome,” she wrote. “If the Board is considering Senator O’Laughlin, I urge you to carefully examine whether her experience and policy positions align with the responsibilities and public mission of this office.”
State law requires the commissioner to “possess an educational attainment and breadth of experience in the administration of public education.”
O’Laughlin’s Senate biography says she has experience “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.”
She chaired the Senate Education Committee from 2020 to 2022, telling public school advocates that she hoped to work with them and that she was not an expert, as The Independent reported in 2021.
Duane Martin, an attorney whose law firm EdCounsel represents public school districts, told The Independent he does not think O’Laughlin meets the legal requirements for the job.
“It is interesting that you would put somebody in a position that is not qualified by statute, who is responsible for the department and reports to the state board that handles all of the licensures for all of the professional educators in the state,” he said.
In 1970, the State Board of Education sought an attorney general’s opinion on a candidate “who is not a certified teacher” but had led the House Education Committee and worked as a part-time professor at Missouri Valley College.
Then-Attorney General John Danforth wrote that the candidate was not qualified, since he lacked experience in administration.
“Executive experience in the field of public education would be invaluable, if not essential, in the performance of (the commissioner’s) duties,” Danforth wrote.
State Board of Education president Brooks Miller, who spoke to The Independent on his way into the department offices Friday morning, said he believes O’Laughlin is qualified.
In a press release, Miller said she “brings a range of skills that will be beneficial to (the department) and the children of Missouri.”
When asked whether his friendship with her has impacted his decision, he said, “not at all.”
Questions about O’Laughlin’s qualifications are not the only concerns raised by opponents of her appointment. Some have also pointed to her record on public education policy.
Former state Sen. Lincoln Hough, a Republican from Springfield, has spoken publicly about O’Laughlin’s leadership in the Senate and said he faced pressure during his time as Senate Appropriations chairman not to fully fund public education.
The two had a falling out amid disagreements over school funding and other Senate issues. In 2025, Hough led the Senate Appropriations Committee in restoring $300 million to fully fund the formula that determines state aid for public schools.
O’Laughlin removed him as appropriations chairman that September, shortly after he opposed Republican efforts to end debate on congressional redistricting and changes to the initiative petition process. O’Laughlin said at the time that the decision would provide continuity on the committee because Hough was approaching the end of his Senate term.
“She is one of very few people in elected office who has actually looked me in the face and said she didn’t want to fund or fully fund the foundation formula the last year that I was the appropriations chairman in the Senate,” Hough told The Independent.
Having O’Laughlin as the chief of the state’s education department is “going to hurt the next generation of students in this state,” he said.
“She’s going to try to systematically dismantle public education,” Hough said.
The department’s press release said O’Laughlin will work to “maintain organizational stability, strengthen relationships with local school districts and the General Assembly, and advance the state board’s strategic priorities.”
“I understand this is an interim assignment and that the state board is undertaking a national search for its next permanent commissioner,” O’Laughlin said in the public release. “My responsibility is to provide the leadership, stability and forward momentum the department needs during that process. I intend to make the most of that opportunity.”
O’Laughlin is a vocal proponent of policies that use public funds for private schools, including the state’s K-12 voucher system, MOScholars. At the end of the legislative session in May, there was a push to remove the program from the State Treasurer’s Office and instead have the education department administer it.
Expanding MOScholars and similar programs has long been a priority for O’Laughlin, who has expressed frustration for years that public schools “have a monopoly on public education.”
Gov. Mike Kehoe also supports expanding private-school options. 
In October, Kehoe declined to share his opinion on Preis’s resignation or O’Laughlin’s possible appointment.
His communications director, Gabby Picard, pointed to the state board’s authority to hire a commissioner.
Kehoe has appointed a majority of the board’s members and “has confidence in their judgment,” Picard said in a statement.
The Missouri Constitution sets up the State Board of Education as an eight-member board with staggered, eight-year terms. This structure is designed to limit how quickly any one governor can reshape the board.
But in recent years, some board members have continued serving after their terms expired. That has allowed Kehoe to make appointments to seven of the eight seats during his first two years in office.
A similar situation occurred under former Gov. Eric Greitens who appointed board members who voted to oust then-Commissioner Margie Vandeven in 2017. When Greitens was forced from office, the board rehired Vandeven.
Martin sees parallels between the two situations, saying the key difference is timing.
“This is very similar to what was being attempted by Governor Greitens,” he said. “It is just at a slower pace.”
This report will be updated.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Google funds $1.3M freshwater habitat at Cape Romain
description: Google gifted $1.3M to to build protective berms at Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge in South Carolina’s Lowcountry.
text:
Audrey Van Belleghem, director of strategy and operations for Google's global data centers, speaks to a crowd of some 100 attendees at the technology company's groundbreaking in Dorchester County Thursday, Sept. 26, 2024. (Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Google gifted $1.3 million to the National Audubon Society to build protective berms at Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge in South Carolina’s Lowcountry.
With public outcry against data centers growing nationwide and in the Palmetto State, the tech giant is taking on this and other projects across the country related to one of opponents’ concerns: water.
SC counties enacting data center moratoriums

“Data centers are the nerve centers of the digital world, powering our daily lives with search, maps, online banking, healthcare and 911 systems,” according to a statement from Google. “As we grow our data center footprint to support these services, we recognize that how we build is just as important as what we build.”
That’s why Google agreed to help protect more than 100 acres of freshwater habitat at Cape Romain, said Marshall Johnson, chief conservation officer at the National Audubon Society.
The 66,000-acre coastal refuge features Bulls Island, maritime forests, hiking trails and lighthouses. It is home to loggerhead sea turtles, alligators, dolphins, shorebirds and red wolves.
This latest grant brings Google’s total investment in what it calls water stewardship projects in South Carolina to more than $5 million.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Past projects include a $4 million smart-irrigation project, working with Arable Labs and farmers on 20,000 acres across the Carolinas to reduce water usage by more than 500 million gallons annually. It also paid to help restore longleaf pine in Francis Marion National Forest.
According to Google, the company has supported 165 water stewardship projects across 97 watersheds nationwide, as of 2025.
The Cape Romain project is part of the company’s latest funding round, for which there were more than 700 applications submitted nationwide.
Of those applications, 22 were for projects in South Carolina. Cape Romain is the state’s only successful applicant so far.
Suzie Shin, Google’s manager of data center sustainability programs, said these and other water-related efforts have resonated with residents of communities where data centers are located.
Social Security, data centers and healthcare: Senate candidates exchange jabs while talking policy

When a Google data center comes into an area, the company pays for upgrades to the water system, which benefits all utility customers, she told the SC Daily Gazette.
“But our commitment extends beyond our four walls. It goes beyond our relationship with the utility and the water-wastewater infrastructure to understand that water is local and it’s interconnected. The headwaters of a national forest can actually be the water source supply for a community 100 miles away,” she said. “So that’s, I think, where we’ve been able to show the connection between the work that we fund within the broader watershed and the community.”
In 2024, a Charleston County man sued the Dorchester County Council when it refused to disclose how much water a new Google data center under construction there would use to cool the servers and chips that power the digital information superhighway, calling that a trade secret.
The county settled a year later, agreeing to publish the numbers. That same year, the California-based company also changed its tune and started disclosing water usage of all of its centers in an annual report.
Google’s Berkeley County data center, which has been in operation since 2008, used more than 900 million gallons in 2025. The company’s other two data centers — located near St. George and Ridgeville in Dorchester County — are still under construction.
Google announces $3.3B investment in SC data centers, 200 new jobs

One of the two planned centers could use 978 million gallons of water annually, according to the published county estimates.
By comparison, Google’s center in Council Bluffs, Iowa, has the heaviest usage — 1.3 billion gallons.
Its centers in Mesa, Arizona, and Pflugerville, Texas, use 100,000 gallons. But there’s a trade off. They’re air-cooled and require more electricity to operate, another pain point.
The largest data centers — known as hyperscalers — are facing pushback due in large part to the massive amount of energy required by the facilities. The need for power is going up at the same time residents are seeing their own monthly power bills continue to rise.
By relying on water cooling, a company can reduce data center energy use by approximately 10% compared to air cooling, according to Google.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Conservative dark-money group sues to block Colorado’s income tax overhaul from taking effect
description: The long-running effort by untraceable conservative “dark money” groups to defeat a Colorado progressive income tax measure shows no signs of stopping after voters approved the measure at the ballot box this month. The right-wing nonprofit Advance Colorado and two GOP state lawmakers sued the state in Denver District Court Thursday, asking a judge to […]
text:
Chris Kennedy, center, president of the Bell Policy Center, spoke as Amendment 87 supporters declared victory at a press conference in Denver's La Raza Park on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The long-running effort by untraceable conservative “dark money” groups to defeat a Colorado progressive income tax measure shows no signs of stopping after voters approved the measure at the ballot box this month.
The right-wing nonprofit Advance Colorado and two GOP state lawmakers sued the state in Denver District Court Thursday, asking a judge to enjoin the state from “collecting any increased taxes under” the new tiered income tax system established by Amendment 87, which the lawsuit argues was adopted in violation of the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights.
“TABOR is a citizen-initiated constitutional measure that requires proposed tax increases be presented to the people through a clear ballot question and an accurate notice so that voters are not confused or misinformed when they vote,” the suit reads. “Amendment 87 was presented to Colorado voters in a form, and with a notice, that directly conflicts with the explicit protections TABOR guarantees.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado voters narrowly approved Amendment 87 on Nov. 3, with 52% in favor and 48% opposed. The measure hikes corporate and individual income tax rates on the top 3% of earners, while the 97% of Coloradans who earn less than $500,000 per year receive a slight income tax reduction.
With all races called, Colorado voters say ‘yes’ to 7 of 14 ballot measures

Together with Proposition NN — a measure also approved by voters this year to raise the annual revenue growth cap established by TABOR — the amendment’s adoption represented the most sweeping set of changes to Colorado tax policy since voters passed TABOR in 1992.
That’s made the measure a target of a powerful, deep-pocketed network of Colorado conservative policy advocates, who sought to block it at every possible stage, including challenging it at the state’s Title Board and suing the secretary of state to remove the amendment from the ballot in a case that was decided just days before Election Day. Advance Colorado also backed a countermeasure, Proposition 136, to block the amendment by capping income tax rates at their current level, but voters rejected it.
The group said Thursday that it had filed the lawsuit on behalf of Republican state Sens. Barbara Kirkmeyer of Brighton and Byron Pelton of Sterling. The complaint alleges that Amendment 87 violated TABOR by consolidating a constitutional amendment — striking language requiring a flat income tax — with a statutory tax increase in the form of its tiered system.
“It’s clear that Amendment 87 should have been filed as two measures, not a single one,” Kirkmeyer said in a statement. “The constitution wasn’t followed, and voters will pay the price if this measure isn’t overturned.”
The complaint also alleges that the state’s 2026 voter information booklet included tables that miscalculated some of the tax changes resulting from Amendment 87, and that it misstated how the revenue raised by the measure would be used, citing recent comments from outgoing Gov. Jared Polis that the new revenue could soon be eaten up by growth in the state’s Medicaid budget.
Absent from the lawsuit, however, are any further assertions that Amendment 87’s passage has resulted in the elimination of tax deductions for Social Security income, veterans’ pensions and other forms of income — a claim that featured prominently in the opposition campaign’s messaging to voters in recent months, despite being repeatedly debunked by fact checkers.
Advance Colorado did not respond to inquiries about whether it still asserts that those deductions will be eliminated when Amendment 87 takes effect on Jan. 1.
New ballot measures
Advance Colorado on Thursday also filed four proposed ballot initiatives for the 2027 election. All are variations on a “graduated income tax” system that would reestablish a top rate of 4.4% for higher income brackets.
Two versions of the proposal would exempt all income under $100,000 from state income taxes, while the other two would exempt the first $50,000 and tax the next $50,000 at 3.71%.
“When people see the economic destruction that Amendment 87 will cause, they will want immediate reform,” Advance Colorado president Michael Fields said in a statement. “Exempting the first $100,000 of income for individuals and businesses will make Colorado more competitive and will put more money in people’s pockets.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump pick to lead agency protecting US elections says Jan. 6 wasn’t ‘attack’
description: Trump nominee to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Michael LoSapio, was questioned by Sen. Blumenthal at a hearing.
text:
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead an agency with a key role in protecting U.S. elections told senators during a confirmation hearing Thursday that he wouldn’t characterize the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection as an “attack.”
The response by Michael LoSapio, nominated to head the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, came as part of an exchange with U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who has made inquiries about the violence and the 2020 election part of his line of questioning for a number of Trump nominees.
It’s also part of Republicans’ rush to confirm Trump’s picks before Democrats take power in Congress early next year.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio told Blumenthal. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.”
The White House did not immediately return a request seeking comment on the remark by LoSapio, who if confirmed would inherit an agency mired in partisan tensions over the role it should play in combating false claims about voting or election fraud.
He also isn’t the first Trump nominee to answer the Jan. 6 question similarly.
During his own June confirmation hearing for the post of Department of Justice inspector general, Don R. Berthiaume — also during questioning from Blumenthal — acknowledged “violence on the Capitol grounds” on Jan. 6, 2021, but also said, “I don’t know if I would use the term attack.”
Several of Trump’s judicial nominees have also shied away from characterizing the violence as an “attack” during their own confirmation hearings.
On Thursday, Blumenthal also asked LoSapio, currently chief information security officer at artificial intelligence firm Palantir, who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed that he won.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said, later adding that his “only involvement” in that election was voting for Trump.
CISA — formed in 2018 during the first Trump administration and nested within the Department of Homeland Security — is charged with protecting the nation’s critical infrastructure, from dams and nuclear power plants to banks and voting systems.
It’s received bipartisan praise from many state and local election officials, but Trump and his allies remain angry over its efforts to counter misinformation about the 2020 presidential election and the coronavirus pandemic.
The agency’s first director, Chris Krebs, was fired by Trump after highlighting election officials’ statement calling the 2020 election the ” most secure in American history.”
CISA has also been without a Senate-confirmed director for nearly two years. Jen Easterly left the agency as Trump returned to office last year, and Nick Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Sean Plankey withdrew in April when his nomination stalled.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Gov-elect says he’s considering new people for every Cabinet agency. At least 11 want to stay.
authors: Jessica Holdman, Katharine Wilson, Seanna Adcox
description: SC Gov.-elect Alan Wilson is asking the state's cabinet agency heads who wish to stay in their position to reapply for their jobs.
text:
South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pam Evette and Gov. Henry McMaster preside over the final Cabinet meeting of their tenure Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson is asking state agency leaders to reapply for their jobs if they want to stay on in his administration — another sign of the biggest turnover at the helm of state government in 16 years.
Wilson sent letters this week to 23 agency directors giving them until Dec. 4 to let his transition team know they “want to be considered for continued service,” it reads.
Eleven of them told the SC Daily Gazette they either intend to reapply or have no plans to leave before their term ends, including several of the state’s longest-serving agency heads.
Gov. Henry McMaster said Wednesday he hopes Wilson keeps all of them.
“It’s a grand group, but every governor’s got to pick the team that he or she wants,” McMaster told reporters at the last Cabinet meeting of his 10-year tenure. “The governors have to make their decisions. That’s the whole point of having a Cabinet agency, that it reports directly to you.”

Left to right, interim South Carolina Department of Public Health Director Dr. Brannon Traxler, Department of Public Safety chief Robert Woods and Hartley Powell, who leads the state’s tax agency, at the final Cabinet meeting of Gov. Henry McMaster’s term Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

It served as both his “thank you” and a farewell gathering, as agency heads publicly outlined their accomplishments ahead of a reception at the Governor’s Mansion.
Wilson, who inherits a Cabinet expanded during McMaster’s tenure, made clear a day earlier he’s made no decisions.
“I have not offered a single Cabinet agency director their job,” Wilson said Tuesday at the first public meeting of his transition team.
Each has the opportunity to be re-interviewed, he said.
“Some will stay, some will go, but we’re going to consider new people for every single Cabinet agency,” Wilson said. “There must be continuity and stability, but there also must be fresh eyes and fresh perspectives and renewed energy and vigor in the governance of our state.”
Not all Cabinet heads got a letter
Two agency directors who report to the governor did not get letters seeking their interest, according to a list provided to the SC Daily Gazette.
They include Dr. Brannon Traxler, who’s been the interim director of the state Department of Public Health since May, after senators refused to confirm her former boss, Dr. Edward Simmer, for the job. Her assignment then became a debate topic in the GOP gubernatorial race.
SC health director out of the job after failing to receive Senate approval

Traxler told the Gazette she had no plans to seek the job permanently anyway. She does hope to stay with the agency in her former role as chief medical officer.
Also not sent a letter was Emily Farr, director of the state Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation for McMaster’s entire tenure. She is leaving the agency at the end of the year, and Wilson’s team knows that, spokeswoman Holly Beeson said about why Farr didn’t get a letter.
And at the Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities, none of the three division directors got a letter. There is no single director of the agency combined from three separate agencies last year.
Agency heads not replaceable anytime soon
Four of the agency leaders receiving letters, according to the provided list, are intentionally insulated by law from political turnovers.
State law sets six-year terms for the chief of the State Law Enforcement Division, while the heads of the state Department of Public Safety and the state Military Department as well as the inspector general have four-year terms. Wilson can remove them before their term ends only under circumstances specified by law, such as incompetence or misconduct. It would be tough for Wilson to make an argument for any of the allowed reasons.

Left to right, Adjutant General Robert Stilwell and State Law Enforcement Division Chief Mark Keel look at Gov. Henry McMaster at the final Cabinet meeting of his tenure Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Wilson is not trying to do so. There are no plans to remove directors with terms, his spokesman told the Gazette on Thursday.
SLED Chief Mark Keel was most recently confirmed by the Senate in May 2024, after he officially came out of a 30-day retirement.
He has no plans to retire for good: “I still enjoy my job,” he told the Daily Gazette.
And he thinks he and Wilson have worked well together over the governor-elect’s 16 years as state attorney general.
Keel, who began his career at SLED in 1979, has led the agency since 2011, which corresponds to Wilson’s first swearing in as the state’s top prosecutor.
Robert Woods, who leads the Department of Public Safety, also said he has no plans to leave early. And he intends to re-apply for the job once his first term is up in a year.
Woods’ appointment brought stability and improved trooper morale at the long-troubled agency that includes the Highway Patrol. Initially put in charge in 2020, the then-30-year veteran of the agency was confirmed as its permanent leader in 2021.
And Maj. Gen. Robin Stilwell has two years left on his term, which he plans to fulfill.
As adjutant general, Stilwell is over the state National Guard. Last year, he became only the second adjutant general chosen by the governor rather than popularly elected.
Other longtime directors
Beyond Keel, two other agency heads appointed by Gov. Nikki Haley at the beginning of her tenure in January 2011 said they hope to stay.
When McMaster ascended to the governor’s office in January 2017, taking over when Haley left to become the first United Nations ambassador in the Trump administration, he largely kept her administration intact. Over the last 10 years, he’s generally replaced directors as they retired or resigned.
Wilson said agency leaders interested in keeping their roles must buy into his vision of a “more modernized and reformed state government.”
SC DMV set to begin massive technology upgrade to agency’s ‘ancient’ computer system

One reason Kevin Shwedo said he wants to stay is to implement a major technology upgrade at the Department of Motor Vehicles that he fought for.
Last year, the Legislature gave him permission to increase document fees by $4 to fund a $100 million overhaul of the DMV’s three-decade-old software systems. By the end of 2027, Shwedo said, South Carolinians will have the option to carry digital driver’s licenses or identification cards on their phones.
Haley hired Shwedo straight from the military. The Army colonel was Fort Jackson’s deputy commanding officer when he retired and took the helm of the DMV.
In 2015, he temporarily left that role when Haley put him in charge of coordinating state and federal disaster relief efforts following historic flooding.
That interim role led to the Legislature creating a new Cabinet agency — the state Office of Resilience — in fall 2020. Its only director, Ben Duncan, was among agency heads declining to say whether he’ll apply with Wilson to stay.

Left to right, South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles Director Kevin Shwedo, and state parks and recreation director Duane Parrish at the final Cabinet meeting of Gov. Henry McMaster’s tenure Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

Duane Parrish, who’s led the state Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism since January 2011, said he will reapply.
At Wednesday’s Cabinet meeting, he touted the expansion of golf in the state, including a PGA Tour stop in Myrtle Beach. This year, the state has opened two new state parks: Black River State Park and Ramsey Grove State Park.
“Thank you for allowing us to promote it to the rest of the world, the rest of the country,” Parrish said to McMaster, after listing golf, fishing, NASCAR and mountains as state tourism products.
Without naming Wilson or his call for modernization, Marcia Adams, director of the Department of Administration, highlighted some of the accomplishments he’ll inherit.
She pointed to improved cybersecurity for agencies, salary studies, and raises for state employees, the reorganizing of the state’s various health-related agencies and a forensic review and correction of multibillion-dollar accounting errors that had lingered on the state books for decade.
“We’ve learned that making accountability visible through independent review and public reporting is very important. That modernizing is a people-and-process effort. Technology and service modernization provides value when the people who understand the business help design that workflow,” Adams said.
She sounded tearful as she concluded: “I am so proud of what the great employees at Admin have been able to do for the state.”
Cabinet expansions over the last decade
Adams’ agency was part of a major government overhaul approved in 2014. It divided duties of the Budget and Control Board, a mammoth bureaucratic agency she led, between the newly created Department of Administration and other agencies. The law, seen as a huge win for Haley, marked the biggest government restructuring in 20 years.
The Legislature added to the governor’s authority during McMaster’s tenure. Three agencies were put directly under the governor’s control as part of restructuring laws:

Last year, the Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities combined three previous agencies: the departments of mental health, disabilities, and alcohol and drug abuse services.
In 2024, the massive Department of Health and Environmental Control was divided in two, becoming the Department of Environmental Services and the Department of Public Health, both in the Cabinet.

Beyond the Office of Resilience, two other agencies in the governor’s Cabinet didn’t exist when McMaster took office:

Legislators approved the Department of Veterans Affairs as a standalone agency in 2019.
The Department on Aging was a division in the lieutenant governor’s office prior to 2019.

The Military Department was put in the Cabinet in 2019, upon implementation of a change in the state constitution, approved by voters in 2014, that made the adjutant general an appointed position answering to the governor.
And the Department of Transportation returns to the governor’s Cabinet on Jan. 1 as part of a modernization law approved by the Legislature earlier this year.
That combination gives Wilson the largest Cabinet of any incoming governor in state history.
All of his picks must be confirmed by the state Senate.
Left to right, South Carolina Department of Administration Director Marcia Adams and state prisons director Joel Anderson listen at the final Cabinet meeting of Gov. Henry McMaster’s term Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

title: $1M settlement proposed in state’s case against Woonsocket sewage plant
description: The cost to clean up a yearslong legal battle with state regulators over repeated environmental violations at Woonsocket’s regional wastewater treatment plant: $1 million. That’s according to a tentative consent agreement on the agenda for the Woonsocket City Council Monday night. The 28-page agreement, which has not been signed by any of the parties, aims [[...]
text:
A tentative settlement would resolve a 2023 state lawsuit against the Woonsocket Wastewater Treatment Facility. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)The cost to clean up a yearslong legal battle with state regulators over repeated environmental violations at Woonsocket’s regional wastewater treatment plant: $1 million.
That’s according to a tentative consent agreement on the agenda for the Woonsocket City Council Monday night. The 28-page agreement, which has not been signed by any of the parties, aims to resolve a March 2023 lawsuit by the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office and Department of Environmental Management (DEM) alleging the city-owned, privately-managed wastewater plant violated state and federal environmental laws by dumping partially untreated sewage into the Blackstone River. 
The Superior Court complaint led to a citywide reckoning in which officials ultimately concluded that they no longer wanted the responsibility — and cost and legal risk — of processing the region’s sludge at the aging sewage treatment facility. The 16-acre Cumberland Hill Road plant hosts one of two incinerators in the state — the other is in Cranston — burning dried sewage products for 30 cities and towns and commercial customers across southern New England.
The state’s lawsuit claims aging equipment was not properly maintained, and poor communication between the two companies that manage the separate sides of the plant caused at least three sewage spills in the previous 12 months.
None of the defendants — the city and its contractors, Jacobs Engineering Group and Synagro Woonsocket LLC — admit liability under the proposed settlement. But the two national companies would pay $500,000 combined in fees to state regulators and funding for environmental programs under the proposed agreement. The remaining $500,000 would be suspended, providing the other financial penalties are paid on time, and that the defendants meet new reporting and monitoring requirements.
“It works out well for the city,” said Council President Dan Gendron, who is sponsoring the resolution calling for the council to approve the tentative agreement. “Not actually being the operator of the facility, and the lawsuit being based on operators, it seems appropriate that the operators who controlled the operation would be the ones to accept the biggest part of the penalty.”
Attorneys for Jacobs and Synagro did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.
Attorney General Peter Neronha remained noncommittal.
“We engaged in settlement discussions with the city and its operators, and those discussions have advanced to a point where an agreement that would achieve accountability for past harm and prevent future harm from the plant may be possible,” Neronha said in an email Friday. “In the event a resolution between parties is finalized, we will have more to say.”
A DEM spokesperson acknowledged but did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Moving on 
Jacobs, a Texas-based company, has already cut ties with the city, severing a 20-year contract signed in 2012 amid service payment disputes. Veolia North America, which provides water and wastewater treatment services for several other cities and towns in the state, was brought on in September to temporarily manage the wastewater treatment side. Synagro Woonsocket, a subsidiary of a Baltimore-based company, is still running the incinerator under its own long-term contract, which doesn’t end until 2032. 
The proposed settlement specifies that both Jacobs and Synagro still have to pay the penalties even if they no longer run the plant, or if it closes.
As laid out in the proposed agreement, each company would pay nearly $76,000 apiece to the Attorney General’s office and DEM, respectively, within the first month. Within three months, they would split the $50,000 cost to set up a third-party grant program to compensate businesses along the Blackstone River that have been negatively impacted by the environmental and health consequences of sewage spills from the plant. And within 10 months, the companies would pay $150,000 apiece toward two state-run environmental programs: one transplanting quahogs into waters designated for shellfishing use, and a second to clean up local waterbodies “impaired by excess aquatic vegetation,” including the Blackstone River.
Both companies, in addition to the city, would also commit to additional staffing and reporting requirements, including monthly “lookbacks” on operations in 30-day increments, and, after 18 months, a comprehensive evaluation of how the incinerator is working.
Gendron thinks the incinerator may no longer be operating by then. 
As mayor-elect, having defeated Mayor Christopher Beauchamp in the Nov. 3 nonpartisan election, Gendron wants to close the sludge side of the operation by June 30, 2027. The city has been trying to shut down the incinerator for more than a year without success. Gendron acknowledged his timeline might be too ambitious, but he also said the ongoing problems caused by aging equipment and lack of maintenance might force the closure without city intervention.
“It’s got so many problems,” Gendron said. “The plant could actually just shut itself down.”
That’s despite more than $2.2 million the city authorized in 2023 to repair the gravity belt thickener used to separate out solid waste. The city estimates another $40 to $50 million would be needed to fully upgrade the 50-year-old incinerator. 
The price of closing 
Woonsocket does not have to pay any of the penalties in the proposed settlement. But if all or a portion of sewage plant closes, it could be costly.
The city brings in $3 million in annual host fees from the two contractors plus a share of royalties from incineration up to $600,000 a year under its contracts with Synagro and Jacobs. And, Woonsocket has its waste treated for free. 
The city’s approved fiscal 2027 budget featured higher sewer fees to cover its expected payments to Veolia, with a $556 annual flat fee per property compared with roughly $440 the year before, Gendron said. The city’s independent wastewater treatment fund is expected to generate $13.5 million in revenue in fiscal 2027, nearly $4 million more than the $9.6 million balance as of June 30, according to city budget documents. 



Quotation







It’s got so many problems. The plant could actually just shut itself down.


– Mayor-elect Dan Gendron


An unsuccessful plan to sell the plant to the Narragansett Bay Commission, a quasi-public agency that already runs the largest wastewater operations in the state, also could have offset projected revenue losses. But negotiations broke down over the summer, Gendron said, when controversy erupted over a separate project for a high-heat sludge processing plant in North Kingstown’s Quonset Business Park.
Narragansett Bay Commission was planning to use the proposed Quonset pyrolysis plant to treat its wastewater byproducts, including from Woonsocket, but the Quonset project is now on hold amid community backlash, a pair of lawsuits, and a soon-to-begin legislative study panel. 
Gendron did not know when the proposed consent agreement could take effect, deferring to City Solicitor Michael Lepizzera, who did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
There are no upcoming hearings in the case, according to the public court docket. 
Outgoing Mayor Christopher Beauchamp also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A separate, federal class-action lawsuit filed by city property owners in July 2023 regarding smells and traffic from the wastewater plant was dismissed in July 2024, court records show.

title: Incoming Kreiss-Tomkins administration names top budget director, chief of staff
description: Alaska Gov.-elect, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, announced the first picks for key leadership positions on Wednesday. Kreiss-Tomkins has named Alexei Painter, former head of the Alaska Legislative Finance Division, the new director of the Office of Management and Budget. Ira Slomski-Pritz will be Kreiss-Tomkins’ chief of staff, and Becky Windt Pearson will be a s[...]
text:
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a candidate for governor, speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Juneau Chamber of Commerce in Juneau on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Gov.-elect, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, announced the first picks for key leadership positions on Wednesday.
Kreiss-Tomkins has named Alexei Painter, former head of the Alaska Legislative Finance Division, the new director of the Office of Management and Budget. Ira Slomski-Pritz will be Kreiss-Tomkins’ chief of staff, and Becky Windt Pearson will be a senior transition advisor for the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority.
“Alaska has no shortage of challenges, and meeting them will require bringing together talented, high-integrity Alaskans who know how to get things done,” Kreiss-Tomkins said in a statement with the announcement. “I’m thrilled to have Ira, Alexei, and Becky helping lead this work. We’re building a team that is ready to move fast and fix things.”
Kreiss-Tomkins is the unofficial winner of the gubernatorial election, garnering 51% of the vote. Official results will be certified on Nov. 25. He is set to take office ten days later, on Dec. 7.     

Alexei Painter, director of the Legislative Finance Division, testifies in front of the Senate Finance Committee on Friday, May 13, 2022 at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
 

Painter, 39, has been the director of the non-partisan Legislative Finance Division that advises the Alaska State Legislature since 2020. He previously worked as a fiscal analyst for the division since 2014, and as an economist for the Alaska Department of Revenue. As lead of the Office of Management and Budget, housed in the executive branch, he’ll oversee the state’s roughly $15.6 billion budget, working across departments.
“With Alaska facing significant fiscal challenges, OMB will play a central role in developing a sustainable budget and aligning state resources with the administration’s priorities,” the announcement said.
The incoming Kreiss-Tomkins administration is charged with submitting a draft budget to the Legislature just one week after inauguration, by Dec. 15.
Slomski-Pritz, 34, will be the new chief of staff for the incoming governor. He has worked for the last six years as a partner for Ship Creek Group, an Anchorage-based political consulting and communications firm. Previously he worked as a special assistant to the former mayors of Anchorage Mayors Ethan Berkowitz and Austin Quinn-Davidson, and in the office of former Gov. Bill Walker. 
As chief of staff, he’ll act as principal advisor to Kreiss-Tomkins, oversee day-to-day operations of the governor’s office and coordinate policy priorities. “He will play a central role in ensuring coordination across state agencies, the legislature, and Alaska stakeholders to advance the administration’s agenda,” the announcement said.
Windt Pearson will serve as senior transition advisor for AIDEA, the state’s economic development agency. “She will work closely with transition leadership to identify priorities, assess opportunities for improvement, and help shape the administration’s approach to AIDEA,” the announcement said.
AIDEA has been on a spending blitz on economic development projects in the last months of the Dunleavy administration authorizing more than $200 million since August. On Thursday, Kreiss-Tomkins called on the seven-member board to pause all action until the new administration takes office.
Most recently Windt Pearson served as head of legal and corporate affairs for Glenfarne Alaska LNG, the Texas-based firm that owns 75% of the project to develop a proposed 800-mile natural gas pipeline from the North Slope to Cook Inlet. The project was the focus of political negotiations this year as Gov. Mike Dunleavy backed a significant state tax break for the proposed gasline, but legislation failed to pass in the Legislature amid a stalemate.
Windt Pearson previously served as municipal manager for the Municipality of Anchorage under Mayor Suzanne LaFrance, and as municipal attorney under former mayor Ethan Burkowitz. She was senior vice president, general counsel and chief administrative officer for GCI, the state’s largest telecommunications provider. 
The Legislature is now hiring to replace Painter. The search and hiring process is conducted by the Legislative Audit and Budget committee, which said in a statement Monday it will begin the process as soon as possible. The goal is to hire a new director of the Legislative Finance Division before the 35th Legislature convenes in January.

text:
A fire burns at Omaha Track’s wood processing facility in Attalla, Ala., on Thursday. (Lee Hedgepeth/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
ATTALLA — April Phillips is worried about her brother Bubba.
The 46-year-old has cerebral palsy and epilepsy and sometimes suffers from difficulty breathing. So when her two-year-old grandson’s preschool messaged to tell her the facility was closing due to smoke from a nearby fire, she fretted not only about the child, but also her brother.
The blaze, she would soon find out, was less than a mile from her home, at a wood processing facility owned by a company called Omaha Track. Just outside, thick, dark smoke rose above the towering pines of Attalla, a town of less than 6,000 people.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Phillips’ worry kicked into overdrive. No public officials had directly informed her family about the plume of smoke billowing through her community. She checked social media. Local officials were saying that an evacuation of residents within a mile had been ordered. Phillips was confused.
“They ain’t told none of us nothing,” Phillips said. “And here we are sitting here and breathing it.”
Jim Slick, director of the Etowah County Emergency Management Agency, said the fire started in a yard where used railroad ties were being stored before being ground into chips of biomass.
Omaha Track and similar companies take wood products, often treated with chemicals, and process and sell them to be burned as industrial fuel. While the industry has billed its products as a renewable energy source because trees and other organic matter can be regrown, environmentalists have critiqued the carbon-intensive practice as “burning trees to save the planet.”
According to its website, Omaha Track’s Attalla facility receives and processes more than 200,000 tons of railroad ties each year. The company could not immediately be reached for comment.
Lynn Battle, chief spokesperson for the Alabama Department of Environmental Management, said in an e-mail Thursday evening that while the overall size of the blaze had been reduced, the fire is ongoing. Several fire departments are applying water to some areas of the site that can be safely reached, she wrote, but there is no significant runoff from the site.
An evacuation order was lifted Thursday afternoon, local officials said.
Slick, the EMA director, said Thursday he believes there to be “very minimal danger to the surrounding areas, if any danger at all.”
“As it is right now, they are burning, but the surrounding areas, the neighborhoods around the yard, so to speak, are safe,” he said.
Tabitha Brown, a certified nursing assistant who lives near the fire, said she was having difficulty breathing after only a few minutes outside Thursday morning and doesn’t believe the fire poses no health risks.
Brown said she suffers from asthma and that those with existing respiratory illnesses often find even limited exposure to air pollution irritating.
“And we haven’t heard anything about what we’re supposed to do,” Brown said.
Tabitha Brown said public officials have done little to inform the public about any risks from Thursday’s fire. (Lee Hedgepeth/Inside Climate News)
Fires of all types lead to air pollution that can cause and exacerbate health issues, according to health experts. Exposure to air pollution from a fire where a chemical like creosote or diesel fuel is burned could lead to additional risks.
Creosote is the name given to a wide variety of products commonly used to protect railroad ties and utility poles from pests and rot.
It can be derived from coal tar, the most widely used source, or wood, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Creosote from coal tar contains a number of potentially harmful chemicals and known carcinogens. Many different creosote products in use may contain various chemical formulations.
The CDC says that “long-term exposure of workers to creosote has been shown to increase cancer in several tissues, including the respiratory tract, skin, lung, pancreas, kidney, scrotum, prostate, rectum, bladder, and central nervous system.”
According to a 1984 technical report prepared by the EPA, burning creosote released potentially hazardous chemicals into the air, including benzo(a)pyrene and dibenzo(a,h)anthracene, pyrene and fluoranthene. The authors found the emissions were roughly 40 percent as potent as coke oven emissions.
Residents living near biomass fuel facilities across the country have repeatedly reported health issues, even from normal facility operations.
Still, Slick said he’s not overly concerned about impacts to residential areas near the fire.
“We looked it up in all of the different manuals and books that we have to look up hazards and things like that, and there’s no—other than if you’re right there involved in the smoke and stuff right on the site, now there would be some inhalation hazards, but the firefighters are using their SCBAs, the self-contained breathing apparatuses, so they’re protected,” Slick said.
Scot Quaranda, communications director for environmental nonprofit Dogwood Alliance, said it’s simply not believable that a fire of this scale doesn’t put residents’ health at risk.
“I don’t know what ‘manuals and books’ they’re reading, but that’s not a little-to-no impact fire,” Quaranda said of local officials in Etowah County. “There’s no way this won’t have health impacts.”
Quaranda said Thursday’s fire is the latest example of an industry that has serious negative consequences for the communities where their industrial plants are located.
“There are countless examples of these facilities that are backed up to neighborhoods and are just not showing the kind of care and safety that they should,” Quaranda said.
Telling the public there is little to no risk to public health is irresponsible, he said: “It seems like a complete disregard for human health.
Smoke from the fire in Attalla has blown well beyond the immediate area of the incident. Emergency management officials in adjacent St.Clair County warned residents to be wary of outdoor activities as first responders fight the flames.
“There are no evacuations ordered in St. Clair County, but those who suffer from respiratory issues may want to avoid being outside while the smoke is in the area,” the agency told a local television station.
Slick said that it will be difficult to completely extinguish the fire, which has reached railroad ties and two diesel fuel tanks.
“I don’t know that they’ll ever get it completely put out because of the amount of cross ties that’s burning, but they can definitely get it under control and be able to manage it a little bit better,” he said.
Omaha Track has been at the center of controversy before over its rail tie biomass facilities.
In 2023, a Nevada news outlet reported that a facility owned by Omaha Track was under investigation for violating several conditions of its operating permit, including having too many rail ties on site, stacking ties too high and failing to meet all requirements imposed by the local fire marshal. A company representative told the news outlet it believed it had complied with the permit requirements.
In 2024, a Wisconsin Omaha Track facility caught fire, leaving first responders struggling to fight what they said was a nearly inextinguishable blaze.
State records show that a staffer with the Alabama Department of Environmental Management inspected the company’s Alabama facility in September following an anonymous complaint that the company was illegally covering spills of fuels and oils with dirt on the site. The inspector wrote in a report that they could not substantiate the claims.
Like Brown and Phillips, Rebecca Riihimaa said she didn’t hear anything about the incident from public officials or law enforcement. She had already sent her children to the bus stop when she found out about the fire and the school cancellations.
“We didn’t hear a siren, weren’t alerted and haven’t been told to evacuate,” Riihimaa said. “The fact that no one came to our neighborhood to warn us is alarming.”
Phillips said she and other family members began planning for the worst when they heard about the smoke. The news brought back memories of a 2019 warehouse fire in the same small town that left ash falling from the sky onto Phillips’ home. Back then, water pressure in the town was nearly nonexistent as first responders fought the inferno.
Phillips had learned her lesson.
So, on Thursday she bought as much drinking water as she could find. Then, she and her loved ones started brainstorming how they would transport her brother Bubba if it came to that.
“My best friend said we can get him into a pickup if we need to,” Phillips said, her brow furrowed with worry. “We may just have to call an ambulance.”

title: Bill to reduce regulations on building energy infrastructure passes US Senate
description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects.The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.  The bill would shorten env[...]
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects.The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.  The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.Opponents voiced concern that NEPA, a bedrock federal statute for environmental protection, would be too severely weakened and that tribes would lose power over the consultation process.Just two Republicans — Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor.The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee’s leaders — GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — along with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair, GOP Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat, Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, negotiated the measure. In a statement celebrating the bill’s passage, Capito said the upper chamber “took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people.” Capito said she has “spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building,” adding that the bill “is the culmination of those efforts.” In his own statement, Heinrich said the measure would bring down electricity costs while preserving environmental standards. The bill “will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” the New Mexico Democrat said. President Donald Trump has backed the measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. In a statement of administration policy this month, the administration said the bill would “deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and economic growth across the United States.”  ‘Deeply disappointing’ But the bill has drawn sharp criticism from many environmental organizations, including the Center for Western Priorities, a public lands group.The Center’s executive director, Aaron Weiss, described the vote as “deeply disappointing,” adding that senators “who promised Westerners they would stand up for our public lands just voted for a bill that sells them out to Big Oil and Big Tech.” Weiss urged the House to reject the bill and allow the next Congress beginning in early January to craft “a permitting bill that builds clean energy without sacrificing America’s public lands.”In the lower chamber, House Natural Resources Committee Chair Bruce Westerman said the Senate vote marked “a strong step forward in fixing our nation’s permitting challenges,” in a statement Friday.The Arkansas Republican said he looks forward “to working with my colleagues in the House to swiftly pass this bipartisan bill that will unleash the full force of American innovation.”
